subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Common Conditions and Emergencies including First Aid
question: (a) Define standing orders and state their uses and precautions. (3 marks) (b) Explain the screening, primary management and referral of common gastrointestinal conditions at the sub-centre/Ayushman Arogya Mandir – abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting, diarrhoea, constipation, jaundice, GI bleeding, dyspepsia, dysphagia and aphthous ulcers. (12 marks)
answer_html:
Introduction At the sub-centre-level Ayushman Arogya Mandir (AAM), the Community Health Officer (CHO) and the multipurpose health workers are the first contact for most illnesses of the village. Gastrointestinal complaints are among the commonest. They manage simple conditions according to standing orders and standard treatment guidelines, recognise red-flag (danger) signs early and refer promptly.

(a) Standing orders

  • Definition – written instructions, prepared and signed by a competent medical authority, that authorise nurses and health workers to carry out specified assessment and treatment in defined situations when a doctor is not immediately available.
  • Uses – prompt care in emergencies and minor ailments; continuity of care in remote areas; decentralisation of health care; uniform, safe practice; protection of the public from quacks; increased confidence and accountability of health workers.
  • Precautions – follow the order exactly and only within one's training; never exceed the stated drug, dose or duration; record every action; review and update the orders periodically; refer whenever the client does not fit the order or does not improve. At AAMs, CHOs also use the national standard treatment guidelines and workflows.

(b) Primary management of common GI conditions

General approach to every client – brief history (onset, duration, character, associated features, drugs, alcohol, pregnancy); vital signs and hydration status; abdominal examination; simple point-of-care tests (haemoglobin, urine pregnancy test, blood sugar, malaria RDT where relevant); symptomatic care; health education; referral for red flags; follow-up and records.

1. Abdominal pain

  • Common causes – dyspepsia and gastritis, colic, gastroenteritis, worms, urinary infection, menstrual pain; serious causes – appendicitis, intestinal obstruction, perforation, pancreatitis, ectopic pregnancy.
  • Primary care – rest; antacid or antispasmodic as per standing orders for mild dyspepsia or colic; avoid painkillers that mask signs; deworming where indicated.
  • Refer urgently – severe or increasing pain; guarding or rigidity; distension with vomiting and no passage of stool or flatus; fever with jaundice; pain with shock, fainting or bleeding; pain in pregnancy or after a missed period; pain in a child that persists for more than a few hours.

2. Nausea and vomiting

  • Rule out pregnancy, dehydration, poisoning and head injury.
  • Give small, frequent sips of ORS or other fluids; light diet once vomiting settles; an anti-emetic only as per standing orders.
  • Refer – vomiting of blood or bile, persistent vomiting with inability to retain fluids, severe dehydration, altered sensorium, severe headache or abdominal pain, vomiting in early pregnancy with weight loss (hyperemesis).

3. Diarrhoea (adults)

  • Assess dehydration (thirst, sunken eyes, dry mouth, reduced urine, skin pinch, pulse, BP).
  • ORS after each loose stool, continued normal feeding and safe drinking water; antibiotics only for dysentery (blood in stool) or suspected cholera, as per protocol; zinc for children.
  • Refer – severe dehydration (for IV fluids), blood with high fever, diarrhoea lasting more than 14 days, elderly or pregnant clients with dehydration.
  • Report clusters of cases to the PHC for outbreak investigation (surveillance).

4. Constipation

  • Advise fibre-rich diet (vegetables, fruits, whole grains), 2–3 litres of fluids daily unless restricted, regular exercise and a regular toilet time; a mild laxative only as per standing orders.
  • Refer – recent change in bowel habit after 45–50 years, blood in stool, weight loss, anaemia, severe pain with distension and vomiting (obstruction).

5. Jaundice

  • Most cases in the community are due to viral hepatitis (A and E through water; B and C through blood).
  • Primary care – rest, adequate calories with a normal balanced diet, plenty of fluids, no alcohol and no unnecessary medicines (especially herbal or self-medication), hygiene and safe water; screen family contacts; hepatitis B vaccination where indicated.
  • Refer – jaundice in pregnancy or in a newborn, drowsiness or confusion, bleeding, persistent vomiting, high fever, ascites, itching with clay-coloured stools (obstruction), jaundice lasting more than two weeks.
  • Notify clusters; link positive cases of hepatitis B and C to the national viral hepatitis programme.

6. GI bleeding (haematemesis, melaena, fresh blood per rectum)

  • An emergency – keep the client lying down, nil by mouth, monitor pulse and BP, start IV fluids if trained and equipped, and refer immediately by 108 ambulance with a health worker.
  • Enquire about painkiller (NSAID) use, alcohol and liver disease; haemorrhoids are a common cause of small amounts of fresh rectal blood but still need medical evaluation.

7. Dyspepsia

  • Burning epigastric pain, fullness and belching; advise small frequent meals, avoiding spicy and fried food, tobacco, alcohol and painkillers; antacid or acid-reducing drug as per protocol.
  • Refer – alarm features: difficulty in swallowing, weight loss, persistent vomiting, anaemia, black stools, new symptoms after 50 years.

8. Dysphagia

  • Difficulty in swallowing is always referred for evaluation (stricture, oesophageal or throat cancer, achalasia), urgently if the client cannot swallow saliva.

9. Aphthous ulcers

  • Small, painful, shallow oral ulcers that heal in 7–14 days; advise salt-water rinses, a soft bland diet, topical soothing gel as per protocol and B-complex if deficiency is suspected.
  • Refer – an ulcer that does not heal in 2–3 weeks, a painless hard ulcer, white or red patches, especially in tobacco users (oral cancer screening).

Summary – GI conditions at the AAM

Condition Primary care at the AAM Refer if
Abdominal pain Rest, antacid or antispasmodic as per orders Guarding, distension, shock, pregnancy
Vomiting ORS sips, light diet Blood or bile, dehydration, drowsiness
Diarrhoea ORS, feeding, zinc for children Severe dehydration, blood with fever, >14 days
Constipation Fibre, fluids, exercise Bleeding, weight loss, obstruction
Jaundice Rest, fluids, no alcohol or unnecessary drugs Pregnancy, confusion, bleeding
GI bleeding Lie flat, nil orally, IV line Always – immediately
Dyspepsia Diet advice, antacid Alarm features
Dysphagia – Always
Aphthous ulcer Rinses, bland diet Non-healing for 2–3 weeks

Role of the ASHA and MPW – preparation and use of ORS at home, early identification and escort of sick clients, follow-up home visits after treatment or discharge, distribution of ORS and zinc, and reporting of unusual numbers of diarrhoea or jaundice cases to the ANM/CHO.

Prevention of GI diseases in the community – safe drinking water and household water treatment; sanitary latrines and an end to open defecation; hand washing with soap before eating and after using the toilet; food hygiene; hepatitis B vaccination; deworming; tobacco and alcohol control; avoiding self-medication with painkillers.

Nursing importance

  • Early recognition of danger signs at the AAM prevents deaths from conditions such as perforation, obstruction and GI bleeding.
  • Rational use of drugs (no unnecessary antibiotics or painkillers) prevents harm and antimicrobial resistance.
  • Health education on safe water, hygiene, diet, tobacco and alcohol reduces recurrence in the whole community.
  • Accurate records and follow-up visits complete the continuum of care.

Conclusion Standing orders allow trained nurses and health workers to give prompt, safe care for common GI complaints at the village level. Careful assessment, simple primary management, health teaching and timely referral of red-flag cases form the basis of effective primary health care.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Common Conditions and Emergencies including First Aid
question: Explain the screening, primary management and referral of common respiratory conditions in adults at the Ayushman Arogya Mandir – acute upper respiratory infections, acute lower respiratory infections (bronchitis, pneumonia and bronchial asthma), haemoptysis and acute chest pain.
answer_html:
Introduction Respiratory infections are among the most frequent reasons for visits to a health centre, and acute chest pain is one of the most important emergencies. At the AAM the nurse or CHO screens, treats simple conditions symptomatically, identifies danger signs and refers sick clients, while avoiding unnecessary antibiotics.

Assessment of a client with a respiratory complaint

  • History – cough (duration, sputum, blood), fever, breathlessness, chest pain, wheeze, smoking, exposure to biomass smoke or dust, TB contact, diabetes, HIV.
  • Examination – temperature, respiratory rate, pulse, BP, oxygen saturation (pulse oximeter), use of accessory muscles, cyanosis, chest examination.
  • Screening – every client with cough for two weeks or more is a presumptive TB case and is tested.

1. Acute upper respiratory infections

  • Common cold (rhinitis) – runny or blocked nose, sneezing, mild fever; viral and self-limiting.
  • Sinusitis – facial pain or pressure, nasal discharge, headache that worsens on bending.
  • Pharyngitis and tonsillitis – sore throat, painful swallowing, enlarged red tonsils, tender neck nodes.
  • Laryngitis – hoarseness of voice, dry cough.
  • Primary management – rest, warm fluids, steam inhalation, warm saline gargles, saline nasal drops, paracetamol for fever or pain, voice rest in laryngitis; antibiotics are not needed for colds and most sore throats.
  • A sore throat with fever, tonsillar exudate, tender nodes and no cough (likely streptococcal) is treated with an antibiotic as per the standard treatment guideline, especially in children and young people, to prevent rheumatic fever.
  • Refer – difficulty in swallowing saliva, drooling or inability to open the mouth (peritonsillar abscess), stridor or noisy breathing, swelling around the eye, high fever not settling, hoarseness for more than three weeks (especially in smokers).

2. Acute lower respiratory infections

  • Acute bronchitis – cough with or without sputum for up to three weeks, mild fever, no fast breathing; usually viral; manage with fluids, steam, paracetamol, stopping smoking; review if not better.
  • Pneumonia – fever, cough with sputum, fast breathing, chest pain on breathing, crepitations on auscultation.
    • Danger signs for urgent referral – confusion, respiratory rate of 30/min or more, low BP, SpO₂ below 94%, age above 65 years with other illness, inability to drink, cyanosis.
    • Give the first dose of antibiotic as per protocol, keep the client propped up, start oxygen if available and refer to the PHC/CHC; follow up after discharge.
  • Bronchial asthma
    • Recurrent wheeze, breathlessness, chest tightness and night-time cough, triggered by dust, smoke, cold air, infection or exercise.
    • Teach the correct inhaler technique with a spacer, use of the reliever (bronchodilator) inhaler for symptoms and regular controller (inhaled steroid) as prescribed; identify and avoid triggers; keep a written action plan.
    • Refer urgently – unable to complete sentences, respiratory rate above 30/min, silent chest, cyanosis, drowsiness, SpO₂ below 92%, or no response to the reliever.

3. Haemoptysis

  • Common causes – tuberculosis, bronchiectasis, pneumonia, lung cancer, mitral stenosis.
  • Primary care – reassure, collect sputum for TB testing (NAAT/microscopy) as per the national TB programme, record and refer for chest X-ray.
  • Massive haemoptysis (a cupful or more) is an emergency – lay the client on the bleeding side, keep calm, give oxygen if available and transfer urgently.

4. Acute chest pain

  • Causes – cardiac (angina, heart attack), pulmonary (pneumonia, pleurisy, pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax), gastro-oesophageal (reflux), musculoskeletal (muscle strain, rib injury), anxiety.
  • Red flags – central crushing or squeezing pain lasting more than 15–20 minutes, spreading to the arm, jaw or back, with sweating, breathlessness, vomiting or fainting; sudden sharp pain with breathlessness.
  • Action – make the client rest, record vitals and SpO₂, perform or arrange an ECG (tele-ECG where available), give chewable aspirin as per the standing order if there is no allergy or bleeding problem, call 108 and refer immediately to a facility capable of thrombolysis; never let the client walk or drive.
  • Pain clearly related to movement or tenderness of the chest wall, with normal vitals, is treated symptomatically and reviewed.

Prevention and health education

  • Stop smoking and avoid second-hand smoke; use clean cooking fuel and ventilation to reduce indoor air pollution.
  • Cough etiquette, hand hygiene and masks during outbreaks.
  • Vaccination – childhood vaccines under the immunisation programme; influenza and pneumococcal vaccines for high-risk adults where available.
  • Early treatment of asthma, diabetes and HIV, and adherence to TB treatment.

Comparison of the common conditions at the AAM

Feature URTI Pneumonia Asthma attack
Fever Mild or absent Often high Usually absent
Breathing Normal rate Fast, with chest pain Fast, with wheeze
Chest findings Normal Crepitations Wheeze
SpO₂ Normal May be low May be low
Care at AAM Symptomatic First dose antibiotic, oxygen, refer Reliever inhaler, refer if severe

Using the pulse oximeter – place the probe on a warm finger without nail polish, wait for a steady reading and a good pulse signal; 95% or above is normal, 90–94% needs evaluation by the medical officer, and below 90% is an emergency needing oxygen and urgent transfer.

Special groups

  • Elderly clients with pneumonia may have no fever and may present with confusion or falls.
  • Pregnant women, persons with diabetes, HIV or heart disease, and young infants are referred early.
  • Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) – chronic cough, sputum and breathlessness in smokers and in women exposed to biomass smoke, usually after 40 years; refer for spirometry and long-term treatment; teach breathing exercises and smoking cessation.

Example – a 58-year-old smoker has fever and cough for 3 days, respiratory rate 32/min and SpO₂ 91%. This is severe pneumonia: give the first dose of antibiotic as per protocol, oxygen if available, keep him propped up and transfer by 108 with the referral slip.

Records and follow-up – record vitals, SpO₂, treatment and referral in the OPD register and the client's health record; follow up by phone or home visit; trace sputum results and start TB treatment through the national programme.

Home-care advice for the family – keep the client warm and well hydrated, continue feeding, steam inhalation for blocked nose, complete the full course of any prescribed medicine, avoid smoke in the house, and return immediately if breathing becomes fast or difficult, lips turn blue, or the client becomes drowsy.

Nursing importance

  • Measuring respiratory rate and SpO₂ at the first contact identifies severe pneumonia and asthma early.
  • Avoiding unnecessary antibiotics for viral infections is an important contribution to antimicrobial stewardship.
  • Systematic TB screening of clients with chronic cough finds missing cases in the community.
  • Rapid recognition and referral of cardiac chest pain saves heart muscle and life.

Conclusion Most respiratory complaints in the community are mild and need only symptomatic care, but pneumonia with danger signs, severe asthma, massive haemoptysis and cardiac chest pain demand urgent referral. Systematic assessment at the AAM ensures that each client receives the right level of care at the right time.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Common Conditions and Emergencies including First Aid
question: Explain the early identification, primary care and referral of heart failure and arrhythmias in the community.
answer_html:
Introduction Heart failure and abnormal heart rhythms are increasing with the rise of hypertension, diabetes and ischaemic heart disease. The community health nurse can identify them early, ensure evaluation by a doctor and support long-term follow-up at home.

1. Heart failure

  • Identification – breathlessness on exertion and later at rest; breathlessness on lying flat (orthopnoea) or waking at night breathless; swelling of feet and ankles; fatigue; weight gain; raised jugular venous pressure; basal crackles.
  • Common causes – uncontrolled hypertension, previous heart attack, rheumatic heart disease (in young people), cardiomyopathy, severe anaemia, thyroid disease.
  • Primary care at the AAM – check BP, pulse, weight, oedema and SpO₂; screen for anaemia and diabetes; refer new cases for confirmation (ECG, echocardiography) and treatment.
  • Follow-up of a diagnosed client
    • adherence to prescribed drugs and regular check-ups;
    • salt restriction (less than 5 g a day) and fluid advice as given by the doctor;
    • daily weight – report a gain of more than 2 kg in 3 days;
    • graded activity, avoiding smoking and alcohol, influenza vaccination;
    • avoiding painkillers (NSAIDs) that worsen fluid retention.
  • Urgent referral – breathlessness at rest, low SpO₂, chest pain, fainting, very low BP, rapidly increasing oedema.

2. Arrhythmias

  • Identification – palpitations, dizziness, fainting, breathlessness or chest discomfort; count the pulse for a full minute and note its rhythm.
  • Important findings
    • an irregularly irregular pulse suggests atrial fibrillation, which carries a high risk of stroke;
    • pulse rate below 50/min or above 120/min with symptoms;
    • fainting during exertion or with palpitations.
  • Primary care – make the client rest, record vitals, obtain an ECG (tele-ECG where available) and refer; never give drugs to "slow the heart" without a prescription.
  • Follow-up – adherence to anti-arrhythmic and anticoagulant drugs, watching for bleeding, regular blood tests if prescribed, and teaching the family to recognise warning signs of stroke.

Prevention – control of BP, diabetes and cholesterol; treatment of sore throat and secondary prophylaxis for rheumatic fever; tobacco cessation; regular physical activity.

Conclusion Simple bedside skills – measuring pulse, BP, weight and oxygen saturation – allow the nurse to recognise heart failure and arrhythmias early, ensure timely referral and keep diagnosed clients stable at home.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Common Conditions and Emergencies including First Aid
question: Explain the approach to a client with a red eye at the Ayushman Arogya Mandir – common causes, danger signs, primary management and referral.
answer_html:
Introduction A red eye is one of the commonest eye complaints in the community. Most causes are mild, but some threaten vision. The nurse must distinguish simple from sight-threatening conditions, give primary care and refer early.

1. Common causes and their features

Condition Key features
Conjunctivitis Diffuse redness, discharge, gritty feeling, vision normal, often both eyes
Subconjunctival haemorrhage Painless bright-red patch, vision normal
Stye Painful, red swelling at the lid margin
Keratitis / corneal ulcer Pain, watering, photophobia, blurred vision, white spot on cornea
Acute iritis Pain, photophobia, redness around the cornea, small pupil
Acute angle-closure glaucoma Severe eye pain, headache, vomiting, haloes, hazy cornea, mid-dilated pupil
Injury / foreign body / chemical History of trauma, pain, watering

2. Danger signs – refer the same day

  • Reduced vision, severe pain, photophobia, a white spot or haze on the cornea, unequal or non-reacting pupils.
  • Penetrating injury or chemical injury; contact-lens wearer with a painful red eye.
  • Red eye with discharge in a newborn (ophthalmia neonatorum).
  • No improvement after 3–5 days of treatment.

3. Primary management

  • Conjunctivitis – clean the eyes with boiled, cooled water and clean cloth; antibiotic eye drops as per standing orders; hand washing and separate towels; avoid rubbing; keep children home during an outbreak.
  • Stye – warm compresses 3–4 times a day; never squeeze; refer if it spreads to the lid.
  • Subconjunctival haemorrhage – reassure; check BP; refer if recurrent or after injury.
  • Foreign body – irrigate with clean water; do not attempt removal of an embedded object; pad the eye and refer.
  • Chemical injury – immediate, continuous irrigation with clean water for at least 15–30 minutes, then urgent referral.
  • Never use steroid eye drops or traditional remedies without a doctor's advice.

4. Related screening and prevention at the AAM

  • Vision screening with charts to detect refractive errors and cataract, and referral under the national programme for control of blindness and visual impairment (free spectacles for school children and the elderly).
  • Trachoma – face washing, environmental sanitation and referral of in-turned eyelashes (trichiasis) for surgery.
  • Health education on eye hygiene, protective eyewear for workers and avoiding unsafe practices such as putting kajal or herbal pastes into the eyes.

Conclusion Careful history and simple examination allow the nurse to treat conjunctivitis and minor problems at the AAM, while promptly referring sight-threatening causes such as corneal ulcer, glaucoma and chemical injury.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Common Conditions and Emergencies including First Aid
question: Explain the primary care and referral of common ENT conditions at the community level – ear pain and acute suppurative otitis media, ear discharge, sore throat, epistaxis and hearing loss.
answer_html:
Introduction Ear, nose and throat problems are common in children and adults. Neglected ear infections are a major cause of preventable deafness. The community health nurse provides first-level care, teaches families and refers complicated cases.

1. Ear pain and acute suppurative otitis media (ASOM)

  • Usually follows a cold; earache, fever, irritability and pulling at the ear in children, sometimes discharge after the drum bursts.
  • Primary care – paracetamol for pain and fever, treatment of the cold, antibiotic as per protocol, keep the ear dry; never put oil or other substances into the ear.
  • Refer – swelling or tenderness behind the ear (mastoiditis), facial weakness, vertigo, severe headache, neck stiffness, high fever, or no improvement in 2–3 days.

2. Ear discharge

  • Discharge for more than two weeks indicates chronic suppurative otitis media.
  • Teach dry mopping with a clean cotton wick 3–4 times a day, keeping water out of the ear while bathing and avoiding swimming; refer for treatment and hearing assessment.
  • Scanty, foul-smelling discharge (possible "unsafe" ear with cholesteatoma) is referred urgently.

3. Sore throat

  • Warm saline gargles, fluids, paracetamol; antibiotics only for suspected streptococcal infection as per guidelines.
  • Refer – difficulty in opening the mouth or swallowing saliva, drooling, stridor, unilateral swelling, hoarseness lasting more than three weeks.

4. Epistaxis (nose bleed)

  • Make the client sit up and lean forward; pinch the soft part of the nose firmly for 10–15 minutes; breathe through the mouth; apply a cold compress over the nose; spit out blood rather than swallowing it.
  • Do not tilt the head back or pack the nose with cloth.
  • Check BP; refer if bleeding continues beyond 20 minutes, is recurrent, follows injury, or occurs in a person on blood-thinning drugs or with uncontrolled hypertension.

5. Hearing loss

  • Screening – ask about difficulty in hearing; whisper test or simple hearing tests at the AAM; observe a baby's response to sound; newborn and child hearing screening under child health programmes; ask the elderly about hearing difficulty.
  • Wax – softening drops as per protocol; do not syringe an ear that has discharged or has a perforation; refer impacted wax.
  • Refer every case of suspected hearing loss for audiometry and rehabilitation, early for children to prevent speech delay.

6. Prevention and health education

  • Avoid inserting objects into the ear; treat colds and throat infections early; breastfeed babies in a semi-upright position.
  • Protect against noise at work and from loud music; immunisation (measles, mumps, rubella) and avoidance of ototoxic drugs without prescription.
  • These activities form part of the national programme for prevention and control of deafness.

Conclusion Simple measures such as dry mopping, correct first aid for nose bleeds and early hearing screening, combined with timely referral, prevent complications and disability from common ENT conditions.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Common Conditions and Emergencies including First Aid
question: Explain the identification, primary management and referral of urinary tract infections in the community – cystitis, pyelonephritis, prostatitis and UTI in children.
answer_html:
Introduction Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are common, especially in women, children and the elderly. Early identification at the community level and correct management prevent kidney damage and unnecessary use of antibiotics.

1. Identification of the types

  • Cystitis (lower UTI) – burning micturition, frequency, urgency, lower abdominal (suprapubic) pain, cloudy or foul-smelling urine, sometimes blood; usually no high fever.
  • Pyelonephritis (upper UTI) – high fever with chills, pain in the flank (loin), vomiting, tenderness at the renal angle; the client looks ill.
  • Prostatitis – men with fever, pain in the perineum or lower back, painful or difficult urination, sometimes retention.
  • UTI in children – fever without an obvious cause, poor feeding, vomiting, irritability, foul-smelling urine, new bedwetting in a previously dry child.

2. Screening at the AAM

  • History of symptoms, previous episodes, pregnancy, diabetes, catheter use.
  • Urine dipstick test – positive nitrite and leucocyte esterase support the diagnosis; check for blood, protein and sugar.
  • Urine microscopy and culture through the PHC laboratory or sample transport, especially before antibiotics in complicated cases.

3. Primary management of uncomplicated cystitis in a non-pregnant woman

  • Plenty of fluids (2–3 litres a day), frequent emptying of the bladder, paracetamol for discomfort.
  • Antibiotic as per standard treatment guidelines and standing orders, for the full course.
  • Review in 2–3 days; refer if symptoms persist.

4. Refer to the medical officer

  • Pyelonephritis (fever, flank pain, vomiting).
  • All men, all children and all pregnant women with suspected UTI.
  • Recurrent infections (three or more a year), blood in urine, stones, diabetes, catheterised clients, urinary retention.

5. Prevention and health teaching

  • Adequate fluid intake; not holding urine for long; perineal hygiene and wiping from front to back; passing urine after intercourse.
  • Hygienic menstrual practices; treatment of constipation in children.
  • Screening for and treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy during antenatal care.
  • Avoid self-medication and incomplete antibiotic courses.

Special points – in the elderly, UTI may present only as confusion, incontinence or falls; untreated or recurrent infection can lead to kidney damage, sepsis and, in pregnancy, preterm labour; every case is recorded and followed up.

Conclusion Recognising the type of UTI, using simple dipstick screening, treating uncomplicated cystitis correctly and referring high-risk groups promptly protect the kidneys and reduce antibiotic misuse.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Common Conditions and Emergencies including First Aid
question: Explain the first aid management of high fever and low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia) at home and in the community.
answer_html:
Introduction High fever and low blood sugar are common emergencies at home. Simple, correct first aid by the family, ASHA or nurse prevents complications such as convulsions, dehydration, brain injury and death, while danger signs indicate the need for urgent referral.

A. High fever

  1. Confirm – measure the temperature with a thermometer; fever is 38 °C (100.4 °F) or more; high fever is above 39 °C.
  2. Cooling measures – remove extra clothing and blankets; keep the room airy; tepid sponging with lukewarm (not cold) water over the trunk and limbs; never use ice-cold water or alcohol rubs.
  3. Fluids – plenty of water, ORS, coconut water or soups; continue feeding; breastfeed infants more often.
  4. Paracetamol – about 15 mg/kg per dose for children, repeated every 4–6 hours if needed (not more than four doses a day); for adults 500 mg–1 g per dose as per standing orders; avoid aspirin in children.
  5. Look for the cause – malaria rapid diagnostic test in endemic areas; dengue, typhoid, UTI and respiratory infection are other common causes.
  6. Refer urgently if – fever with convulsions, neck stiffness, drowsiness or confusion, rash or bleeding, breathlessness, persistent vomiting, severe dehydration; fever in an infant under two months; fever lasting more than 3 days; fever in a pregnant woman.

B. Low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia)

  1. Recognise – sweating, trembling, palpitations, hunger, pallor, headache, confusion, irritability, slurred speech, unusual behaviour, drowsiness and finally fits or unconsciousness, especially in persons with diabetes on insulin or tablets, after a missed meal, extra exercise or alcohol.
  2. Confirm if possible – blood glucose by glucometer below 70 mg/dl; if a glucometer is not available and the person is diabetic with symptoms, treat as hypoglycaemia.
  3. If conscious and able to swallow – the "rule of 15"
    • give 15–20 g of fast-acting sugar: 3–4 teaspoons of sugar or glucose dissolved in water, or about 150 ml of fruit juice or sweetened drink, or glucose tablets;
    • recheck after 15 minutes; repeat if still low or symptoms persist;
    • once better, give a snack or meal with complex carbohydrate (roti, bread, biscuits).
  4. If unconscious or unable to swallow
    • give nothing by mouth; place in the recovery position; keep the airway clear;
    • call 108; intravenous dextrose by a trained person or glucagon injection if available.
  5. After the episode – find the cause, inform the doctor, and teach regular meals, carrying sugar or sweets, adjusting doses with the doctor, glucose monitoring, and wearing a diabetic identity card.

Conclusion Correct cooling and paracetamol for fever, and quick sugar by mouth for a conscious hypoglycaemic person, are life-saving first aid measures, while danger signs and unconsciousness always demand urgent referral.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Common Conditions and Emergencies including First Aid
question: Explain the first aid kit for a sub-centre/Ayushman Arogya Mandir and for community first-aid volunteers – contents, uses and maintenance.
answer_html:
Introduction A well-stocked and well-maintained first aid kit enables the health worker, CHO or trained volunteer to give immediate care for injuries and emergencies before the victim reaches a health facility. Every sub-centre/AAM, school, workplace and community volunteer group should have one.

1. Contents

  • Dressing materials – sterile gauze pads of different sizes, cotton wool, adhesive plasters, micropore tape, non-adherent dressings for burns.
  • Bandages – roller bandages (5 cm, 7.5 cm, 10 cm), crepe bandages, triangular bandages (for slings and pads), eye pads.
  • Instruments and items – scissors, forceps, safety pins, disposable gloves, face masks, a pocket mask or face shield for CPR, torch, thermometer, BP apparatus and glucometer (at the AAM), pulse oximeter where available.
  • Splints – padded wooden or SAM splints, cervical collar at the AAM.
  • Solutions and medicines (as per standing orders) – povidone-iodine or other antiseptic, clean water and soap, ORS packets, glucose, paracetamol, antacid, calamine lotion, sterile saline for eye irrigation.
  • Other – plastic bags for waste, a notebook and pen, a first aid manual, a list of emergency numbers (108 ambulance, 102 transport, police, poison centre) and addresses of the nearest PHC/CHC.

2. Uses

  • Wounds, bleeding, burns, fractures and sprains; fainting, fever, hypoglycaemia, dehydration, eye injuries.
  • First response during road accidents, school and workplace injuries, and disasters.
  • Training ASHAs, teachers and volunteers in basic first aid.

3. Principles of maintenance

  • Use a strong, waterproof, clearly marked box with a red cross or green cross symbol, kept in a known, accessible place, out of reach of small children.
  • Keep a contents list inside the lid; check the kit monthly and after every use; replace used and expired items promptly.
  • Store away from heat and moisture; keep sterile items sealed.
  • Record the items used and the persons treated, and report to the PHC.
  • One person (the ANM or CHO) is responsible for the kit at the sub-centre.

Kits for special settings – schools and hostels (emphasis on injuries, fainting and fever); workplaces, where the occupational safety law requires first aid boxes and trained first-aiders; and disaster or relief camps (larger stock of dressings, ORS, water purification tablets and splints).

Conclusion A complete, regularly checked first aid kit and a trained person to use it turn the sub-centre and the community into the first link in the chain of emergency care.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Common Conditions and Emergencies including First Aid
question: Explain the first aid management of fainting.
answer_html:
• Fainting (syncope) is a sudden, brief loss of consciousness due to a temporary fall in blood flow to the brain, with spontaneous recovery.
  • First aid – lay the person flat on the back and raise the legs about 30 cm; loosen tight clothing; ensure fresh air and keep onlookers away; check breathing; turn into the recovery position if vomiting or not recovering; give nothing by mouth until fully conscious, then sips of water or a sweet drink; let the person sit up slowly.
  • Seek medical help if recovery takes more than a minute or two, or if there is injury, chest pain, palpitations, pregnancy, known heart disease or repeated fainting.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Common Conditions and Emergencies including First Aid
question: List the danger (red-flag) signs in a client with abdominal pain that need urgent referral.
answer_html:
• Severe or steadily increasing pain, or pain that wakes the client from sleep.
  • Guarding or rigidity of the abdomen; distension with vomiting and no passage of stool or flatus (obstruction).
  • Pain with vomiting of blood, black stools or rectal bleeding.
  • Pain with fainting, low BP or fast pulse (shock).
  • Pain in pregnancy or after a missed period (ectopic pregnancy).
  • Fever with jaundice or with right lower abdominal pain (appendicitis); new pain with weight loss in an older person.
  • Abdominal pain in a child that persists for more than a few hours, or with bilious vomiting.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Common Conditions and Emergencies including First Aid
question: List the warning signs of blood cancers and bleeding disorders to be looked for at the Ayushman Arogya Mandir.
answer_html:
• Unexplained pallor and fatigue, persistent or recurrent fever and infections.
  • Easy bruising, petechiae, bleeding gums, frequent nose bleeds, prolonged bleeding after minor cuts or tooth extraction, very heavy menstrual bleeding.
  • Painless enlarged lymph nodes, enlarged liver or spleen, bone pain, night sweats, weight loss.
  • Swollen, painful joints after minor injury in a boy (possible haemophilia).
  • Such clients are referred for a complete blood count and peripheral smear and specialist evaluation.
  • Early referral improves the chances of cure, especially in childhood leukaemia.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Common Conditions and Emergencies including First Aid
question: What are aphthous ulcers? Write their primary management.
answer_html:
• Aphthous ulcers are small, round, shallow, painful ulcers of the mouth lining with a yellowish base and red margin; they are often recurrent and linked to stress, minor injury, deficiency of iron, folate or vitamin B12, or certain foods.
  • Management – salt-water or plain warm-water rinses, a soft bland diet, avoiding spicy food, a topical soothing gel as per protocol, vitamin supplements if deficiency is suspected, and good oral hygiene.
  • Refer an ulcer that does not heal in 2–3 weeks, a painless hard ulcer, or ulcers with fever and weight loss (to rule out oral cancer or systemic disease).

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Common Conditions and Emergencies including First Aid
question: What is the SAFE strategy for trachoma?
tags: elimination as a public health problem
answer_html:
• SAFE is the WHO strategy for the elimination of trachoma, a chronic infection of the eye by Chlamydia trachomatis:
    • S – Surgery for trichiasis (in-turned eyelashes);
    • A – Antibiotics (mass or individual treatment, mainly azithromycin);
    • F – Facial cleanliness (regular face washing, especially of children);
    • E – Environmental improvement (water supply, sanitation, latrines, fly control).
  • With these measures India was validated by WHO in 2024 as having eliminated trachoma as a public health problem; surveillance for new cases and trichiasis continues.
  • The nurse's role is face-washing education in schools and referral of trichiasis.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health
question: (a) Explain the current status of reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health in India. (5 marks) (b) Describe the life-stage approach and key interventions of the RMNCH+A strategy, with its health-system strengthening measures. (6 marks) (c) Explain the management, monitoring and evaluation of RMNCH+A at the district level. (4 marks)

diagram.caption: Continuum of care in the RMNCH+A strategy
labels: Horizontal arrow across the life stages – adolescence
infancy and childhood – crossed by three vertical levels of care – household and community
and facility – with key interventions written in each cell

answer_html:
Introduction India launched the Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health (RMNCH+A) strategy in 2013 under the National Health Mission. The "+" emphasises adolescents as a distinct life stage. It is built on the idea of a continuum of care – across the life stages and across home, community, outreach and facility levels – so that each woman and child receives essential interventions at the right time.

(a) Current status of RMNCH+A in India

Indicator Latest level
Maternal mortality ratio (SRS 2022–24) 87 per 1,00,000 live births (130 in 2014–16)
Infant mortality rate (SRS 2024) 24 per 1,000 live births
Neonatal mortality rate (SRS 2024) 18 per 1,000 live births
Under-five mortality rate (SRS 2024) 28 per 1,000 live births
Total fertility rate 1.9 (SRS 2024); 2.0 (NFHS-6)
Institutional births (NFHS-6, 2023–24) 90.6%
Births assisted by skilled personnel (NFHS-6) 91.3%
ANC in the first trimester / four or more ANC visits (NFHS-6) 76.2% / 65.2%
Contraceptive prevalence rate / unmet need (NFHS-6) 69.1% / 8.5%
Women aged 20–24 married before 18 years (NFHS-6) 20.1%
Children under five stunted / wasted / underweight (NFHS-6) 29.3% / 19.0% / 31.8%
  • Achievements – steep falls in maternal and child mortality; near-universal institutional delivery; replacement-level fertility; better immunisation and child growth.
  • Remaining challenges – wide differences between states and districts; neonatal deaths form the largest share of under-five deaths; anaemia and undernutrition in women and children; early marriage and adolescent pregnancy in some areas; quality of care; rising caesarean rates in the private sector.
  • Targets – the Sustainable Development Goals call for an MMR below 70, an NMR of 12 or less and a U5MR of 25 or less by 2030.

(b) Life-stage approach and key interventions The strategy identifies high-impact interventions for each of five life stages (often presented as a "5 × 5 matrix").

  1. Reproductive age (including pre-conception)
    • family planning counselling and a basket of contraceptive choices; spacing between births;
    • prevention and management of RTIs/STIs; pre-conception folic acid and nutrition;
    • prevention of sex-selective practices and promotion of gender equity.
  2. Pregnancy (maternal health)
    • early registration, at least four (preferably eight) antenatal contacts, IFA, calcium and deworming, Td vaccination;
    • detection and management of high-risk pregnancies, birth preparedness;
    • safe abortion services.
  3. Childbirth and the postnatal period (mother and newborn)
    • skilled birth attendance at functional delivery points, use of the labour care guide and safe childbirth checklist;
    • active management of the third stage, management of complications, free referral transport;
    • essential newborn care, early breastfeeding, kangaroo mother care, postnatal and home-based newborn care visits, special newborn care units.
  4. Childhood
    • exclusive breastfeeding and complementary feeding, full immunisation, vitamin A, deworming;
    • management of diarrhoea and pneumonia, management of severe acute malnutrition;
    • child health screening and early intervention for defects, diseases, deficiencies and developmental delays.
  5. Adolescence
    • adolescent-friendly health services, nutrition and weekly iron–folic acid supplementation;
    • menstrual hygiene, sexual and reproductive health, mental health, substance-use prevention;
    • prevention of injuries and violence, and delaying marriage and first pregnancy.

Health-system strengthening measures (cross-cutting)

  • Infrastructure – operationalising delivery points and first referral units, newborn care units, nutrition rehabilitation centres.
  • Human resources – skilled birth attendants, staff nurses, ANMs, ASHAs and specialists; training and mentoring.
  • Free entitlements and demand generation – free drugs, diagnostics, diet, blood and transport for pregnant women and sick infants; conditional cash transfers for institutional births; ASHA incentives.
  • Supply chain – uninterrupted availability of essential drugs, vaccines, contraceptives and commodities.
  • Community processes – ASHAs, village health, sanitation and nutrition committees and Village Health, Sanitation and Nutrition Days.
  • Quality improvement – quality standards and certification of labour rooms and maternity operation theatres.
  • Information systems – name-based tracking of mothers and children through the RCH portal and HMIS.

(c) Management, monitoring and evaluation at the district level

  • Prioritisation – the most lagging districts were identified as high priority districts and given additional resources, technical support and close monitoring.
  • Planning – RMNCH+A activities are included in the district health action plan and the state programme implementation plan under the NHM.
  • Monitoring tools
    • HMIS and RCH portal data on registration, ANC, deliveries, immunisation and family planning;
    • scorecards that rank districts and blocks on key indicators, highlighting gaps for action;
    • supportive supervision visits with checklists, and monthly review meetings at the block and district levels.
  • Reviews of deaths – maternal death surveillance and response and child death review identify preventable causes and lead to corrective action.
  • Evaluation – periodic surveys such as SRS and NFHS measure outcomes and impact.

Role of the community health nurse

  • Registers every pregnant woman early, tracks high-risk mothers and newborns and completes the continuum of care.
  • Delivers or organises the interventions at each life stage at the sub-centre, VHSND and home visits.
  • Counsels families on nutrition, birth spacing, breastfeeding, immunisation and adolescent health.
  • Maintains accurate records and uploads data, and participates in death reviews and supportive supervision.

Major national schemes that support the strategy

  • Janani Suraksha Yojana (cash assistance for institutional delivery) and Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (free delivery, caesarean section, drugs, diagnostics, diet, blood and transport for mothers and sick infants).
  • Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan (assured ANC by doctors on the 9th of every month) and SUMAN (assured, respectful maternity care).
  • LaQshya (quality of labour rooms and maternity theatres) and the Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana (maternity benefit).
  • Home-based newborn care and home-based care for the young child by ASHAs; Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram; the Mothers' Absolute Affection breastfeeding programme; SAANS for childhood pneumonia; Anaemia Mukt Bharat; Mission Indradhanush for immunisation.
  • Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram for adolescents and Mission Parivar Vikas for family planning in high-fertility districts.

Equity focus – special attention to high priority districts, tribal and hard-to-reach areas, urban slums, migrants and the poorest households; addressing gender discrimination, early marriage and son preference, which affect every stage of the life cycle.

Indicators the nurse monitors in her area – proportion of pregnant women registered in the first trimester, women receiving four or more ANC visits and 180 IFA tablets, institutional deliveries, mothers and newborns visited at home after delivery, children fully immunised by one year, cases of diarrhoea treated with ORS and zinc, eligible couples using a modern contraceptive, adolescents counselled, and every maternal, infant and child death reported and reviewed.

Conclusion India has made striking progress in maternal, newborn and child survival, but gaps in neonatal survival, nutrition and adolescent health remain. The RMNCH+A strategy, with its life-stage interventions, health-system strengthening and data-driven district monitoring, gives the community health nurse a clear framework for closing these gaps.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health
question: Explain the high-risk approach in maternal care at the community level – early identification, primary (pre-referral) management, referral and follow-up of pregnant women with antepartum haemorrhage, pre-eclampsia/eclampsia, severe anaemia, gestational diabetes, hypothyroidism and syphilis.
answer_html:
Introduction The high-risk approach means identifying, early in pregnancy, those women who are more likely to develop complications, giving them extra attention, planning their delivery at an appropriate facility and referring them in time. Since most complications cannot be predicted, every pregnancy is also watched for danger signs. At the community level the ANM, CHO and ASHA play the key role.

1. Early identification of high-risk pregnancies

  • From history – age below 18 or above 35 years; fifth or later pregnancy; short interval (less than two years) since the last birth; previous caesarean section, stillbirth, neonatal death, repeated abortions, PPH, APH or eclampsia; chronic illness (hypertension, diabetes, heart, kidney or thyroid disease, TB, HIV).
  • From examination – height below 145 cm, low weight or poor weight gain, BP of 140/90 mm Hg or more, pallor, oedema of face and hands, abnormal lie or presentation, twins, excessive or poor uterine growth.
  • From investigations – haemoglobin below 11 g/dl, proteinuria, raised blood sugar, Rh-negative blood group, positive tests for syphilis, HIV or hepatitis B.
  • Action – mark the woman as high-risk on the MCP card (red sticker during the monthly PMSMA clinic), enter her in the high-risk line list, inform the ASHA and PHC, and plan delivery at an appropriate facility.

2. Antepartum haemorrhage (APH)

  • Any bleeding per vagina after 20 weeks is an emergency (placenta praevia or abruption).
  • Never do a vaginal examination at the sub-centre; record pulse, BP and fetal heart; keep the woman lying on her left side; start an IV line with Ringer lactate if trained; arrange blood donors.
  • Refer immediately by 108/102 to a first referral unit with blood transfusion and caesarean facilities, with a health worker accompanying.

3. Pre-eclampsia and eclampsia

  • Detection – measure BP at every contact; test urine for protein by dipstick; ask about severe headache, blurred vision, epigastric pain, reduced urine and swelling.
  • Mild pre-eclampsia – refer to the medical officer for confirmation and an antihypertensive; teach danger signs; more frequent visits.
  • Severe pre-eclampsia or eclampsia (fits)
    • protect the airway, turn on the left side, prevent injury, give oxygen if available;
    • give the pre-referral loading dose of magnesium sulphate as per national guidelines (the intramuscular dose can be given by the trained ANM/SBA; the full loading dose with an antihypertensive is given at the PHC);
    • catheterise the bladder if trained and refer urgently to a first referral unit, with a written note of the dose and time.

4. Severe anaemia

  • Detection – haemoglobin estimation at every ANC visit (digital haemoglobinometer at point of care); pallor, breathlessness, fatigue, swelling.
  • Management at the community level – prophylactic IFA for all; for anaemia, therapeutic oral iron and follow-up of compliance and Hb; deworming after the first trimester; diet counselling.
  • Refer to the PHC/FRU – for intravenous iron after the first trimester as per the national anaemia guidelines; women with severe anaemia (Hb below 7 g/dl), breathlessness or heart failure for evaluation; very severe anaemia for blood transfusion.
  • Plan the delivery at a facility with blood transfusion.

5. Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM)

  • Screening as per national guidelines – a single-step 75 g oral glucose test (non-fasting) with a 2-hour plasma glucose value; 140 mg/dl or more indicates GDM; testing is done at the first contact and repeated at 24–28 weeks.
  • Management – medical nutrition therapy and physical activity for two weeks; refer to the medical officer for insulin or other treatment if sugar remains high; regular follow-up; delivery at a facility; a repeat glucose test about six weeks after delivery.

6. Hypothyroidism

  • Screening of pregnant women by a TSH test at the first visit, as recommended by national guidelines, especially those with goitre, symptoms, previous thyroid disease or recurrent pregnancy loss.
  • Refer women with raised TSH to the medical officer for levothyroxine and dose monitoring; ensure the newborn's thyroid screening.

7. Syphilis

  • Point-of-care testing for syphilis (along with HIV) at the first antenatal contact.
  • A positive woman is treated promptly with benzathine penicillin at the PHC as per protocol, her partner is also treated, and the baby is followed up after birth – this prevents congenital syphilis and stillbirth.

8. Referral process

  • Stabilise the woman before transfer; write a referral slip with findings and treatment given; inform the receiving facility by phone; use free referral transport (102/108); send a health worker or ASHA with her; follow up to know the outcome.

9. Follow-up and records

  • Monthly or more frequent visits by the ANM; ASHA home visits; birth preparedness and complication readiness plan with the family.
  • Entry in the ANC register, high-risk line list, MCP card and RCH portal for name-based tracking until 42 days after delivery; feedback to the ASHA.
  • Review of every maternal death through maternal death surveillance and response.

Danger signs taught to every pregnant woman and her family – bleeding from the vagina; severe headache, blurred vision or fits; high fever; severe abdominal pain; leaking of fluid; reduced or absent fetal movements; swelling of face and hands; breathlessness or palpitations. The family must bring her to the facility at once if any of these occur.

Role of the ASHA – early registration, accompanying high-risk women to PMSMA clinics and the PHC, ensuring IFA and calcium intake, monitoring danger signs during home visits, helping the family prepare a birth plan (place, transport, money, blood donor, companion), escorting the woman for delivery and visiting her after birth.

Example – a 20-year-old first-time mother at 34 weeks has BP 150/100 mm Hg, 2+ proteinuria on dipstick and a severe headache. She has severe pre-eclampsia. The ANM lays her on her left side, gives the pre-referral magnesium sulphate dose as per guidelines, calls 108, informs the FRU, sends the MCP card and referral slip, and accompanies her. The ASHA follows her up after delivery for BP and danger signs.

Other high-risk situations – an Rh-negative mother is referred for antibody testing and anti-D prophylaxis as per protocol; women with twins, malpresentation, previous caesarean section or heart disease are counselled to deliver at an FRU and are admitted early.

Nursing importance

  • Most maternal deaths are due to haemorrhage, hypertensive disorders, sepsis and anaemia, which can be detected early in the community.
  • Pre-referral treatment (left lateral position, IV fluids, magnesium sulphate) keeps the woman alive until she reaches the right facility.
  • Tracking of high-risk mothers reduces the "three delays" – in deciding to seek care, reaching the facility and receiving care.

Conclusion The high-risk approach at the community level combines universal screening, special care for identified women, prompt pre-referral management and organised referral and follow-up. Done well by the ANM, CHO and ASHA, it is one of the most effective ways to prevent maternal and perinatal deaths.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health
question: Explain the early identification, pre-referral management and referral of intrapartum and immediate postpartum emergencies at the sub-centre/primary health centre delivery point – preterm labour, fetal distress, prolonged and obstructed labour, perineal tears, rupture of the uterus and postpartum haemorrhage.
answer_html:
Introduction Many deliveries in rural India take place at sub-centre and PHC delivery points conducted by skilled birth attendants (ANMs and staff nurses). Complications of labour can arise suddenly in any woman. The SBA must monitor labour carefully, recognise complications early, give life-saving first-level treatment and refer in time to a first referral unit (FRU) with caesarean, blood transfusion and newborn care facilities.

General principles at the delivery point

  • Monitor every labour with the labour care guide (or partograph); record maternal pulse, BP and temperature, fetal heart rate, contractions, cervical dilatation and descent.
  • Follow the WHO safe childbirth checklist at admission, before pushing, soon after birth and before discharge.
  • Keep the emergency drug tray, IV fluids, oxytocin, magnesium sulphate and resuscitation equipment ready.
  • Decide on referral early – a woman transferred in good condition has a far better outcome.

1. Preterm labour (before 37 weeks)

  • Identification – regular painful contractions with cervical changes, show or leaking fluid before 37 weeks.
  • Pre-referral care – confirm gestation; give antenatal corticosteroids (dexamethasone) as per national guidelines between 24 and 34 weeks where gestational age is reliable and facilities for care of the preterm baby are available; treat any infection as per protocol.
  • Refer for in-utero transfer to a facility with a special newborn care unit – it is safer to transfer the baby inside the mother than after birth.

2. Fetal distress

  • Identification – fetal heart rate persistently below 110 or above 160 beats per minute, or decelerations; thick meconium-stained liquor.
  • Action – turn the mother on her left side, stop any oxytocin, give IV fluids, correct maternal fever or dehydration, recheck the fetal heart; if it remains abnormal in the first stage, refer urgently; in the second stage, expedite delivery if possible and be ready for newborn resuscitation.

3. Prolonged and obstructed labour

  • Identification – progress slower than expected on the labour care guide (alert threshold crossed); prolonged second stage; signs of obstruction – a tired, dehydrated woman with fast pulse, fever, retraction ring, a tender lower segment, caput and moulding, no descent despite good contractions, blood-stained urine.
  • Pre-referral care – IV fluids, empty the bladder (catheterise), antibiotics as per protocol if labour is prolonged or membranes have been ruptured long; never give oxytocin for obstructed labour; refer immediately.

4. Perineal tears

  • Identification – inspect the perineum, vagina and cervix after every delivery.
  • First- and second-degree tears are repaired by the trained SBA under local anaesthesia with aseptic technique.
  • Third- and fourth-degree tears (involving the anal sphincter or rectal mucosa) and cervical tears are packed, bleeding controlled and the woman referred for repair by a specialist.

5. Rupture of the uterus

  • Risk factors – obstructed labour, previous caesarean scar, misuse of oxytocin, grand multiparity.
  • Identification – sudden severe abdominal pain, cessation of contractions, vaginal bleeding, shock, fetal parts easily felt, absent fetal heart.
  • Action – treat shock (two IV lines, fluids, oxygen, keep warm), arrange blood donors and transfer urgently to the FRU for laparotomy.

6. Postpartum haemorrhage (PPH)

  • Prevention – active management of the third stage of labour with an uterotonic (oxytocin) for every woman; misoprostol where oxytocin cannot be used; close observation for the first two hours after birth.
  • Early detection – measure blood loss; watch for a soft uterus, rising pulse and falling BP; act early, as recommended by recent WHO guidelines, when bleeding is heavy or accompanied by abnormal vital signs.
  • First-level management
    • call for help; massage the uterus and expel clots; start IV fluids; give a further uterotonic as per protocol;
    • empty the bladder; check that the placenta is complete and look for tears;
    • give tranexamic acid where available and permitted;
    • bimanual uterine compression or aortic compression while arranging transfer; keep the woman warm.
  • Refer immediately if bleeding continues, the placenta is retained, or she shows signs of shock.

7. Referral process

  • Stabilise; write a referral slip with the labour findings, drugs given and times; phone the receiving facility; use free transport (102/108) under the free maternity entitlement scheme; send the SBA or ASHA with the woman and the baby; carry blood donors where possible; record and follow up the outcome.

Readiness of the delivery point for emergencies – a clean, well-lit labour room with a functioning newborn corner; an emergency drug tray (oxytocin, magnesium sulphate, antihypertensive, antibiotics, IV fluids, calcium gluconate); trays for delivery, episiotomy and the baby; a resuscitation bag and mask; a 24-hour phone and ambulance number list; trained staff who rehearse emergency drills.

Retained placenta – if the placenta is not delivered within 30 minutes after the baby despite active management, empty the bladder, repeat controlled cord traction and the uterotonic as per protocol; if bleeding is present or the placenta remains, start IV fluids and antibiotics and refer for manual removal (or perform it if trained and authorised).

Shoulder dystocia – call for help, avoid fundal pressure, use the McRoberts position with suprapubic pressure, and be ready to resuscitate the baby.

Newborn resuscitation – every delivery point keeps a trained person and equipment ready; the "golden minute" approach (drying, stimulation, clearing the airway if needed and bag-and-mask ventilation within one minute) prevents birth asphyxia deaths.

Example – at a PHC, a woman's labour care guide shows no progress in cervical dilatation for four hours, with maternal tachycardia and caput formation. The staff nurse recognises probable obstruction, starts IV fluids, catheterises the bladder, gives antibiotics as per protocol, does not give oxytocin, calls 108, phones the FRU and sends her with the filled labour care guide and referral slip.

Records and reporting – labour room register, referral register and MCP card; any maternal death is notified within 24 hours for maternal death surveillance and response; near-miss cases are reviewed to improve care.

Monitoring in the first two hours after birth – check the mother's pulse, BP, uterine tone and vaginal bleeding every 15 minutes for the first hour and every 30 minutes for the second hour; keep the baby skin-to-skin with the mother, start breastfeeding within an hour, and check the baby's breathing, colour and temperature. Most PPH and many newborn emergencies are detected during this period, so the mother and baby are not left alone.

Respectful care during emergencies – explain what is happening to the woman and her companion, obtain consent, maintain privacy and dignity, and keep the family informed during transfer; fear and confusion delay decisions.

Nursing importance

  • Early use of the labour care guide converts emergencies into planned referrals.
  • Life-saving first-level care at the delivery point (left lateral position, uterotonics, uterine massage, IV fluids) prevents deaths during transfer.
  • Clear documentation and communication avoid delays at the receiving facility.

Conclusion Intrapartum complications are unpredictable, but careful monitoring, prompt first-level treatment and organised referral by the skilled birth attendant at the delivery point save the lives of mothers and babies.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health
question: Explain youth-friendly (adolescent-friendly) health services and the attitudes expected of nurses – privacy, confidentiality, non-judgemental care and respect for client autonomy.
answer_html:
Introduction Adolescents often avoid health services because of fear, shame, lack of privacy or judgemental attitudes of providers. Youth-friendly health services are services that adolescents find easy to reach, comfortable and trustworthy. Under the national adolescent health programme they are offered through adolescent-friendly health clinics at different levels of health facilities, with counsellors and trained staff.

1. Characteristics of youth-friendly services

  • Equitable – available to all adolescents, married or unmarried, boys and girls, in and out of school.
  • Accessible – convenient timings (after school hours), free or low cost, no need for an appointment.
  • Acceptable – a welcoming, private space; trained, respectful staff; information materials designed for young people.
  • Appropriate – the right package of services: counselling, nutrition, menstrual and sexual health, contraception, RTI/STI care, mental health, substance use, injuries and violence.
  • Effective – evidence-based care by competent providers, with referral links.

2. Attitudes expected of nurses

  • Privacy – counsel and examine the adolescent alone in a separate room or screened area; ask whether they would like a parent or friend present; avoid discussing problems in front of others.
  • Confidentiality – assure the adolescent that information will not be shared without their consent; keep records secure. Explain honestly the limits of confidentiality – situations of danger to life, sexual abuse (which must be reported under the POCSO Act) or serious harm.
  • Non-judgemental care – accept the adolescent without blaming or moralising about sexual activity, substance use, pregnancy or sexual orientation; use a calm tone and neutral words; focus on helping, not punishing.
  • Respect for autonomy – give accurate, age-appropriate information and options; help them make their own informed decisions; involve parents only with their agreement, except where the law or safety requires otherwise.
  • Empathy and good communication – listen actively; use simple language; take their concerns seriously; maintain eye contact; avoid interrupting.
  • Gender sensitivity – equal respect for boys and girls; a female provider for girls where preferred.

3. Supporting measures

  • Trained peer educators in the village, school health activities, adolescent health days and helplines.
  • Linkages with schools, youth clubs and anganwadi centres.

Conclusion When nurses provide services with privacy, confidentiality, respect and a non-judgemental attitude, adolescents use them early, share their real problems and receive timely help.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health
question: Explain the identification, primary management and referral of common gynaecological conditions in women and girls in the community – premenstrual syndrome, abnormal vaginal discharge, breast lump and mastitis, chronic pelvic pain and pelvic organ prolapse.
answer_html:
Introduction Many women and adolescent girls suffer gynaecological problems silently because of shame or lack of access. The nurse at the AAM can identify these conditions, give primary care and counselling, and refer those that need specialist treatment.

1. Premenstrual syndrome (PMS)

  • Physical and emotional symptoms – bloating, breast tenderness, headache, irritability, mood swings, poor concentration – in the week or two before menstruation, relieved when bleeding starts.
  • Management – a symptom diary for two cycles to confirm the pattern; regular exercise, adequate sleep, small frequent meals, less salt, sugar and caffeine; relaxation techniques; a simple analgesic for pain.
  • Refer if symptoms are severe enough to disturb studies, work or relationships, or there are thoughts of self-harm (possible premenstrual dysphoric disorder).

2. Abnormal vaginal discharge

  • Ask about colour, smell, itching, burning, lower abdominal pain, fever and partner's symptoms; normal clear or white discharge without symptoms needs only reassurance.
  • Management – syndromic treatment as per national RTI/STI guidelines at the PHC; treatment of the partner; condom use; completing the full course; personal and menstrual hygiene; avoiding douching.
  • Refer – discharge with fever or lower abdominal pain (pelvic inflammatory disease), blood-stained or foul discharge, discharge after menopause, or pregnancy.

3. Breast lump and mastitis

  • Clinical breast examination is done at the AAM as part of screening for breast cancer in women aged 30 years and above; teach breast self-awareness.
  • Any lump – especially a hard, painless, irregular one, with skin dimpling, nipple retraction or discharge, or axillary nodes – is referred for evaluation.
  • Mastitis in a lactating mother – painful, red, swollen area with fever; continue breastfeeding (or expressing) from both breasts, correct attachment, warm compresses, rest, fluids, analgesic and antibiotic as per protocol; refer if a fluctuant swelling (abscess) develops.

4. Chronic pelvic pain

  • Pain in the lower abdomen for six months or more; causes include chronic PID, endometriosis, fibroids, adhesions and urinary or bowel problems.
  • Record its relation to menstruation and intercourse; treat any infection; refer for evaluation.

5. Pelvic organ prolapse

  • Feeling of something coming down, a mass at the vulva, backache, urinary or bowel symptoms; common in multiparous and older women and those who do heavy work.
  • Teach pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises, treatment of cough and constipation, avoidance of heavy lifting; refer for a pessary or surgery.
  • Prevention – skilled birth attendance, avoiding prolonged second stage, birth spacing and postnatal exercises.

Conclusion A sensitive approach, simple examination, correct syndromic and primary care, and timely referral at the community level relieve much hidden suffering and help detect cancers early.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health
question: Explain the counselling of parents and teenagers on adolescent health issues using a balanced counselling approach.
answer_html:
Introduction Adolescence brings rapid physical, emotional and social changes. Parents often feel unprepared to discuss these issues, and teenagers often feel misunderstood. The nurse counsels both, helping them communicate and make healthy choices. A balanced counselling approach gives the right amount of information, tailored to the client's needs, and supports the client's own decision.

1. Steps of balanced counselling

  1. Build rapport – greet warmly, ensure privacy, explain confidentiality and its limits.
  2. Assess needs – ask open questions about concerns (school, friends, body changes, mood, relationships, risk behaviours); listen without judging.
  3. Give focused information – only what is relevant, in simple language, using pictures or leaflets; correct myths.
  4. Help the client decide – discuss options and their consequences; let the teenager (and parent) choose a plan.
  5. Confirm understanding and plan follow-up – summarise, check what has been understood, give a date for review and information about services and helplines.

2. Key topics for teenagers

  • Puberty changes, menstruation and menstrual hygiene, nocturnal emissions.
  • Nutrition, physical activity, sleep, screen time, anaemia prevention.
  • Stress, examination pressure, emotions, coping skills and where to seek help.
  • Avoiding tobacco, alcohol and drugs; road safety.
  • Healthy relationships, consent, protection from sexual abuse and exploitation, safe internet use.
  • Delaying marriage and pregnancy, contraception and protection from RTIs/STIs when needed.

3. Key advice for parents

  • Talk openly and regularly; listen more than lecture; respect the teenager's growing need for privacy and independence.
  • Set clear, reasonable limits with explanations; praise good behaviour.
  • Know the child's friends and online activities; be a role model (no smoking or alcohol misuse at home).
  • Recognise warning signs – withdrawal, falling school performance, sleep or appetite changes, persistent sadness, aggression, talk of self-harm, unexplained money needs or smell of substances – and seek help early.
  • Support girls' education and oppose child marriage.

4. Joint sessions – help parents and teenagers express concerns to each other, agree on rules and plan family activities together.

Barriers to overcome – embarrassment, cultural taboos, lack of time, generation gap and fear of punishment; the nurse addresses these by meeting each party separately first and then together.

Conclusion Balanced counselling that respects the adolescent and involves parents improves family communication, prevents risk behaviours and links adolescents to services when needed.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health
question: Why are iron and folic acid given together during pregnancy?
answer_html:
• Both are needed to form red blood cells – iron for haemoglobin and folic acid for DNA synthesis and cell division; the demand for both rises sharply in pregnancy for the expanded maternal blood volume, the placenta and the growing fetus.
  • Diets in India are often deficient in both, so iron-deficiency and folate-deficiency (dimorphic) anaemia commonly occur together; giving both prevents and treats anaemia more effectively.
  • Folic acid also helps prevent neural tube defects (when taken early) and supports fetal growth.
  • A single combined IFA tablet (60 mg elemental iron with 500 µg folic acid) daily from the second trimester through pregnancy and lactation improves compliance and simplifies supply.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health
question: Enlist the common health problems of adolescents.
answer_html:
• Nutritional – undernutrition, anaemia, obesity and unhealthy eating.
  • Reproductive and sexual health – menstrual problems, early marriage and teenage pregnancy, unsafe abortion, RTIs/STIs, lack of information.
  • Mental health – stress, depression, anxiety, examination pressure, self-harm and suicide.
  • Substance use – tobacco, alcohol and drugs.
  • Injuries and violence – road traffic injuries, drowning, bullying, sexual abuse, gender-based violence.
  • Non-communicable disease risk factors – physical inactivity, excessive screen time; acne and skin problems.
  • Educational and social problems – school dropout, learning difficulties, child labour and early marriage.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health
question: What are maternity (birth) waiting homes?
answer_html:
• Maternity waiting homes are simple residential facilities located close to a first referral unit or a delivery point, where pregnant women from remote, hilly or tribal areas, or with high-risk pregnancies, stay during the last days or weeks before delivery.
  • They reduce the delay in reaching a facility when labour starts, ensuring skilled care and quick access to emergency obstetric services.
  • Food, basic facilities and health education are provided, and a family member may stay with the woman.
  • In India such homes, often called birth waiting homes, operate in tribal and remote districts, linked to free referral transport.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health
question: What are L1, L2 and L3 delivery points?
answer_html:
• Health facilities conducting deliveries are classified into three levels according to the services they provide:
    • L1 – mainly sub-centres (and some PHCs) conducting normal deliveries, with stabilisation and referral of complications;
    • L2 – 24 × 7 PHCs and non-FRU CHCs that manage normal deliveries and some complications (basic emergency obstetric and newborn care);
    • L3 – first referral units (district hospitals, FRU-CHCs, medical colleges) providing comprehensive emergency obstetric care, including caesarean section and blood transfusion, and newborn care units.
  • The classification guides the planning of staff, supplies and referral linkages.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Demography, Surveillance and Interpretation of Data
question: (a) Define demography and explain its scope. (3 marks) (b) Describe the demographic cycle (demographic transition) with its stages. (6 marks) (c) Explain the population trends in India. (6 marks)

diagram.caption: The demographic cycle (demographic transition)
labels: Graph with time on the x-axis and rates per 1
000 on the y-axis; a birth-rate line and a death-rate line passing through five stages – high stationary
low stationary and declining – with the shaded gap between the lines showing natural increase and an arrow marking India's present position near the end of the late expanding stage

answer_html:
Introduction Every health programme is planned for a population. Its size, age and sex structure and the speed at which it grows determine the needs for maternal and child care, schools, jobs and care of the elderly. Demography provides the numbers and trends on which health planning is based.

(a) Definition and scope

  • Demography is the scientific study of human populations – their size, composition (age, sex and other characteristics) and distribution, and the changes in these brought about by fertility, mortality and migration.
  • Scope
    • population statics – size, density, distribution and structure at a point of time (census data);
    • population dynamics – births, deaths, migration and growth over time;
    • social demography – marriage, family, literacy, employment and urbanisation;
    • applications – population projections, health and family welfare planning, and evaluation of programmes.

(b) The demographic cycle (demographic transition) The demographic cycle describes how a population moves from high birth and death rates to low birth and death rates as a society develops. Five stages are commonly described.

  1. First stage – high stationary
    • high birth rate and high death rate, cancelling each other;
    • population stable or growing very slowly (India until about 1920).
  2. Second stage – early expanding
    • the death rate begins to fall with better food, sanitation and control of epidemics, while the birth rate remains high;
    • population grows fast (many developing countries in the mid-twentieth century).
  3. Third stage – late expanding
    • the death rate falls further and the birth rate also starts to fall;
    • growth continues but more slowly (India in recent decades).
  4. Fourth stage – low stationary
    • low birth rate and low death rate;
    • population becomes stable (many developed countries).
  5. Fifth stage – declining
    • the birth rate falls below the death rate;
    • population declines (some European and East Asian countries).

India's position – India has reached the end of the late expanding stage and is moving towards the low stationary stage. The crude birth rate fell from 21.0 in 2014 to 18.3 per 1,000 in 2024, the crude death rate is 6.4 and the total fertility rate is 1.9 (SRS 2024) – below the replacement level of 2.1. Population will still grow for some decades because of the large number of young people entering reproductive age (population momentum).

(c) Population trends in India

  1. Growth of population (Census)
Year Population (crore) Remarks
1901 23.8 Slow growth
1921 25.1 "Year of the great divide" – population fell during 1911–21 because of epidemics and famine; growth continuous thereafter
1951 36.1 Start of rapid growth after Independence
1971 54.8 Fastest growth decades (about 2.2% a year)
2001 102.9 Crossed one billion
2011 121.1 Decadal growth 17.7%, the lowest since Independence
  • India became the most populous country in the world in 2023, with about 145 crore people (UN estimates); growth is expected to peak and then decline in the second half of the century. 2. Fertility – the TFR has fallen from 3.4 (NFHS-1, 1992–93) to 2.0 (NFHS-5 and NFHS-6); most states are now below replacement, while a few northern states such as Bihar remain above it. 3. Mortality and life expectancy – death rates and infant mortality have fallen steadily (IMR 24 in 2024); life expectancy at birth has risen to about 70 years. 4.
