Age structure – children's share of the population is falling, the working-age share is rising (demographic dividend) and the proportion of elderly (60 years and above, 8.6% in 2011) is growing rapidly, bringing the challenge of ageing. 5. Sex ratio – 943 females per 1,000 males in 2011; the child sex ratio fell to 918; the sex ratio at birth was 918 in 2022–24 (SRS), showing continuing son preference. 6. Density and urbanisation – density 382 persons per sq km in 2011; 31% of people lived in urban areas and urbanisation is increasing rapidly through migration. 7. Literacy – 74% in 2011, with a gender gap that is narrowing. 8. Census 2027 – India's 16th census and the first digital one; house listing was held between April and September 2026 and population enumeration is scheduled for February 2027, with the reference date of 1 March 2027 (1 October 2026 for snow-bound areas). It will provide the first full population count since 2011.

Implications for health

  • Continued investment in family planning, maternal and child health in high-fertility states.
  • Planning for the health needs of a growing elderly population and for non-communicable diseases.
  • Using the demographic dividend through education, nutrition, skills and adolescent health.
  • Addressing urban health, migration and the adverse sex ratio.

Why the transition happened in India – the death rate fell first with the control of famines and epidemics (smallpox, plague, cholera, malaria), antibiotics, vaccines and better food supply; the birth rate fell later with female education, family planning, urbanisation, rising age at marriage and better child survival.

Changing population pyramid – India's age pyramid has changed from a broad-based, triangular (expansive) shape with many children, to a narrower base with a bulge in the young adult ages; it is gradually moving towards a more rectangular (stationary) shape with a growing elderly top.

Common demographic indicators – crude birth and death rates, natural growth rate, general and total fertility rates, net reproduction rate, sex ratio, dependency ratio, life expectancy, density, literacy and urban proportion.

Regional differences – fertility and birth rates are highest in Bihar (CBR 26.8, TFR 2.9 in SRS 2024) and lowest in states such as Kerala (CBR 11.1) and Delhi (TFR 1.2); therefore population programmes must be tailored to each state and district.

Population projection – using the present age structure and assumed future fertility, mortality and migration, demographers project the future population; such projections guide the planning of schools, jobs, health facilities and elderly care. Projections need revision once new census data become available, which is why Census 2027 is so important for planning.

Migration – the third component of population change; internal migration from rural to urban areas and between states for work creates crowded urban slums and leaves the elderly and women behind in villages, with implications for continuity of care, immunisation and maternal health of migrant families.

Nursing importance

  • The community health nurse collects demographic data during community surveys and maintains eligible couple, birth and death registers.
  • Knowledge of the local population structure helps in planning services and setting targets for the sub-centre or PHC.
  • Health education on small family norm, birth spacing and gender equality contributes to population stabilisation.

Conclusion Demography explains how populations change. India has moved through the demographic cycle to near-replacement fertility and falling death rates, but population momentum, ageing, regional differences and an adverse sex ratio remain important challenges for health planning.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Demography, Surveillance and Interpretation of Data
question: Explain the sources of vital statistics in India, with their uses and limitations.
tags: Registration of Births and Deaths Act 1969
answer_html:
Introduction Vital statistics are numerical records of vital events – births, deaths, marriages, divorces, foetal deaths and migration – and the rates calculated from them. They are essential for measuring health status and planning services.

1. Census

  • A complete count of the population every ten years by the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, giving size, age, sex, literacy, occupation, housing and amenities.
  • The last census was in 2011; Census 2027 (reference date 1 March 2027) is the first digital census.

2. Civil Registration System (CRS)

  • Compulsory registration of births and deaths under the Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1969 – births and deaths are to be reported within 21 days to the local registrar (gram panchayat secretary, municipal officer, or the facility).
  • The 2023 amendment (in force from 1 October 2023) created a national digital database and made the birth certificate a key document for admission to school, voter registration and other services.
  • Includes the Medical Certification of Cause of Death (MCCD) in hospitals.

3. Sample Registration System (SRS)

  • A dual-record system – continuous enumeration by a resident part-time enumerator plus an independent half-yearly survey – in a representative sample of villages and urban blocks; started on a pilot basis in 1964–65 and fully in 1969–70.
  • Provides reliable annual estimates of birth rate, death rate, IMR, TFR, MMR and sex ratio at birth at state and national level.

4. National Family Health Survey (NFHS) and other surveys

  • Large household surveys giving data on fertility, family planning, maternal and child health, nutrition and NCD risk factors; NFHS-6 (2023–24) fact sheets were released in May 2026.
  • Other surveys – Comprehensive National Nutrition Survey, Longitudinal Ageing Study in India, National Sample Survey.

5. Health service records – HMIS and RCH portal data from health facilities, notification of diseases under surveillance, hospital records, disease registers (cancer, TB) and records of special programmes.

Uses – measuring health status and trends; comparing areas; identifying problems and high-risk groups; planning, implementing and evaluating programmes; research; legal and administrative purposes (age proof, inheritance, citizenship).

Limitations – incomplete and late registration (especially of deaths and of births at home); errors in the cause of death; long intervals between censuses; survey sampling errors; differences between sources; poor-quality data at the facility level.

Role of the nurse – encourage and help families register every birth and death on time, fill records accurately and use local data for planning.

Conclusion India uses several complementary sources – census, CRS, SRS, surveys and service records – each with strengths and weaknesses; complete registration and good-quality records at the grassroots are the foundation of reliable vital statistics.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Demography, Surveillance and Interpretation of Data
question: Explain the sex ratio and child sex ratio in India – trends, causes and social implications, with measures to improve them.
answer_html:
Introduction The sex ratio is a sensitive indicator of the status of women in a society. In India it has been adverse to females for more than a century.

1. Definitions

  • Sex ratio – number of females per 1,000 males in the population.
  • Child sex ratio (CSR) – number of girls per 1,000 boys in the 0–6 years age group.
  • Sex ratio at birth (SRB) – number of girls born per 1,000 boys born; the natural value is about 950 (943–954).

2. Trends

  • Overall sex ratio (Census) – 972 in 1901, 946 in 1951, 927 in 1991, 933 in 2001 and 943 in 2011.
  • Child sex ratio – 945 in 1991, 927 in 2001 and 918 in 2011, the lowest since Independence.
  • Sex ratio at birth (SRS) – a slight improvement to 918 in 2022–24, but still well below the natural level, with wide state differences (lowest in some northern states, highest in some central and southern states).

3. Causes

  • Son preference – sons seen as old-age security, carriers of the family name and performers of rituals; daughters seen as an economic burden because of dowry.
  • Sex-selective abortion after prenatal sex determination; female infanticide in the past.
  • Neglect of girls – poorer nutrition, delayed treatment and lower immunisation, leading to higher female child mortality.
  • Maternal deaths and migration patterns (men moving to cities) also affect local ratios.

4. Social implications

  • Shortage of brides ("marriage squeeze") – trafficking of girls, bride buying, child marriage.
  • Increased violence and crimes against women.
  • Further lowering of the status of women and an unbalanced population structure.

5. Measures

  • Strict enforcement of the Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (PC-PNDT) Act, 1994 – registration of ultrasound centres, prohibition of sex determination and advertisements, records (Form F), decoy operations, penalties.
  • Beti Bachao Beti Padhao (launched 2015) – improving the child sex ratio and girls' education through awareness and community action.
  • Schemes for the girl child – savings and conditional cash transfer schemes, free education, scholarships.
  • Women's empowerment, education and employment; legal rights of daughters to property; campaigns against dowry.
  • Complete registration of births, tracking of pregnancies and audit of female infant deaths.

Role of the community health nurse – early registration and tracking of every pregnancy and its outcome; counselling families against sex selection and in favour of equal care for girls; reporting suspected sex-selective practices; celebrating the birth of girls in the community; ensuring equal nutrition and immunisation.

Conclusion India's adverse sex ratio reflects deep-rooted son preference. Legal enforcement, social change and the active involvement of health workers are needed to ensure that every girl is born, survives and thrives.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Demography, Surveillance and Interpretation of Data
question: Explain the calculation and interpretation of common mortality and morbidity indicators, with a worked example from a PHC area.
answer_html:
Introduction Health workers collect births, deaths and cases of illness in their area. Converting these numbers into rates and ratios allows comparison between areas and over time, and shows where action is needed.

1. Worked example – a PHC area with a mid-year population of 30,000 in one year

  • Live births 540; total deaths 195; infant deaths 13 (of which 10 were neonatal); maternal deaths 1; women aged 15–49 years 7,800.
Indicator Formula Calculation Result
Crude birth rate (CBR) Live births ÷ mid-year population × 1,000 540 ÷ 30,000 × 1,000 18.0 per 1,000
Crude death rate (CDR) Deaths ÷ mid-year population × 1,000 195 ÷ 30,000 × 1,000 6.5 per 1,000
Natural growth rate (CBR – CDR) ÷ 10 (18.0 – 6.5) ÷ 10 1.15% a year
Infant mortality rate (IMR) Infant deaths ÷ live births × 1,000 13 ÷ 540 × 1,000 24.1 per 1,000 live births
Neonatal mortality rate (NMR) Neonatal deaths ÷ live births × 1,000 10 ÷ 540 × 1,000 18.5 per 1,000 live births
Maternal mortality ratio (MMR) Maternal deaths ÷ live births × 1,00,000 1 ÷ 540 × 1,00,000 185 per 1,00,000 live births
General fertility rate (GFR) Live births ÷ women 15–49 × 1,000 540 ÷ 7,800 × 1,000 69.2 per 1,000 women

2. Morbidity indicators

  • Incidence rate – new cases in a period ÷ population at risk; for example, 45 new TB cases in a year in 30,000 people = 150 per 1,00,000 per year.
  • Prevalence – all existing cases at a point of time ÷ population; for example, 2,400 persons with hypertension among 18,000 adults = 13.3%.

3. Interpretation

  • Compare with national figures (SRS 2024: CBR 18.3, CDR 6.4, IMR 24, NMR 18; MMR 87 in 2022–24). In the example, birth and death rates and infant mortality are close to national levels, but three-fourths of infant deaths are neonatal, pointing to the need to strengthen newborn care.
  • One maternal death gives an MMR of 185 – with small numbers, rates fluctuate widely from year to year; therefore, small areas should use actual numbers and death reviews, and combine data over several years.
  • Check data quality first – missed home births and deaths make rates falsely low.

Conclusion Simple calculations turn local registers into meaningful indicators. Interpreted carefully, with attention to small numbers and data quality, they guide priorities for the sub-centre and PHC.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Demography, Surveillance and Interpretation of Data
question: Explain the Mother and Child Tracking System (MCTS) and its successor, the RCH portal – features, information flow and benefits.
answer_html:
Introduction Earlier, health reports gave only aggregate numbers (how many ANC visits, how many vaccinations), which could not show which woman or child had missed a service. The Mother and Child Tracking System (MCTS) introduced name-based tracking of every pregnant woman and child, and was later upgraded to the Reproductive and Child Health (RCH) portal.

1. Features

  • Registration of each beneficiary with a unique RCH ID – eligible couples, pregnant women (from early pregnancy to 42 days after delivery) and children (from birth to immunisation completion).
  • Records of every service – ANC visits, tests, IFA, Td, high-risk conditions, place and outcome of delivery, postnatal visits, newborn details, vaccinations, family planning method.
  • Due lists and work plans generated for each ANM and ASHA, listing who needs which service on which date.
  • Tracking of high-risk pregnancies and of children who miss vaccines (drop-outs and left-outs).
  • SMS messages to beneficiaries and health workers; tablet-based data entry by ANMs.
  • Reports and dashboards for block, district, state and national managers.

2. Information flow

  • ASHA identifies and mobilises beneficiaries → ANM registers them and records services (directly on a tablet or through the block data-entry operator) → data compiled at the PHC/block → district and state → national level.
  • Due lists flow back from the portal to the ANM and ASHA for action.

3. Benefits

  • Ensures that every woman and child gets the full package of services on time; identifies and follows up left-outs and drop-outs.
  • Early detection and tracking of high-risk mothers and sick newborns.
  • Improves planning of sessions, vaccine and drug requirements.
  • Provides reliable data for monitoring and accountability, and for payments under schemes.
  • Strengthens the continuum of care across levels.

4. Challenges – incomplete or delayed data entry, duplicate records, migration of beneficiaries, connectivity problems and the extra workload on ANMs.

Role of the nurse – registers every pregnant woman and newborn early with complete and correct details, updates every service on time, uses the due lists for planning sessions and home visits, and verifies the data during supervision.

Conclusion Name-based tracking through MCTS and the RCH portal changed the focus from counting services to reaching every individual woman and child, making the ANM's work more targeted and accountable.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Demography, Surveillance and Interpretation of Data
question: What is disaggregation of data? Why is it important?
answer_html:
• Disaggregation is the breaking down of aggregated (total) data into sub-groups – by sex, age, rural/urban area, village or hamlet, caste or tribe, income, disability or other characteristics.
  • Importance – it reveals inequalities hidden in averages and helps target action to the groups most in need.
  • Example – full immunisation coverage of 90% in a PHC area may hide a coverage of only 65% in a tribal hamlet or among children of migrant workers.
  • The Sustainable Development Goals call for disaggregated data so that "no one is left behind".

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Demography, Surveillance and Interpretation of Data
question: What is the dependency ratio? How is it calculated?
answer_html:
• The dependency ratio is the number of dependents (children aged 0–14 years and elderly aged 65 years and above) per 100 persons of working age (15–64 years).
  • Dependency ratio = (population 0–14 + population 65+) ÷ population 15–64 × 100.
  • Example – 9,000 children and 1,800 elderly in a population with 19,200 persons aged 15–64 give a ratio of 56.25.
  • A falling young-dependency ratio creates a demographic dividend; a rising old-age dependency ratio indicates the need for elderly care.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Demography, Surveillance and Interpretation of Data
question: What is demographic dividend?
answer_html:
• Demographic dividend is the potential for faster economic growth that arises when the share of the working-age population (15–64 years) is large compared with dependent children and elderly, as happens after fertility declines.
  • It is a time-limited window of opportunity; India is in this phase now.
  • It is realised only if the young population is healthy, educated, skilled and employed – hence the importance of adolescent health, nutrition, education and women's participation in work.
  • If these conditions are not met, a large young population can instead become a burden of unemployment.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Demography, Surveillance and Interpretation of Data
question: Define net reproduction rate (NRR). Write its significance.
answer_html:
• Net reproduction rate is the average number of daughters that a woman would bear in her lifetime who would survive to the mother's age at their birth, given the current age-specific fertility and mortality rates.
  • NRR = 1 means each generation of women exactly replaces itself – the replacement level, which corresponds roughly to a TFR of 2.1.
  • An NRR above 1 indicates a growing population and below 1 a declining one; achieving an NRR of 1 was a long-standing goal of India's population policy.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: (a) Explain population explosion and its impact on the individual, family, society and national development. (5 marks) (b) Describe the measures for population control – women's empowerment, social, economic and educational development, and limiting family size. (6 marks) (c) Explain the role of the nurse in family welfare. (4 marks)
tags: role of the nurse in family welfare
answer_html:
Introduction Population explosion refers to a rapid and large increase in population, when the birth rate remains high while the death rate falls sharply. India's population grew from 36 crore in 1951 to 121 crore in 2011, and India is now the most populous country in the world. Although fertility has now fallen to about the replacement level, the large base of young people means that population will keep growing for some decades.

(a) Population explosion – causes and impact Causes – a steep fall in death rates through better health care without an equal fall in birth rates; early marriage; poverty and illiteracy; son preference; high infant mortality (parents having more children to ensure survival); religious and cultural beliefs; lack of access to contraception; the large proportion of people in the reproductive age group (momentum).

Impact

  • On the individual – poorer health and nutrition, especially of women who have frequent pregnancies; less opportunity for education and employment.
  • On the family – lower income per head, poor housing and sanitation, malnutrition of children, inadequate attention and care for each child, stress on the mother.
  • On society – overcrowding, slums, unemployment, crime, pressure on schools, hospitals, transport and water supply; social unrest.
  • On national development – the benefits of economic growth are spread thinly; low per-capita income; high spending on basic services; food insecurity; environmental degradation – deforestation, pollution, water scarcity, loss of biodiversity and climate stress.
  • On health services – more people to cover with the same staff and facilities, increasing the workload of health workers and reducing quality.

(b) Measures for population control 1. Women's empowerment

  • Education of girls beyond secondary level, raising the age at marriage (legal minimum 18 for girls), employment and economic independence.
  • Equal rights in decision-making, property and political participation; prevention of violence.
  • Empowered women marry later, have fewer and healthier children and make better use of health services.

2. Social development

  • Reduction of infant and child mortality, so that parents feel secure with fewer children.
  • Social security for old age, which reduces the need for many sons.
  • Mass media and community leaders promoting the small family norm and gender equality.

3. Economic development

  • Poverty reduction, employment generation, industrialisation and urbanisation, which raise the cost of rearing many children and the value of educating each child.

4. Educational development

  • Universal school education, adult literacy, adolescent life-skills and population education.

5. Limiting family size – the small family norm

  • Temporary (spacing) methods
    • natural – fertility awareness methods, lactational amenorrhoea;
    • barrier – condoms and diaphragm;
    • chemical – spermicides;
    • hormonal – combined oral pills, the weekly non-hormonal pill centchroman, injectable contraceptive, implant;
    • intrauterine devices – Copper-T (including postpartum and post-abortion insertion).
  • Terminal (permanent) methods – female sterilisation (tubectomy) and male sterilisation (no-scalpel vasectomy).
  • Emergency contraception for unprotected intercourse.
  • A basket of choices with informed choice, quality services, free supplies and compensation for sterilisation, and home delivery of contraceptives by ASHAs.

(c) Role of the nurse in family welfare

  • Survey and registration – maintain the eligible couple register; identify couples with unmet need.
  • Information, education and counselling – about methods, their benefits and side-effects; correct myths; counsel couples together; respect free and informed choice.
  • Service provision – distribute condoms and pills, give injectables, insert IUCDs (trained nurses), prepare clients for sterilisation and give post-operative care, provide emergency contraception.
  • Postpartum and post-abortion family planning counselling and services.
  • Follow-up – manage side-effects, check continuation and switch methods if needed; detect complications early.
  • Special groups – newly married couples, adolescents, couples with one child (spacing), men (male participation).
  • Coordination – with ASHAs, AWWs, self-help groups and leaders; organise family welfare camps and observe population fortnights.
  • Records and reports – accurate entries in the eligible couple register, stock registers, the RCH portal and monthly reports.

Magnitude – India has about 18% of the world's population living on only about 2.4% of the world's land area, which magnifies the pressure on natural resources and services.

Contraceptive services in the public health system

Method Provider Place
Condoms, oral pills, emergency pills ASHA, ANM Home, sub-centre
Centchroman (weekly pill) ANM, CHO, MO Sub-centre/AAM and above
Injectable contraceptive Trained ANM, staff nurse Sub-centre/AAM, PHC and above
IUCD (interval, postpartum, post-abortion) Trained ANM, staff nurse, MO Sub-centre, PHC, delivery points
Female sterilisation Trained doctors PHC/CHC fixed-day services, district hospital
No-scalpel vasectomy Trained doctors CHC, district hospital

Inter-sectoral support – education, women and child development (anganwadi services), panchayati raj institutions, NGOs, self-help groups and the media all contribute to population stabilisation.

Quality and rights in family planning services – voluntary, informed choice using the medical eligibility criteria; screening and counselling before every method; fixed-day, facility-based sterilisation services in place of camps (as directed by the Supreme Court in 2016); management of side-effects and complications; privacy and dignity.

Example of the nurse's work – a newly married couple in the village is visited by the ANM and ASHA, who explain the benefits of delaying the first child, discuss condoms and oral pills, correct the myth that pills cause infertility, give a three-month supply and arrange a follow-up visit; after the birth of their first child, the couple is counselled on postpartum IUCD or injectable contraception for spacing.

Indicators the nurse monitors – the proportion of eligible couples using modern methods, unmet need, use of spacing methods by young couples, postpartum family planning acceptance, continuation rates, and complications or failures reported.

Challenges in population control – deep-rooted son preference, early marriage in some regions, low male participation (vasectomy forms a very small share of sterilisations), myths about side-effects, gaps in quality of services, and wide differences between states. Overcoming these requires sustained behaviour change communication, men's involvement and a strong primary health care system.

Ethical principles – no coercion or incentives that pressure people, full information on all methods, respect for the couple's decision, confidentiality, and equal access for the poor, adolescents and marginalised groups.

Population education – teaching adolescents and young adults about population, family life, gender equality and responsible parenthood in schools and youth groups helps the next generation to adopt the small family norm by conviction.

Male participation – the nurse involves husbands in counselling, promotes condoms and no-scalpel vasectomy (a simple, safe procedure with no effect on strength or sexual function), and uses the vasectomy fortnight to reach men through male health workers and community leaders.

Nursing importance

  • Family planning saves the lives of women and children by preventing high-risk, closely spaced and unwanted pregnancies.
  • The nurse is the most trusted source of family planning information for many rural women.
  • Rights-based, non-coercive counselling builds long-term acceptance.

Conclusion Population growth affects every aspect of individual and national life. Lasting population stabilisation comes from development – especially women's empowerment, education and child survival – together with easy access to a wide range of contraceptive methods, in which the nurse plays a central part.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain the National Population Policy, 2000 – its objectives, national socio-demographic goals and strategies.
answer_html:
Introduction The National Population Policy (NPP), 2000 was adopted by the Government of India to provide a framework for advancing goals and prioritising strategies for population stabilisation and improving the quality of life. It reaffirmed a voluntary, target-free, rights-based approach.

1. Objectives

  • Immediate – address the unmet needs for contraception, health infrastructure and personnel, and provide integrated service delivery for basic reproductive and child health care.
  • Medium-term – bring the TFR to replacement level (2.1) by 2010 through vigorous implementation of inter-sectoral strategies.
  • Long-term – achieve a stable population by 2045, consistent with sustainable economic growth, social development and environmental protection.

2. National socio-demographic goals (selected)

  • Make school education up to age 14 free and compulsory and reduce drop-outs.
  • Reduce the IMR below 30 per 1,000 live births and the MMR below 100 per 1,00,000 live births.
  • Achieve universal immunisation of children against vaccine-preventable diseases.
  • Promote delayed marriage of girls – not earlier than 18 and preferably after 20 years.
  • Achieve 80% institutional deliveries and 100% deliveries by trained persons.
  • Achieve universal access to information, counselling and services for fertility regulation and contraception, with a wide basket of choices.
  • Achieve 100% registration of births, deaths, marriages and pregnancies.
  • Prevent and control communicable diseases and contain the spread of HIV/AIDS.
  • Integrate Indian systems of medicine in reproductive and child health services.
  • Promote the small family norm vigorously; bring about convergence of related social sector programmes.

3. Strategies

  • Decentralised planning and implementation through panchayats; convergence of services at the village level.
  • Empowering women for improved health and nutrition; child health and survival.
  • Meeting unmet needs for family welfare services; services for under-served groups (urban slums, tribal and hilly areas, adolescents); increased male participation.
  • Diverse health care providers, collaboration with NGOs and the private sector; information, education and communication; research.

4. Institutional arrangements – a National Commission on Population chaired by the Prime Minister and state commissions to oversee implementation; a population stabilisation fund (later Jansankhya Sthirata Kosh).

Achievements – the replacement-level TFR was reached later than planned (TFR 2.0 in NFHS-5 and NFHS-6), and the IMR and MMR goals have since been surpassed nationally, though not in all states.

Conclusion NPP 2000 shifted India's population effort from targets to people-centred reproductive and child health and social development, a direction that has contributed to the present near-replacement fertility.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain the evolution of the National Family Welfare Programme in India and its present services.
answer_html:
Introduction India was the first country in the world to launch a national family planning programme, in 1952. Over the decades the programme changed from a narrow focus on birth control to a broad reproductive, maternal and child health approach.

1. Evolution

  • 1952 – clinical approach: family planning clinics in hospitals; people had to come to the clinic.
  • 1960s – extension education approach: services taken to the community through health workers; IUCD and sterilisation camps; a separate Department of Family Planning (1966).
  • 1975–77 – Emergency period: coercive sterilisation targets caused a public backlash.
  • 1977 – renamed the Family Welfare Programme, emphasising voluntary acceptance and maternal and child welfare.
  • 1996 – target-free approach, later called the community needs assessment approach: targets abolished; planning based on the needs assessed at the sub-centre level.
  • 1997 – Reproductive and Child Health (RCH) Programme Phase I, following the International Conference on Population and Development (Cairo, 1994) – integrated family planning with maternal, child and reproductive health.
  • 2005 – RCH Phase II under the National Rural Health Mission, later the National Health Mission (2013).
  • 2013 – RMNCH+A strategy – family planning as part of the continuum of care across life stages.

2. Present services

  • Basket of choices – condoms, combined oral pills, the weekly pill centchroman, injectable contraceptive (MPA), IUCDs (interval, postpartum and post-abortion), female sterilisation (minilaparotomy and laparoscopic), no-scalpel vasectomy, emergency contraceptive pills; newer options such as the subdermal implant and subcutaneous injectable in selected facilities.
  • Community-level services – home delivery of contraceptives and pregnancy testing kits by ASHAs; counselling for spacing after marriage and after the first child.
  • Postpartum and post-abortion family planning at facilities.
  • Compensation and insurance – compensation to sterilisation acceptors for wage loss and an indemnity (insurance) scheme for failure, complications or death.
  • Mission Parivar Vikas – intensified services in high-fertility districts.
  • Campaigns – World Population Day fortnight (July) and the vasectomy fortnight (November–December).
  • Supply chain – an online family planning logistics management information system tracks contraceptive stocks down to the ASHA level.

Conclusion From a clinic-based birth-control programme, India's family welfare programme has become a voluntary, target-free, rights-based service integrated with maternal and child health, contributing to near-replacement fertility.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain the small family norm – its meaning, benefits and the factors affecting its acceptance.
answer_html:
Introduction The small family norm is the idea, accepted by a couple and the community, that a family should have only one or two children, born by choice and adequately spaced. It is a goal of India's family welfare programme.

1. Benefits

  • Mother – fewer pregnancies mean less risk of maternal death, anaemia and complications; better health and more time for self-development and work.
  • Children – better nutrition, care, education and survival; healthier growth with adequate spacing between births.
  • Family – higher income per head, better housing and living standards, less stress, savings for the future.
  • Community and nation – reduced pressure on land, water, housing, schools and health services; higher per-capita income; better environment and quality of life.

2. Factors affecting acceptance

  • Education, especially of women – educated couples accept the norm more readily.
  • Son preference – families continue to have children until a son is born.
  • High infant and child mortality – parents have more children to ensure survival of some.
  • Age at marriage – early marriage lengthens the reproductive span.
  • Economic factors – children seen as working hands and old-age security in poor families.
  • Religious and cultural beliefs and pressure from elders.
  • Access to and quality of contraceptive services, and fear of side-effects or myths.
  • Status of women and their role in decision-making.

3. Promotion by the nurse

  • Health education through home visits, group meetings, mass media and role models of small, happy families.
  • Ensuring child survival through immunisation and nutrition; counselling for spacing.
  • Providing easily accessible contraceptive services and follow-up.
  • Working with leaders, self-help groups and schools; supporting girls' education and later marriage.

4. Common myths to correct – "contraceptives cause infertility or cancer", "vasectomy makes a man weak", "a Copper-T moves in the body", "it is God's will to have many children" – the nurse corrects these with facts and examples of satisfied users.

5. Simple messages – "small family, happy family"; "the right age for marriage – girls 18, boys 21"; "the second child after at least three years".

Conclusion The small family norm benefits every member of the family and the nation. It is accepted most readily where children survive, women are educated and empowered, and good family welfare services are available.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain the community-based distribution of contraceptives by ASHAs and the supply chain for family planning commodities.
tags: family planning logistics management information system
answer_html:
Introduction Many women, especially in rural areas, find it difficult to visit a health facility for contraceptives. Community-based distribution brings family planning commodities to the doorstep through the ASHA, improving access, continuation and privacy.

1. Home delivery of contraceptives

  • The ASHA keeps a stock of condoms, combined oral contraceptive pills and emergency contraceptive pills, and supplies them to eligible couples at home for a nominal charge (which forms part of her incentive), or free as per state policy.
  • She also uses pregnancy testing kits for early detection of pregnancy, so that women can register early for ANC or seek safe abortion services.

2. Counselling and spacing

  • The ASHA identifies newly married couples and couples with one child and counsels them on spacing – delaying the first child after marriage and keeping a gap of at least three years between children – and on postpartum family planning.
  • She refers women for IUCD, injectable contraceptive and sterilisation, and accompanies them if needed.
  • She is given performance-based incentives for ensuring spacing and for motivating sterilisation acceptors, as per the national scheme.

3. Follow-up and records

  • Follow-up of new users for side-effects and continuation; referral of problems to the ANM or PHC.
  • Records of beneficiaries and commodities given, reported monthly to the ANM.

4. Supply chain for family planning commodities

  • Supplies flow from the national level through state and district warehouses to the PHC, sub-centre and ASHA.
  • An online family planning logistics management information system captures stock, consumption and requirements at each level, generates indents and alerts for stock-outs or expiry, and makes the system transparent.
  • The ANM checks the ASHA's stock monthly, replenishes it and ensures that expired items are removed.

5. Benefits and challenges

  • Benefits – better access and privacy, increased use of spacing methods, early pregnancy detection, empowerment of women.
  • Challenges – irregular supplies, myths, lack of male involvement, workload and training needs of ASHAs.

Example – an ASHA learns that a young mother of a six-month-old baby wants to avoid another pregnancy for some years. She explains the options, supplies condoms immediately, refers her to the ANM for an IUCD or injectable, and records the visit for follow-up.

Conclusion Doorstep delivery of contraceptives by ASHAs, backed by a reliable logistics system and supervision by the ANM, has made family planning more accessible and acceptable in rural communities.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: What were FP2020 and FP2030?
answer_html:
• FP2020 (Family Planning 2020) was a global partnership launched at the London Summit on Family Planning in July 2012 to enable 120 million additional women and girls in the world's poorest countries to use modern contraceptives by 2020, through rights-based, voluntary family planning.
  • India was a major partner and committed to expanding its basket of choices, postpartum family planning and investment in contraceptive services.
  • Its successor, FP2030, launched in 2021, continues the partnership with a broader, country-led vision of rights-based family planning by 2030.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: What was the Jansankhya Sthirata Kosh (JSK)?
answer_html:
• Jansankhya Sthirata Kosh (originally the National Population Stabilisation Fund) was an autonomous society under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, set up under the National Population Policy 2000 with a government corpus of ₹100 crore, to promote population stabilisation.
  • It ran the Prerna scheme (rewarding couples who delayed marriage and the first child and kept spacing), the Santushti scheme (public–private partnership for sterilisation) and a national family planning helpline.
  • It was discontinued in February 2019 following a Cabinet decision, and its functions were absorbed into the Ministry's family planning programme.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: What is the target-free approach (community needs assessment approach) in family welfare?
answer_html:
• Introduced in 1996, the target-free approach abolished the centrally fixed method-specific targets for family planning workers.
  • Instead, the ANM assesses the needs of her community – eligible couples, pregnant women, children – and prepares a sub-centre action plan; this was later called the community needs assessment approach (CNAA).
  • It emphasises quality, informed choice and the overall reproductive and child health needs of the community rather than the number of acceptors.
  • It followed the spirit of the International Conference on Population and Development (Cairo, 1994).

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: (a) Define occupational health and occupational health nursing, and state the objectives and functions of the occupational health nurse. (4 marks) (b) Classify occupational health hazards and list the common occupational diseases. (5 marks) (c) Explain the national and state occupational health programmes, institutions and legislation in India. (6 marks)
tags: state directorates of industrial safety and health
Occupational Safety Health and Working Conditions Code 2020
National Policy on Safety Health and Environment at Workplace

diagram.caption: Classification of occupational health hazards
labels: Central box "Worker" with five arrows to boxes – physical (heat

answer_html:
Introduction Workers spend a third of their day at work, and the working environment strongly influences their health. India has a vast workforce, most of it in the unorganised sector (agriculture, construction, small industries, domestic work), where protection is weakest. Occupational health aims to keep workers healthy and productive and to make workplaces safe.

(a) Definitions, objectives and functions

  • Occupational health (joint ILO/WHO Committee) is the promotion and maintenance of the highest degree of physical, mental and social well-being of workers in all occupations; the prevention of ill-health caused by working conditions; the protection of workers from risks; and the placing and maintenance of workers in an environment adapted to their physical and mental capacities – in short, adapting work to the worker and each worker to the job.
  • Occupational health nursing is the specialty practice of nursing that provides health services to workers and worker populations, focusing on the promotion, protection and restoration of workers' health within a safe and healthy work environment.
  • Objectives – prevent occupational diseases and injuries; promote health and productivity; provide first aid, emergency and primary care; ensure early diagnosis, treatment and rehabilitation; maintain a safe and healthy workplace.
  • Functions of the occupational health nurse
    • pre-placement, periodic and special medical examinations with the medical officer;
    • first aid and emergency care; treatment of minor illnesses as per standing orders;
    • health education (safe work practices, personal protective equipment, nutrition, tobacco and alcohol, NCDs, HIV);
    • surveillance of workers exposed to hazards and of the work environment, with records;
    • counselling, rehabilitation and return-to-work support; care of women workers;
    • immunisation (tetanus, hepatitis B for health workers); maintenance of records and statutory reports;
    • liaison with management, safety committees, ESIC and community health services.

(b) Occupational health hazards and diseases 1. Physical hazards

  • Heat (heat stroke, heat cramps), cold, light (eye strain, nystagmus), noise (noise-induced hearing loss), vibration (vibration white finger), ionising radiation (cancers, radiation sickness), ultraviolet radiation, high or low pressure (decompression sickness). 2. Chemical hazards

  • Dusts causing pneumoconioses – silicosis (stone quarrying, mining, sandblasting, glass and ceramics), coal workers' pneumoconiosis, asbestosis, byssinosis (cotton dust), bagassosis (sugar-cane fibre), farmer's lung.

  • Gases – carbon monoxide, hydrogen sulphide, chlorine, ammonia.
  • Metals – lead (battery, paint, printing), mercury, cadmium, manganese, chromium.
  • Solvents (benzene – leukaemia), pesticides (agricultural workers), dyes (bladder cancer). 3. Biological hazards – tuberculosis, hepatitis B and C and HIV (health workers), anthrax and brucellosis (animal handlers), leptospirosis (farmers, sewer workers), fungal infections. 4. Mechanical hazards – injuries from unguarded machinery, falls from heights, collapse of structures, road accidents during work. 5. Ergonomic and psychosocial hazards – poor posture, heavy lifting and repetitive movements (back pain, carpal tunnel syndrome), shift and night work, long hours, monotony, job insecurity, harassment and stress.

Common occupational diseases – pneumoconioses; metal poisoning; occupational asthma; occupational cancers (skin, lung, bladder, leukaemia, mesothelioma); occupational dermatoses; noise-induced hearing loss; heat illnesses; musculoskeletal disorders; occupational infections; poisoning by pesticides; and accidents. Many of these are notifiable under labour law.

(c) National and state occupational health programmes, institutions and legislation 1. Legislation – the four labour codes

  • From 21 November 2025 India brought into force four labour codes that consolidate 29 central labour laws:
    • the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, which merges 13 earlier laws (including the Factories Act, Mines Act and laws for construction, dock, contract and migrant workers) – it provides for national safety standards, a National Occupational Safety and Health Board, safety committees, limits on working hours, welfare facilities, notification of occupational diseases and accidents, and free annual health check-ups for workers aged 40 years and above;
    • the Code on Social Security, 2020, which includes the employees' state insurance, provident fund, maternity benefit and employees' compensation provisions, extends ESIC coverage across the country (including hazardous establishments with even one worker) and covers gig and platform workers;
    • the Code on Wages, 2019 and the Industrial Relations Code, 2020.
  • The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013 protects women workers.

2. National institutions

  • ICMR-National Institute of Occupational Health (NIOH), Ahmedabad, with regional centres – research, surveillance, training and technical support for the prevention and control of occupational diseases.
  • Directorate General Factory Advice Service and Labour Institutes (DGFASLI), Mumbai – advises on safety and health in factories and ports, with the Central and Regional Labour Institutes.
  • Directorate General of Mines Safety (DGMS) – safety and health of mine workers.
  • Employees' State Insurance Corporation (ESIC) – medical care and cash benefits for insured workers through dispensaries and hospitals.
  • The National Policy on Safety, Health and Environment at Workplace (2009) sets the national goals of preventing work-related injuries and diseases.

3. Health-sector programmes

  • Programmes for control and treatment of occupational diseases implemented with ICMR-NIOH; screening of workers for TB, silicosis and NCDs through NHM and NCD programmes; noise and hearing services under the deafness programme; heat-related illness action plans.
  • Ayushman Arogya Mandirs provide screening and primary care to workers in villages and urban areas.

4. State-level services

  • State Directorates of Industrial Safety and Health (factory inspectorates) enforce safety and health provisions in factories.
  • State labour departments run ESIC hospitals and welfare boards for building and other construction workers, and some states have special policies – for example, schemes for screening, compensation and rehabilitation of workers with silicosis.
  • Registration of unorganised workers on the national e-Shram portal links them to social security schemes.

Prevention – the hierarchy of controls

  1. Elimination or substitution – remove the hazard or replace it with a safer material (for example, lead-free paints, less toxic pesticides).
  2. Engineering controls – enclosure of processes, local exhaust ventilation, wet methods for dust suppression, machine guards, noise barriers.
  3. Administrative controls – job rotation, rest breaks in heat, limits on exposure time, training, safe work procedures, warning signs.
  4. Personal protective equipment – masks and respirators, ear plugs, goggles, gloves, helmets, safety shoes – the last line of defence.
  5. Medical measures – pre-placement and periodic examinations, biological monitoring, immunisation, early treatment and rehabilitation.

Example – in a stone-crushing unit, wet drilling, water sprays and ventilation reduce silica dust; workers use respirators; the nurse arranges periodic chest X-rays and TB screening, educates workers about tobacco cessation, and helps those with silicosis obtain compensation and rehabilitation.

Nursing importance

  • Most occupational diseases are irreversible but entirely preventable through engineering controls, protective equipment and early detection.
  • The nurse is often the only health professional at the workplace or in the village who can recognise a work-related illness and link the worker to compensation and care.
  • Health education and periodic screening protect workers in the unorganised sector, who lack formal occupational health services.

Conclusion Occupational health protects the people who keep the economy running. Knowledge of workplace hazards and diseases, the new labour codes and the institutions that support workers' health enables the occupational and community health nurse to prevent disease, detect it early and help workers obtain care and compensation.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain the Employees' State Insurance (ESI) scheme – its coverage, contributions and benefits.
answer_html:
Introduction The Employees' State Insurance (ESI) scheme, started under the ESI Act of 1948 and now governed by the Code on Social Security, 2020, is an integrated social security scheme that protects workers and their families against sickness, maternity, disability and death due to employment injury. It is administered by the Employees' State Insurance Corporation (ESIC) under the Ministry of Labour and Employment.

1. Coverage

  • Factories and specified establishments employing 10 or more persons; from November 2025 the scheme is being extended to all districts, and establishments engaged in hazardous processes are covered even with a single worker.
  • Employees earning wages up to the notified ceiling (currently ₹21,000 a month; higher for persons with disability) are insured persons; coverage includes their dependent family members.

2. Contributions

  • Employer – 3.25% and employee – 0.75% of wages; workers with very low daily wages are exempt from their share.
  • State governments share part of the cost of medical care.

3. Benefits

  • Medical benefit – full medical care (outpatient, inpatient, specialist, drugs, investigations) for the insured person and family from the first day of insurable employment, through ESI dispensaries, hospitals and tie-up hospitals.
  • Sickness benefit – cash payment at about 70% of wages for certified sickness for up to 91 days in a year; extended sickness benefit for certain long-term diseases; enhanced benefit during sterilisation.
  • Maternity benefit – full wages for up to 26 weeks of maternity leave (with shorter periods for miscarriage and for adopting or commissioning mothers), and confinement expenses where facilities are not available.
  • Disablement benefit – temporary disablement benefit (about 90% of wages) during incapacity due to employment injury; permanent disablement benefit in proportion to the loss of earning capacity.
  • Dependants' benefit – monthly payment (about 90% of wages) shared among dependants when an insured person dies due to employment injury.
  • Funeral expenses, unemployment allowance for insured persons who lose their job involuntarily, and vocational and physical rehabilitation.

4. Role of the nurse

  • Provide care in ESI dispensaries and hospitals; educate workers about their entitlements; help in certification, referral and follow-up; encourage registration of eligible workers.

Conclusion The ESI scheme provides workers with comprehensive health care and income security; its expansion under the new labour code brings more workers and families under this protection.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain sickness absenteeism in industry – its measurement, causes and prevention.
answer_html:
Introduction Sickness absenteeism is the absence of a worker from work attributed to sickness by the worker and accepted as such by the employer. It is an important indicator of the health of the workforce and the quality of working conditions.

1. Measurement

  • Frequency – number of spells of sickness absence per 100 workers per year.
  • Severity – average number of days lost per spell or per worker per year.
  • Sickness absence rate – days lost due to sickness as a percentage of the total working days available.
  • Records are kept by the health department and personnel office; patterns are analysed by department, age, season and cause.

2. Causes

  • Medical – respiratory infections, diarrhoeal diseases, injuries, musculoskeletal pain, fevers, chronic diseases (hypertension, diabetes), mental health problems.
  • Occupational – exposure to dust, chemicals, heat and noise; accidents; ergonomic strain; shift work and fatigue.
  • Social – festivals, marriages and other ceremonies, harvest seasons (many industrial workers have farms), family illness, child care responsibilities of women workers.
  • Economic and personal – alcoholism and substance use, indebtedness, long commuting distances, poor housing.
  • Organisational – low morale, job dissatisfaction, poor relations with supervisors, monotony, lack of incentives.

3. Effects – loss of production, extra costs of overtime and replacements, overload on other workers, loss of wages and welfare for the worker.

4. Prevention

  • Health promotion and protection – health education, immunisation, nutrition, safe drinking water and canteens, sanitation, control of workplace hazards, personal protective equipment.
  • Medical examinations – pre-placement, periodic and special examinations; early treatment of illness; management of chronic diseases at the workplace.
  • Welfare measures – housing, transport, crèches, recreation, social security and medical benefits under ESIC.
  • Good management – fair treatment, job rotation, grievance redressal, incentives for good attendance, flexible leave for genuine social needs.
  • Counselling and rehabilitation – for alcohol and drug problems, stress and family problems; employee assistance programmes.
  • Analysis of absence records to identify and correct underlying problems.

5. Role of the occupational health nurse – maintain sickness records, analyse patterns, provide early care, conduct health education and counselling, follow up absent workers and support their return to work.

Conclusion Sickness absenteeism reflects both health and morale. A combination of good occupational health services, welfare measures and supportive management keeps absence low and productivity high.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain the occupational health problems of women workers and the measures for their protection.
answer_html:
Introduction Women form a large part of India's workforce, especially in agriculture, construction, domestic work, garment and food industries and health care. Besides the hazards faced by all workers, they face special problems due to their reproductive role, social position and the double burden of paid work and household responsibilities.

1. Health problems

  • Reproductive hazards – exposure to pesticides, lead, solvents, anaesthetic gases, radiation and heavy physical work can cause abortion, preterm birth, low birth weight and congenital anomalies.
  • Musculoskeletal disorders – from prolonged standing, squatting, carrying heads loads and repetitive work (back pain, varicose veins).
  • Nutritional problems – anaemia and undernutrition, worsened by heavy work and repeated pregnancies.
  • Lack of facilities – no clean toilets or menstrual hygiene facilities, leading to urinary infections and reduced water intake; no crèches.
  • Psychosocial – sexual harassment, discrimination in wages and promotion, long hours, stress and fatigue from the double burden.
  • Unorganised sector – no maternity protection, job insecurity, exposure to violence and trafficking.

2. Measures for protection

  • Maternity protection (now under the Code on Social Security) – paid maternity leave of 26 weeks for the first two children (12 weeks thereafter), benefits for adopting and commissioning mothers, crèche facilities in larger establishments, nursing breaks, and protection from dismissal during maternity.
  • Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 – every workplace with 10 or more employees must have an Internal Committee; a Local Committee at the district level serves smaller workplaces and the unorganised sector.
  • Equal pay for equal work under the Code on Wages.
  • Night work permitted with the woman's consent and with safety, transport and security arrangements under the occupational safety code; protective restrictions on exposure to specific hazards during pregnancy.
  • Welfare facilities – separate toilets, washing and rest rooms, safe drinking water.
  • Social security – ESIC medical and maternity benefits; maternity benefit schemes for unorganised workers; registration on the e-Shram portal.

3. Role of the nurse

  • Health education on nutrition, hygiene, safe work practices and rights; anaemia screening and IFA; antenatal care and counselling on hazards in pregnancy; screening for cervical and breast cancer; support for breastfeeding at work; help in reporting harassment.

Conclusion Protecting women workers protects two generations. Legal safeguards, workplace facilities and sensitive health services ensure that women can work safely without risking their own health or that of their children.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: What is the ICMR-National Institute of Occupational Health (NIOH)? State its functions.
answer_html:
• The ICMR-National Institute of Occupational Health, located at Ahmedabad, is the national institute of the Indian Council of Medical Research for research and services in occupational health, with regional centres in other parts of the country.
  • Functions – research on occupational diseases and hazards (silicosis, pesticide poisoning, heat stress, noise); environmental and biological monitoring of workers; surveillance and field studies; training of doctors, nurses and safety personnel; and technical advice to governments and industries on prevention and control of occupational diseases.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Write the main features of the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020.
tags: Occupational Safety Health and Working Conditions Code 2020
National Occupational Safety and Health Board
answer_html:
• One of the four labour codes in force from 21 November 2025, it merges 13 earlier laws (including the Factories Act and the Mines Act) on safety, health and working conditions.
  • Main features – national safety standards set through a National Occupational Safety and Health Board; safety committees in larger establishments; working hours limited to 48 hours a week; free annual health check-up for workers aged 40 years and above; welfare facilities (drinking water, toilets, canteens, crèches); reporting of accidents and notifiable occupational diseases; women allowed to work at night with consent and safety arrangements; a single registration and licence for employers.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: What are notifiable occupational diseases?
answer_html:
• Notifiable occupational diseases are diseases listed in labour law that the employer and the medical practitioner must report to the authorities (the factory inspectorate) when they occur in a worker.
  • Examples – lead and mercury poisoning, silicosis, asbestosis, byssinosis, coal workers' pneumoconiosis, benzene poisoning, occupational cancers, noise-induced hearing loss, toxic jaundice, anthrax.
  • Notification enables inspection of the workplace, correction of hazards, protection of other workers and compensation to the affected worker.
  • The nurse should know the list and report suspected cases through the medical officer.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: (a) What is comprehensive elderly care? Explain its key components. (8 marks) (b) Describe the National Programme for Health Care of the Elderly (NPHCE). (7 marks)

diagram.caption: Levels of care under the NPHCE
labels: Pyramid with the base "Sub-centre/AAM – domiciliary visits
PG courses" and at the top "National Centres for Ageing (AIIMS New Delhi

answer_html:
Introduction India's elderly population (60 years and above) is growing rapidly – from 8.6% of the population in 2011 to a much larger share in the coming decades – because of falling fertility and rising life expectancy. Older people have multiple chronic diseases, disabilities and social and economic needs. Comprehensive elderly care is a holistic, continuous and coordinated approach that addresses all these needs, delivered as close to home as possible.

(a) Comprehensive elderly care and its key components Comprehensive elderly care is the integrated provision of promotive, preventive, curative, rehabilitative, long-term and palliative services, together with social, psychological and financial support, to maintain the older person's functional ability and quality of life, centred on the person and the family.

1. Health promotion and healthy ageing

  • Balanced diet with adequate protein, calcium, vitamin D and fluids; regular physical activity (walking, yoga, balance exercises); adequate sleep.
  • Avoiding tobacco and alcohol; social participation; lifelong learning; spiritual well-being.
  • The WHO Decade of Healthy Ageing (2021–2030) promotes maintaining functional ability.

2. Prevention and screening

  • Screening for hypertension, diabetes, common cancers, cataract, hearing loss, osteoporosis risk, depression, dementia and falls risk.
  • Immunisation (influenza and pneumococcal vaccines where available; tetanus).
  • The WHO Integrated Care for Older People (ICOPE) approach screens six domains of intrinsic capacity – cognition, mobility, nutrition, vision, hearing and psychological well-being – and links any decline to a personalised care plan.

3. Curative care

  • Accessible primary care at the AAM, with weekly geriatric clinics at the PHC and specialist geriatric services at higher levels.
  • Rational prescribing and review of polypharmacy; management of chronic diseases; priority queues and age-friendly facilities.

4. Rehabilitation

  • Physiotherapy and occupational therapy after stroke, fractures and arthritis.
  • Aids and appliances – spectacles, hearing aids, walking sticks, walkers, wheelchairs, dentures.

5. Long-term care

  • Domiciliary (home-based) care of the bedridden by health workers and trained family caregivers.
  • Day-care centres, respite care and institutional care in old-age homes for those without family support.

6. Palliative and end-of-life care – pain and symptom relief, psychological and spiritual support, advance care planning and dignified death, through community-based palliative care.

7. Mental health – prevention and early detection of depression, anxiety, dementia and loneliness; counselling; support groups.

8. Social support and protection

  • Family and community support, senior citizens' associations, intergenerational activities.
  • Prevention of elder abuse and neglect; legal protection under the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007; the national helpline for senior citizens (Elderline 14567).

9. Financial protection – old-age pensions; health insurance – all citizens aged 70 years and above are entitled to Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY coverage (Ayushman Vay Vandana card) regardless of income.

10. Caregiver support and age-friendly environments – training and respite for family caregivers; ramps, rails, good lighting and accessible transport.

(b) National Programme for Health Care of the Elderly (NPHCE)

  • Launched by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare in 2010–11, in line with the National Policy on Older Persons and the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act.
  • Vision – to provide accessible, affordable, high-quality, long-term, comprehensive and dedicated care to an ageing population, to create a new "architecture" for ageing, and to promote active and healthy ageing.
  • Objectives
    • easy access to promotive, preventive, curative and rehabilitative services through a community-based primary health care approach;
    • identification of health problems of the elderly and their appropriate management;
    • referral services through district hospitals and regional medical institutions;
    • training of health personnel and caregivers; convergence with NHM, AYUSH and the Ministry of Social Justice.
  • Service delivery at different levels
    • Sub-centre/AAM – the ANM and male health worker make domiciliary visits to the elderly and bedridden, give health education, screen, provide simple aids and appliances and train caregivers; elderly and palliative care is one of the service packages of AAMs.
    • PHC – a weekly geriatric clinic by a trained medical officer, screening and management of common problems, and referral.
    • CHC – a geriatric clinic, rehabilitation unit with physiotherapy, and the first referral unit for the elderly.
    • District hospital – geriatric OPD, a 10-bedded geriatric ward, physiotherapy and rehabilitation, and laboratory services.
    • Regional Geriatric Centres – established in 19 medical colleges in 18 states, with a dedicated geriatric OPD, a 30-bedded geriatric ward, postgraduate courses in geriatric medicine, training and research.
    • National Centres for Ageing – two apex centres at AIIMS, New Delhi and Madras Medical College, Chennai, for advanced care, training and research. The tertiary component is known as the Rashtriya Varishth Jan Swasthya Yojana.
  • Other components – IEC on healthy ageing, capacity building of health workers, provision of equipment and drugs, and monitoring through the NCD and NHM systems.

Role of the community health nurse

  • Prepare a register of the elderly in her area and identify the bedridden, those living alone and the frail.
  • Screen for chronic diseases, functional decline, depression and dementia; ensure follow-up and medication adherence.
  • Teach families home care, fall prevention, nutrition and exercise; arrange aids and appliances.
  • Link the elderly to pensions, PM-JAY, helplines and social welfare schemes; detect and report abuse.

Common health problems of the elderly – hypertension, diabetes, heart disease, stroke, arthritis, osteoporosis and fractures, cataract and hearing loss, chronic respiratory disease, cancers, urinary problems, dementia, depression, malnutrition, dental problems and falls; many have several conditions at once (multimorbidity).

Challenges in providing elderly care in India – the "feminisation" of ageing (more widows, often poor and dependent), most elderly living in rural areas, migration of younger family members, poverty and lack of pensions, shortage of geriatric specialists and trained caregivers, poor access to transport and facilities, and neglect or abuse.

Example of a comprehensive care plan – a 72-year-old widow living alone has knee arthritis, hypertension and poor vision. The nurse checks her BP and adherence, arranges cataract surgery and a walking stick, teaches knee exercises, makes the house safer (lighting, bathroom rails), links her to the old-age pension and the PM-JAY card, involves a neighbour and the local self-help group for daily contact, gives her the Elderline number and visits monthly.

Principles of comprehensive elderly care – person-centred (based on the older person's own goals), continuous (follow-up over time), coordinated (between home, AAM, hospital and social services), accessible and affordable, respectful of dignity and autonomy, and involving the family and community.

Community participation – senior citizens' associations, day-care and recreation centres run by panchayats or NGOs, volunteer visitors for those living alone, and intergenerational programmes with schools reduce isolation and keep older people active.

Conclusion Comprehensive elderly care looks beyond disease to function, independence and dignity. The NPHCE provides a structure for delivering this care from the home to tertiary centres, and the community health nurse is the key link at the first level.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain the screening of older adults in the community for functional decline and common geriatric problems.
answer_html:
Introduction Many problems of old age – loss of vision or hearing, falls, memory loss, depression, malnutrition – develop slowly and are dismissed as "normal ageing". Simple screening during home visits or at the AAM detects them early, when help can still preserve independence.

1. Functional ability

  • Activities of daily living (ADL) – bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, continence and feeding (Katz index).
  • Instrumental ADL (IADL) – using the telephone, shopping, cooking, housework, managing money and medicines, travelling (Lawton scale).
  • Decline in IADL is often the first sign of illness or cognitive impairment.

2. Mobility and falls risk

  • Ask about falls in the past year and fear of falling.
  • Timed Up and Go test – the person rises from a chair, walks 3 metres, turns, returns and sits; taking more than about 12 seconds suggests an increased risk of falls.
  • Check gait, balance, footwear and home hazards.

3. Vision and hearing

  • Vision chart or finger counting at a distance; ask about difficulty reading or recognising faces (cataract, refractive error, glaucoma).
  • Whisper test or simple questions about hearing difficulty; check for wax.

4. Cognition

  • Mini-Cog – recall of three words after a clock-drawing task; difficulty suggests the need for further evaluation for dementia.
  • Ask family members about forgetfulness, getting lost or repeating questions.

5. Mood

  • Two-question screen for depression (low mood and loss of interest in the past two weeks) or a short geriatric depression scale; ask about loneliness and thoughts of death.

6. Nutrition

  • Weight and BMI; unintentional weight loss; appetite; dental problems; mid-arm circumference.

7. Other areas

  • Urinary incontinence and constipation; review of all medicines (polypharmacy); oral health; BP, blood sugar and other NCD screening; skin and feet.
  • Social situation – living alone, caregiver support, finances; signs of elder abuse or neglect.

8. Integrated approach – the WHO ICOPE screening covers cognition, mobility, nutrition, vision, hearing and psychological well-being; any positive finding is followed by a fuller assessment and a care plan.

9. Action after screening – health education and simple interventions at home; referral to the PHC geriatric clinic, CHC rehabilitation unit or district geriatric unit; arrangement of aids; regular follow-up visits; records in the elderly register.

Conclusion Regular, simple screening of older adults in the community identifies treatable problems early and helps them remain independent and active for longer.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain the primary management of common geriatric ailments at the Ayushman Arogya Mandir – counselling and supportive treatment.
answer_html:
Introduction Most older people first seek help for common, chronic complaints that affect their comfort and independence. At the AAM, the CHO and nurse can relieve many of these with counselling, lifestyle advice and simple, safe treatment, while referring those who need specialist care.

1. Joint pain and osteoarthritis

  • Weight reduction, regular gentle exercises (quadriceps strengthening, range-of-motion), warm compresses, knee supports, a walking stick in the opposite hand.
  • Paracetamol as per protocol; avoid long-term painkillers (NSAIDs) because of kidney and stomach effects; refer for severe deformity or physiotherapy.

2. Sleep problems

  • Sleep hygiene – regular timings, daytime activity, avoiding long day-time naps, tea or coffee in the evening and heavy meals at night; treat pain, frequent urination or depression.
  • Avoid sleeping tablets, which increase confusion and falls.

3. Constipation

  • Fibre, fluids, activity, a regular toilet routine; review drugs causing constipation; mild laxative as per orders; refer for bleeding or weight loss.

4. Urinary problems

  • Incontinence – bladder training, scheduled toileting, pelvic floor exercises, treating constipation and urinary infection, easy access to the toilet, absorbent pads and skin care.
  • Men with poor stream, frequency or retention (prostate enlargement) – refer for evaluation.

5. Vision and hearing problems

  • Refer for cataract surgery and spectacles under the blindness control programme; refer for hearing aids; remove wax as per protocol; advise good lighting and face-to-face communication.

6. Dizziness and falls

  • Check BP lying and standing (postural hypotension), blood sugar and medicines; advise rising slowly, home safety (lighting, non-slip floors, rails), proper footwear and balance exercises.

7. Memory complaints, loneliness and low mood

  • Screen for depression and dementia; encourage social activities, senior citizens' groups and family involvement; refer for evaluation; teach caregivers.

8. Medication management

  • Review all medicines at each visit; simplify regimens; use pill boxes; check for side-effects and duplication.

9. When to refer – sudden confusion, chest pain, breathlessness, weakness of a limb, a fall with injury or inability to walk, weight loss, blood in urine or stool, or any condition not improving.

Conclusion Patient counselling and safe, simple treatment at the AAM can greatly improve the comfort and independence of older people, provided warning signs are recognised and referred promptly.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: What is the Rashtriya Varishth Jan Swasthya Yojana? Name the National Centres for Ageing.
answer_html:
• The Rashtriya Varishth Jan Swasthya Yojana is the name given (in 2016–17) to the tertiary-care component of the NPHCE.
  • Under it, Regional Geriatric Centres function in 19 medical colleges in 18 states with geriatric OPDs, 30-bedded wards and postgraduate training in geriatric medicine.
  • Two National Centres for Ageing – at AIIMS, New Delhi and Madras Medical College, Chennai – provide advanced geriatric care, training and research.
  • They also develop training modules and guide the lower levels of the programme.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: What is the WHO Integrated Care for Older People (ICOPE) approach?
answer_html:
• ICOPE is a WHO approach for community and primary care that aims to maintain the functional ability of older people by preventing declines in their intrinsic capacity.
  • It screens six domains – cognition, mobility, nutrition (vitality), vision, hearing and psychological well-being – using simple questions and tests.
  • Any decline leads to a fuller assessment and a person-centred care plan, involving the family and community, with regular follow-up.
  • It can be used by nurses and community health workers.
  • India's AAM elderly care package follows a similar approach.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain the role of the community health nurse in the screening, early identification, initiation of treatment and follow-up of persons with common mental disorders in the community – depression, anxiety, acute psychosis, schizophrenia, dementia, suicide risk and alcohol and substance use.
tags: mental neurological and substance use disorders
initiation of treatment as per protocol
answer_html:
Introduction Mental disorders are common in every village and town, but most affected persons never receive treatment because of stigma, lack of awareness and the shortage of specialists. The community health nurse, CHO and ASHA, working through the Ayushman Arogya Mandirs and the District Mental Health Programme, can close this "treatment gap" by screening, early identification, initiating care as per protocol, referral and long-term follow-up.

1. Community awareness and case finding

  • Health talks and IEC to explain that mental illness is common and treatable; reduce stigma and myths (possession, black magic).
  • Involve ASHAs, teachers, self-help groups, religious and community leaders as "eyes and ears" to identify persons who are withdrawn, behaving unusually, misusing alcohol or talking of death.

2. Screening at the AAM and during home visits

Condition Simple screening tool Positive finding
Depression PHQ-2, followed by PHQ-9 Low mood or loss of interest for two weeks; PHQ-9 score of 10 or more
Anxiety GAD-2, followed by GAD-7 Excessive worry, nervousness; GAD-7 score of 10 or more
Alcohol use AUDIT-C Score of 4 or more in men, 3 or more in women
Dementia Mini-Cog, history from family Poor recall or abnormal clock drawing
Psychosis Observation and history Hallucinations, delusions, disorganised behaviour
Suicide risk Asking directly about thoughts, plans and past attempts Any current plan or recent attempt
  • Screening is offered especially to persons with chronic illness, postnatal mothers, the elderly, adolescents and persons under stress (debt, crop failure, bereavement).

3. Early identification and initial management of specific conditions

  • Depression – persistent sadness, loss of interest, sleep and appetite changes, fatigue, hopelessness. Counselling (problem-solving, behavioural activation), family support, refer to the medical officer/DMHP for antidepressants; follow up adherence.
  • Anxiety – excessive worry, palpitations, restlessness; reassurance, relaxation and breathing exercises, address stressors; refer if severe or with panic attacks.
  • Acute psychosis – sudden onset of strange behaviour, hallucinations, agitation. Ensure safety of the person and others, rule out fever, injury or substance use, refer urgently to the DMHP or district hospital; never use chains or confinement.
  • Schizophrenia (chronic) – after diagnosis and prescription by the psychiatrist, the nurse ensures continuation of antipsychotic medicines, monitors side-effects (stiffness, tremor, restlessness), and teaches the family early relapse signs (sleeplessness, withdrawal, suspiciousness, stopping medicines).
  • Dementia – progressive memory loss and difficulty in daily activities; refer for evaluation; teach caregivers about safety, routine, nutrition, communication and their own stress.
  • Suicide risk – ask directly and calmly; do not leave a person with a plan alone; remove means (pesticides, medicines, ropes); involve the family; refer the same day; give the Tele-MANAS helpline (14416); follow up after any attempt.
  • Alcohol and substance use – brief intervention (feedback, advice, setting goals); refer for detoxification and treatment; watch for withdrawal fits or delirium; involve the family; link to de-addiction services and self-help groups.

4. Initiating and continuing treatment as per protocol
