  • Under the national mental health programme, medicines for common mental disorders are available at the AAM and PHC; the CHO and nurse continue and dispense treatment prescribed by the medical officer or psychiatrist as per standard protocols, and manage simple side-effects.
  • Tele-consultation (eSanjeevani, Tele-MANAS) links the AAM with specialists.

5. Follow-up and rehabilitation

  • Regular home visits to check adherence, side-effects, improvement and relapse signs; a reminder system for review dates.
  • Psychoeducation of the family – nature of the illness, importance of medicines, coping with difficult behaviour, avoiding criticism and over-involvement.
  • Psychosocial rehabilitation – return to school or work, vocational training, self-help groups, disability certificates and welfare benefits.
  • Physical health care of persons with severe mental illness (NCD screening, tobacco cessation).

6. Protection of rights

  • Respect dignity, confidentiality and informed consent; prevent chaining and abuse; inform families about free treatment and rights under the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017.

7. Records and reporting – register of persons with mental illness in the area, treatment cards, referral and follow-up records, monthly reports to the DMHP.

Magnitude – national surveys show that a significant proportion of adults in India have a mental disorder, with depression, anxiety and substance use the commonest, and a treatment gap of more than 70% for most conditions.

Brief intervention for alcohol and substance use (5 As) – Ask about use; Advise clearly and personally; Assess readiness to change; Assist with a plan, coping skills and referral; Arrange follow-up. Brief interventions of 5–15 minutes reduce harmful drinking.

Communication skills – a calm, private setting; active listening without interrupting; empathy and non-judgemental language; simple explanations; involving the client in decisions; avoiding arguments with a person who has delusions; giving hope.

Example – during a postnatal home visit, the ASHA notices that a mother is tearful, not sleeping and not caring for herself. The nurse screens her with the PHQ-9 (score 16), asks about thoughts of self-harm, refers her the same day to the medical officer and DMHP team, counsels the husband and mother-in-law, ensures breastfeeding support and follows her up weekly.

Referral pathway – ASHA → nurse/CHO at the AAM → medical officer at the PHC → DMHP team or district hospital psychiatry unit → medical college or mental health institute; tele-consultation through Tele-MANAS at any level.

Care of the caregiver – family members caring for persons with severe mental illness or dementia often suffer stress and depression; the nurse listens to them, teaches coping skills, links them to support groups and respite services, and screens them too.

Special groups needing attention – postnatal mothers (perinatal depression), adolescents (examination stress, self-harm, substance use), the elderly (depression and dementia), persons with chronic illness or disability, victims of violence and disasters, migrants and the homeless mentally ill; each group needs targeted screening and outreach.

Monitoring indicators – number of persons screened, identified and referred; number on regular treatment; drop-outs traced; suicide attempts followed up; and community awareness activities held.

Self-care for the nurse – working with distressed clients is emotionally demanding; the nurse needs supervision, peer support and attention to her own mental health to provide sustained, empathetic care.

Mental health promotion – promoting life skills in schools, stress management for workers and farmers, support groups for women, healthy parenting and community activities builds resilience and prevents many mental disorders.

Nursing importance

  • Early detection and continued treatment in the community prevent chronic disability, suicide and family breakdown.
  • Task-sharing with trained nurses and CHOs is the only practical way to reach the large number of people needing mental health care.
  • Integration of mental health into primary care reduces stigma and cost.

Conclusion With simple screening tools, protocols for initial care, clear referral pathways and regular follow-up, the community health nurse becomes the backbone of community mental health care, ensuring that persons with mental disorders are identified, treated and supported close to home.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain the Drug De-addiction Programme and the services for drug demand reduction in India, with the role of the community health nurse.
tags: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
National Action Plan for Drug Demand Reduction
Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment
answer_html:
Introduction Substance use – alcohol, cannabis, opioids, inhalants and sedatives – is a major public health and social problem in India. The government responds through a health-sector treatment programme and a social-sector demand-reduction programme, supported by law enforcement.

1. Drug De-addiction Programme (DDAP) – Ministry of Health and Family Welfare

  • Started in the late 1980s to provide treatment for substance use disorders through de-addiction centres in government hospitals and medical colleges.
  • The National Drug Dependence Treatment Centre (NDDTC), AIIMS is the apex centre for treatment, training, research and national surveys.
  • Addiction treatment facilities in government hospitals provide outpatient treatment, including medicine-assisted treatment for opioid dependence (for example, buprenorphine), with training and support from NDDTC.
  • Treatment of substance use is also part of the District Mental Health Programme and of services at medical colleges.

2. National Action Plan for Drug Demand Reduction (NAPDDR) – Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment

  • Integrated Rehabilitation Centres for Addicts (IRCAs) – residential treatment and rehabilitation run with NGOs.
  • Outreach and Drop-in Centres (ODICs) and Community Peer-Led Interventions – screening, counselling and referral, especially for adolescents and youth.
  • District De-addiction Centres in districts lacking facilities; de-addiction services in prisons.
  • Awareness programmes in schools, colleges and communities; capacity building of service providers.

3. Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan – a nationwide campaign launched in 2020, first in the most affected districts and later extended across the country, mobilising youth, educational institutions, NGOs and communities against substance use; a national toll-free helpline (14446) offers counselling and referral.

4. Legal support – under the NDPS Act, a person dependent on drugs who volunteers for treatment is protected from prosecution (section 64A), encouraging people to seek help.

5. Role of the community health nurse

  • Screening for tobacco, alcohol and drug use during routine contacts (AUDIT-C and simple questions).
  • Brief intervention – give feedback, advise reduction or abstinence, help set goals, and follow up.
  • Referral to de-addiction centres, addiction treatment facilities or IRCAs; recognition and urgent referral of withdrawal emergencies (fits, delirium) and overdose.
  • Follow-up after treatment – encourage adherence, attendance at self-help groups (Alcoholics Anonymous, Narcotics Anonymous) and relapse prevention.
  • Family counselling – support for spouse and children, dealing with co-dependency and violence.
  • Prevention – life-skills education in schools, awareness campaigns, working with youth clubs and panchayats.

Conclusion Treatment through the health-sector de-addiction programme and rehabilitation and awareness through the demand-reduction programme together form India's response to substance use; the community health nurse connects individuals and families to these services and supports their recovery.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: What is AUDIT-C? How is it interpreted?
tags: alcohol use disorders identification test consumption
answer_html:
• AUDIT-C is a short three-question screening test for hazardous drinking, derived from the WHO Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test.
  • It asks about how often the person drinks, how many drinks on a typical drinking day, and how often six or more drinks are taken on one occasion; each is scored 0–4 (total 0–12).
  • A score of 4 or more in men and 3 or more in women is considered positive and calls for brief intervention or full assessment; higher scores indicate greater risk.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: List the "red flags" in a person with a mental disorder that need urgent referral.
answer_html:
• Suicidal thoughts with a plan, or a recent suicide attempt.
  • Violence or threats to harm others; severe agitation.
  • Refusal to eat or drink, extreme withdrawal or catatonic stupor.
  • Sudden confusion with fever or physical illness (delirium).
  • First episode of psychosis, or psychosis after childbirth (postpartum psychosis).
  • Severe drug side-effects – high fever with stiffness, severe tremor or vomiting in a person on lithium.
  • Alcohol or drug withdrawal with fits or delirium.
  • Severe self-neglect, or abuse and chaining by others.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Who is a "gatekeeper" in suicide prevention?
answer_html:
• A gatekeeper is any community member who comes in regular contact with people – such as teachers, ASHAs, anganwadi workers, pharmacists, police, religious and community leaders – and who is trained to recognise the warning signs of suicide.
  • Gatekeepers ask directly about suicidal thoughts, persuade the person to seek help, and refer them to health services or helplines (the "question, persuade, refer" approach).
  • Gatekeeper training is an important community strategy under the national suicide prevention strategy.
  • ASHAs and nurses can train such gatekeepers.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: (a) Explain the Health Management Information System (HMIS) – its meaning, objectives and data elements. (5 marks) (b) Describe the recording and reporting formats and the flow of information from the sub-centre to the national level. (6 marks) (c) Explain the common data quality issues and the measures to improve data quality. (4 marks)

diagram.caption: Flow of information in the HMIS
labels: Bottom-to-top flow chart – ASHA (village) → ANM/CHO at the sub-centre/AAM (registers
medical officer) → block (data manager) → district (district programme management unit
HMIS portal) → state → Ministry of Health and Family Welfare; a return arrow on the side labelled "feedback

answer_html:
Introduction Every day, health workers record thousands of services – ANC visits, deliveries, vaccinations, treatments. A health management information system (HMIS) converts these records into information that managers at every level use to plan, monitor and improve services. In India, a web-based HMIS was introduced under the National Rural Health Mission, through which every public health facility reports its services monthly.

(a) Meaning, objectives and data elements

  • Meaning – HMIS is an organised system for the collection, compilation, analysis, transmission and use of health-service data, so that decisions are based on evidence.
  • Objectives
    • to provide timely, reliable information on the performance of health facilities and programmes;
    • to monitor progress against targets and indicators of the National Health Mission;
    • to identify gaps, under-served areas and high-risk groups;
    • to support planning (district health action plans, state programme implementation plans) and allocation of resources;
    • to provide information for evaluation, research and accountability.
  • Data elements – a data element is a single item of data collected, such as "number of pregnant women registered in the first trimester" or "number of children given measles–rubella first dose". HMIS formats contain data elements on:
    • reproductive and maternal health – ANC registration, visits, tests, high-risk cases, deliveries (place, type), postnatal care;
    • newborn and child health – live births, birth weight, breastfeeding, immunisation, childhood diseases, deaths;
    • family planning – methods provided, complications, failures;
    • disease control programmes – malaria, TB, leprosy, NCD screening;
    • outpatient and inpatient services, laboratory tests, surgeries;
    • infrastructure, human resources, drugs and equipment (in periodic formats).
  • Indicators are calculated from data elements (for example, percentage of pregnant women registered in the first trimester = first-trimester registrations ÷ total ANC registrations × 100).

(b) Recording and reporting formats and flow of information 1. Recording at the sub-centre/AAM

  • Eligible couple register and family planning register.
  • Maternal and child health register – ANC, delivery and postnatal care.
  • Immunisation register and due lists; birth and death register.
  • OPD and treatment register, NCD screening records (including the community-based assessment checklist), drug and stock registers, cold chain records.
  • ASHA diaries and village health registers; MCP cards held by families.
  • Increasingly, records are entered directly into tablets or portals (RCH portal, NCD application, Ni-kshay for TB, the AAM portal and the IHIP for surveillance).

2. Reporting formats

  • Monthly service delivery report for each facility type – sub-centre, PHC, CHC, sub-district and district hospital – with standard data elements.
  • Quarterly and annual formats for infrastructure, human resources and facility profile.
  • Programme-specific reports and weekly surveillance reports (S, P and L forms under the integrated disease surveillance programme).
  • Immediate reporting of events such as maternal deaths, outbreaks and adverse events following immunisation.

3. Flow of information

  • ASHA → ANM/CHO (sub-centre/AAM) – the ANM compiles village data and prepares the monthly report.
  • Sub-centre → PHC – the PHC compiles reports of all its sub-centres and its own services; the medical officer verifies them.
  • PHC → block → district – data are entered on the HMIS portal facility-wise; the district data manager checks completeness and quality.
  • District → state → national – the state and the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare analyse the data, prepare dashboards and scorecards and use them in reviews.
  • Feedback – analysed information and rankings flow back to districts, blocks and facilities for corrective action; without feedback, the system becomes a burden rather than a tool.

(c) Data quality issues and their improvement Common issues

  • Incompleteness – missing reports or missing data elements, non-reporting by private facilities.
  • Delay – reports submitted late.
  • Inaccuracy – arithmetic errors, wrong entries, double counting, guesswork, inflated figures to show achievement of targets.
  • Inconsistency – different figures for the same item in different registers or portals; illogical data (more deliveries than ANC registrations).
  • Poor use of data – data collected only for reporting and not analysed or used locally.
  • Heavy workload due to multiple registers and portals; lack of training and IT support.

Measures for improvement

  • Standard definitions in a data dictionary; simplified, integrated formats; reducing duplication by linking portals through the digital health mission.
  • Built-in validation rules in the portal to flag impossible values.
  • Regular data quality assessments and verification of reports against registers during supervision visits.
  • Training and supportive supervision of ANMs, CHOs and data operators; timely feedback.
  • Triangulation with surveys (NFHS, SRS) and programme data.
  • Monthly review meetings at the PHC and block in which the data are discussed and acted upon, building a culture of data use.

Role of the nurse

  • Records every service accurately at the time it is given; maintains registers neatly and completely.
  • Prepares and submits reports on time; cross-checks totals before submission.
  • Uses her own data to identify gaps – drop-outs, low coverage hamlets – and plans action.
  • Participates in review meetings and data quality checks.

Uses of HMIS data at different levels

  • Sub-centre/AAM – preparing due lists and micro-plans, tracking drop-outs, identifying hamlets with poor coverage.
  • PHC and block – comparing the performance of sub-centres, planning supervision visits, assessing drug and vaccine needs.
  • District – preparing the district health action plan, ranking blocks, deciding where to place staff and resources, detecting unusual trends.
  • State and national – monitoring programme indicators, allocating funds, evaluating policies and reporting on national and SDG targets.

Example of data use – the PHC's monthly review shows that one sub-centre has only 70% full immunisation compared with 92% elsewhere; disaggregation reveals that a brick-kiln settlement is missed. The ANM revises her micro-plan, adds an outreach session at the kiln and the ASHA mobilises families; coverage rises within three months.

Link with digital health – under the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission, individuals receive a digital health ID and facilities and professionals are entered in national registries, allowing records from different programmes to be linked over time, reducing duplicate entries.

Confidentiality and security – health data are personal; registers must be kept safely, passwords protected, and information shared only with authorised persons and for authorised purposes.

Qualities of a good HMIS – simple and standardised formats, a minimum essential data set, timely flow, built-in analysis and feedback, linkage between programmes, trained users and a clear focus on decision-making rather than on collecting data for its own sake.

Private-sector reporting – private hospitals and clinics provide a large share of services; their reporting of notifiable diseases, births, deaths and key services into the national systems is essential for a complete picture of community health.

Nursing importance

  • Accurate data protect the community – a missed high-risk pregnancy or an unreported outbreak can cost lives.
  • Good records also protect the nurse legally and show the value of her work.

Conclusion HMIS links the work of the health worker in the village to decisions taken at the district, state and national levels. Its value depends on the quality of data recorded at the grassroots and on how well that information is analysed and used, at every level, to improve services.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain the analysis of community data for a needs assessment and the preparation of a health action plan for a sub-centre/village.
answer_html:
Introduction A health action plan is a written plan stating what health problems will be addressed in an area, how, by whom, when and with what resources. It is prepared after a community needs assessment – the systematic collection and analysis of data about the health status and needs of the community.

1. Collection of data – community survey (households, population by age and sex, eligible couples, pregnant women, children, elderly, persons with chronic illness or disability); sub-centre registers and HMIS reports; environmental data (water, sanitation); discussions with the VHSNC, ASHAs, self-help groups and leaders.

2. Analysis of data

  • Calculate indicators – registration of pregnancies in the first trimester, institutional deliveries, full immunisation, contraceptive use, NCD screening coverage, births and deaths.
  • Estimate expected numbers using the population and birth rate (for example, a population of 5,000 with a birth rate of about 18 per 1,000 gives about 90 births and about 100 pregnancies a year).
  • Compare achievements with expected numbers, previous years and district or state averages.
  • Disaggregate by hamlet, caste or tribe, and age group to find pockets of low coverage.
  • Identify gaps and problems – for example, only 60% of expected pregnancies registered; low immunisation in a migrant settlement; many cases of diarrhoea in one hamlet.

3. Prioritisation – rank problems by magnitude, seriousness, vulnerability of the affected group, feasibility of action and community concern (a simple scoring matrix can be used).

4. Preparing the action plan – for each priority problem write:

  • objective (specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound) – for example, "to increase first-trimester ANC registration from 60% to 85% within one year";
  • activities – house-to-house survey by ASHAs, use of pregnancy testing kits, monthly ANC sessions at the VHSND, counselling of newly married women;
  • responsible person, timeline, resources (staff, materials, funds from untied grants) and indicators for monitoring.

5. Implementation, monitoring and evaluation – carry out activities; review progress monthly at sub-centre and VHSNC meetings; revise the plan; evaluate at the end of the year.

Conclusion Careful analysis of community data turns numbers into priorities, and a clear action plan turns priorities into results that the community can see.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Differentiate between a data element and an indicator, with examples.
answer_html:
• A data element is a single, raw item of data that is counted and recorded – for example, "number of pregnant women registered in the first trimester" or "number of children fully immunised this month".
  • An indicator is a measure calculated from data elements, usually as a rate, ratio or percentage, that shows the level of performance or health status – for example, "percentage of pregnant women registered in the first trimester" or "full immunisation coverage (%)".
  • Indicators allow comparison between areas and over time; data elements are their building blocks (numerators and denominators).

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: How is the expected number of pregnancies, births and infants estimated for a sub-centre area?
answer_html:
• Expected live births = population × crude birth rate ÷ 1,000; for a sub-centre population of 5,000 and a birth rate of 18 per 1,000, about 90 births a year.
  • Expected pregnancies = expected births plus about 10% (to allow for abortions and stillbirths) – about 99–100 pregnancies a year.
  • Expected infants for immunisation are taken as equal to the expected live births (about 90).
  • These figures act as denominators for planning sessions, vaccines and supplies and for judging coverage.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Delivery of Community Health Services
question: (a) Explain the planning of health services at the sub-centre/AAM, PHC and CHC levels. (5 marks) (b) Describe the budgeting and the sources of funds for these facilities. (5 marks) (c) Explain material management, including drugs, equipment and supplies, at the sub-centre and PHC. (5 marks)
answer_html:
Introduction Primary health facilities must deliver a wide range of services with limited staff, money and supplies. Good planning, budgeting and material management ensure that the right services, staff, drugs and equipment are available to the community at the right time. The nurse, CHO and ANM are directly involved in all three at the sub-centre and PHC.

(a) Planning of health services 1. Bottom-up planning under the National Health Mission

  • Village health plan prepared with the Village Health, Sanitation and Nutrition Committee (VHSNC) on the basis of local needs.
  • Sub-centre/AAM action plan – prepared by the CHO and ANM from the community needs assessment: expected pregnancies, births and children, eligible couples, NCD screening population, and the services, sessions and supplies needed.
  • PHC and block plans – compiled from the sub-centre plans, with the PHC's own requirements (staff, equipment, drugs, training, outreach, referral transport).
  • District health action plan – integrates all block plans and programme needs.
  • State programme implementation plan (PIP) – prepared annually from district plans, submitted to the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, and approved with a record of proceedings that becomes the basis for releasing funds.

2. Steps of planning at the facility level

  • Situation analysis (population, health status, existing resources, gaps); fixing priorities; setting objectives and targets using expected numbers; planning activities (clinics, VHSND sessions, home visits, campaigns, screening); assigning responsibilities; estimating resources; preparing a calendar (micro-plan); and deciding indicators for monitoring.
  • Specific micro-plans are prepared for immunisation, NCD screening, family planning and outreach to hard-to-reach areas.

(b) Budgeting and sources of funds 1. Budget – a financial plan estimating expected income and expenditure for a year; prepared on the basis of needs, norms, previous expenditure and approved activities.

2. Sources of funds

  • State government budget – salaries of regular staff, buildings, drugs and routine running costs.
  • National Health Mission funds – shared between the Centre and states (generally 60:40, and 90:10 for north-eastern and Himalayan states) for programme activities, contractual staff, training, incentives to ASHAs, free entitlements and infrastructure.
  • Untied funds and annual maintenance grants for sub-centres/AAMs, PHCs and CHCs – used flexibly for local needs such as minor repairs, cleanliness, emergency supplies, referral transport in emergencies and patient amenities, with approval of the facility committee (Jan Arogya Samiti or Rogi Kalyan Samiti) and proper records.
  • Funds of the facility committee – user charges where applicable, donations and grants.
  • Grants through local bodies – health grants recommended by the Finance Commission, released through panchayats and urban local bodies for primary health infrastructure and diagnostics.
  • Pradhan Mantri Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission (PM-ABHIM) – a centrally sponsored scheme for strengthening primary, secondary and tertiary health infrastructure and disease surveillance.
  • Performance-linked payments to AAM teams based on agreed service indicators.

3. Budget process – preparation of estimates → approval → release of funds → expenditure as per guidelines → accounting and statement of expenditure → utilisation certificate → audit.

(c) Material management 1. Drugs and consumables

  • Facility-specific essential medicines lists under the free drugs service initiative (for example, about 105 medicines at a sub-centre-level AAM) and a list of free diagnostic tests (about 14 at the sub-centre).
  • Indenting – estimate monthly needs from consumption plus a buffer stock; indent through the PHC or the online drugs and vaccines distribution management system.
  • Receipt – check quantity, batch number, expiry date and condition; enter in the stock register.
  • Storage – clean, dry, cool, well-ventilated store; shelves off the floor; protection from light, rodents and dampness; labelled bins; separate storage for vaccines (cold chain) and for expired items.
  • Issue – follow FEFO (first expiry, first out); keep a daily issue register; maintain minimum and maximum stock levels; avoid stock-outs and overstocking.

  • Monitoring – monthly physical stock verification; reporting near-expiry items for redistribution; condemnation and safe disposal of expired drugs as per rules. 2. Equipment

  • Inventory (dead-stock) register of all equipment and furniture; periodic checking; preventive maintenance through the biomedical equipment maintenance programme; repair requests; condemnation of unserviceable items through a committee. 3. Vaccines and cold chain – ice-lined refrigerators, deep freezers, vaccine carriers and ice packs; twice-daily temperature recording; stock and wastage records. 4. Linen, stationery, registers and IEC materials – stock registers and periodic indents.

Example – immunisation micro-plan at a sub-centre

  • List all villages and hamlets with their populations; estimate the expected number of infants and pregnant women; fix session sites and days (for example, every Wednesday by rotation); assign the ASHA and AWW for mobilisation; estimate vaccine, syringe and diluent needs; plan alternate vaccine delivery from the PHC; prepare a due list for each session; include hard-to-reach and migrant areas; define a plan for tracking drop-outs.

Planning tools – activity calendars and Gantt charts, simple tables of who will do what and when, and a SWOT analysis (strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats) of the facility help to make plans realistic.

Community participation in planning – the VHSNC and the Jan Arogya Samiti identify local priorities, approve the use of untied funds and monitor services; public hearings and social audits make the facility accountable to the community.

Documentation of materials – stock register and bin cards for drugs, issue register, indent book, dead-stock (inventory) register for equipment, cold chain temperature log, vaccine stock register, condemnation register, and records of untied fund expenditure with bills and vouchers.

Example – preventing stock-outs at an AAM – the CHO reviews the stock register every week, notes that the stock of antihypertensive tablets will last only ten days because of increased screening, raises an indent through the online system, borrows a buffer from the PHC and informs the pharmacist; no patient misses treatment.

Financial records and accountability – every expenditure from untied or programme funds is supported by approval of the committee, bills and vouchers, cash book entries and a monthly statement of expenditure; utilisation certificates are sent to the PHC/block; funds are used only for permitted purposes; records are kept ready for audit.

Monitoring the plan – progress is reviewed monthly against targets (sessions held, beneficiaries served, stock position, expenditure), problems are discussed in staff and committee meetings, and the plan is revised mid-year if needed.

Nursing importance

  • Stock-outs of essential drugs, test kits or vaccines lead directly to missed treatment and loss of community trust.
  • Careful use and accounting of funds and supplies protect the nurse from audit objections and ensure value for public money.
  • Planning based on local data makes services responsive to real community needs.

Conclusion Bottom-up planning, realistic budgeting from multiple sources and disciplined material management are the managerial foundations of effective primary health care. At the sub-centre and PHC, the nurse and CHO translate these principles into everyday practice.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Delivery of Community Health Services
question: Explain manpower planning in community health services, with the staffing of the sub-centre/AAM, PHC and CHC as per the Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS) 2022.
answer_html:
Introduction Manpower (human resource) planning is the process of estimating the number and type of health personnel needed, and arranging for their recruitment, training, deployment and retention, so that services are delivered to the expected standard. The Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS) 2022 give population norms and staffing norms for each level of public health facility, distinguishing between essential (minimum) and desirable staff.

1. Steps in manpower planning

  • Assess the population, workload and services to be provided.
  • Compare with norms (IPHS) and existing staff to identify gaps.
  • Plan recruitment (regular or contractual), redeployment and task-sharing.
  • Plan pre-service and in-service training, supervision and career progression.
  • Ensure retention – housing, incentives for difficult areas, safe working conditions.
  • Review periodically.

2. Population norms (IPHS 2022)

Facility Plain areas Hilly, tribal and difficult areas
Sub-centre/AAM 5,000 3,000
PHC (rural) 30,000 20,000
CHC 1,20,000 80,000
Urban PHC About 50,000 urban population –

3. Staffing of the sub-centre-level AAM

  • Community Health Officer – a B.Sc. Nursing or GNM nurse or an Ayurveda practitioner trained through the certificate programme in community health (or a B.Sc. in community health).
  • Two multipurpose workers – one female and one male, or both female.
  • ASHAs – one per 1,000 population (about five).

4. Staffing of the PHC (minimum team) – a medical officer (MBBS), staff nurses, a pharmacist, a laboratory technician, a lady health visitor/health assistant (female) and supporting staff; additional medical officers (including an AYUSH doctor) and more nurses for 24 × 7 PHCs with delivery services. Urban PHCs have multipurpose workers and urban ASHAs for their population.

5. Staffing of the CHC – a 30-bedded first referral unit with specialists (medicine, surgery, obstetrics and gynaecology, paediatrics, anaesthesia, and others such as ophthalmology and dental surgery), general duty medical officers, staff nurses for wards, labour room and operation theatre, pharmacists, laboratory and radiography technicians, a public health nurse and administrative and support staff.

6. Issues – shortages of specialists in CHCs, vacancies in rural and tribal areas, uneven distribution, and heavy workload of ANMs; strategies include contractual hiring under NHM, multi-skilling, mid-level health providers (CHOs), incentives for hard areas and telemedicine.

Conclusion Manpower planning based on IPHS norms ensures that each facility has the right team to deliver its expected services; nurses form the largest and most essential part of this team.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Delivery of Community Health Services
question: Explain the organisation, staffing and functions of urban health services in India.
answer_html:
Introduction More than a third of India's people live in towns and cities, and a large proportion of the urban poor live in slums with poor sanitation, overcrowding and poor access to health care. The National Urban Health Mission (NUHM, 2013), now part of the National Health Mission, created a structured urban primary health care system alongside municipal and other services.

1. Organisation

  • Urban Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (urban health and wellness centres) – small clinics near slums, with a medical officer, staff nurse or pharmacist and support staff, offering primary care and NCD services closer to the community.
  • Urban PHC (UPHC) – one for about 50,000 population, preferably located in or near a slum, working in convenient hours (often afternoon to evening) for daily-wage earners; provides OPD, MCH, immunisation, family planning, NCD screening, basic laboratory services and outreach.
  • Urban CHC – a 30–50-bedded referral facility for a larger population (several lakhs), providing inpatient care and deliveries in larger cities.
  • Municipal and corporation hospitals, dispensaries and maternity homes run by urban local bodies.
  • Special clinics – TB, STI/RTI, ICTC, de-addiction, mental health, cancer screening and other programme clinics.
  • District hospitals and medical colleges as referral centres.
  • Other providers – ESIC, CGHS, railways, defence, NGOs and the large private sector.

2. Community-level structures

  • Urban ASHAs – one for every 1,000–2,500 population (200–500 households) in slums, linking families to services.
  • Mahila Arogya Samiti (MAS) – a women's group for every 50–100 households that promotes health awareness, sanitation and use of services and manages a small untied grant.
  • Outreach sessions in slums by ANMs (urban MPWs) for immunisation, ANC and health education; special outreach camps.

3. Functions – preventive and promotive services (MCH, immunisation, family planning, nutrition), curative primary care, NCD screening and management, communicable disease control, health education, and referral to higher centres.

4. Challenges – rapid growth of slums, migration and floating populations, unregistered settlements, multiple agencies with poor coordination, high out-of-pocket spending in the private sector, and weak data on the urban poor.

Conclusion Urban health services combine NUHM facilities, municipal services and community structures to reach the urban poor; the community health nurse works through outreach and ASHAs to bring vulnerable slum dwellers into the system.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Delivery of Community Health Services
question: Explain the health services provided by other government agencies – defence, railways, ESIC, CGHS and public sector undertakings.
answer_html:
Introduction In addition to the general health services run by the state health departments, several government agencies provide health care to their own employees, families and specific populations. These services form an important part of India's health care delivery system.

1. Defence – Armed Forces Medical Services (AFMS)

  • Comprises the medical services of the Army, Navy and Air Force, the Army Medical Corps and the Military Nursing Service, with command, base and field hospitals and medical units.
  • Provides preventive, curative and rehabilitative care to service personnel and families; plays a major role in disaster relief and humanitarian assistance.
  • The Ex-Servicemen Contributory Health Scheme (ECHS) serves retired personnel through polyclinics and empanelled hospitals.
  • The Armed Forces Medical College, Pune and military nursing colleges train doctors and nurses.

2. Railway health services

  • The Indian Railways run central, zonal and divisional hospitals and health units across the country for railway employees and their families, retired staff and passengers in emergencies.
  • Services include occupational health of railway workers (drivers' fitness, vision testing), first aid at stations and trains, and disaster response at accident sites.

3. Employees' State Insurance Corporation (ESIC)

  • Medical care and cash benefits for insured workers and families through ESI dispensaries, hospitals and medical colleges, under the Code on Social Security.

4. Central Government Health Scheme (CGHS)

  • Started in 1954 in Delhi, it provides comprehensive health care to central government employees, pensioners, members of Parliament and certain other categories, through wellness centres (dispensaries), polyclinics and empanelled hospitals in many cities.
  • Services include OPD care, medicines, specialist consultation, investigations and hospitalisation.

5. Public sector undertakings and others

  • Large public sector undertakings (steel, coal, oil, power) run hospitals and occupational health services for workers and nearby communities; mines, ports and plantations have their own health services.
  • Police, paramilitary forces and prisons have their own medical units.

6. Role of nurses – nurses work in all these services as nursing officers, occupational health nurses and community health nurses, providing clinical care, health education, screening and disaster response.

Conclusion These agency-based services reduce the load on general services and provide organised care to large groups; coordination with them strengthens referral, disease control and disaster response in the community.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Delivery of Community Health Services
question: Explain the referral system in community health services – levels, procedure, problems and strengthening.
answer_html:
Introduction A referral system is the organised process by which a client whose needs cannot be met at one level of care is sent to a higher (or more appropriate) level, and is then sent back with advice for continuing care. A good referral system makes the whole network of facilities work as one.

1. Levels of care and referral pathway

  • Home and community (ASHA, AWW) → sub-centre/AAM (CHO, MPWs) → PHC (medical officer) → CHC/first referral unit (specialists, caesarean section, blood transfusion) → district hospital → medical college and tertiary hospitals.
  • Two-way referral – upward referral for diagnosis or treatment, and back-referral (counter-referral) with a discharge summary for follow-up near home.

2. Procedure for referral

  1. Assess and decide on referral early; explain the reason to the client and family and obtain consent.
  2. Stabilise the client (airway, IV fluids, first dose of drugs as per protocol, keeping warm).
  3. Fill the referral slip – identification, date and time, history, findings, vital signs, treatment given, reason for referral, name of the referring person and facility.
  4. Inform the receiving facility by phone.
  5. Arrange transport – 108 emergency ambulance, 102 patient transport (free for pregnant women and sick infants), or other means.
  6. Send a health worker or ASHA with the client when needed; carry previous records (MCP card).
  7. Enter in the referral register; follow up the outcome; act on the back-referral advice.

3. Problems in the referral system

  • Self-referral and bypassing of primary facilities, overcrowding of tertiary hospitals.
  • Delays due to distance, lack of transport, cost and lack of escort.
  • Incomplete referral notes; no communication with the receiving facility; no back-referral or follow-up.
  • Gaps in specialists, beds or blood at FRUs; unnecessary or "defensive" referrals.

4. Strengthening the referral system

  • Clear referral protocols and directories of facilities and services; hub-and-spoke linkages between AAMs and PHCs/CHCs.
  • Teleconsultation with specialists so that many clients can be managed locally.
  • Free and reliable ambulance networks; birth-waiting homes for remote areas.
  • Standard referral and back-referral formats, referral registers and audits; feedback to referring staff.
  • Strengthening first referral units with staff, blood storage and equipment.

Conclusion An effective two-way referral system ensures that every client gets the right care at the right level, avoids delays and duplication, and keeps the primary health care team at the centre of continuing care.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Delivery of Community Health Services
question: Explain the role of AYUSH and indigenous systems of medicine in community health services.
tags: AYUSH doctors at PHC and CHC
answer_html:
Introduction India has rich traditions of medicine. AYUSH stands for Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Sowa-Rigpa and Homoeopathy. A separate Ministry of AYUSH was created in 2014, and AYUSH is integrated into public health services to widen choice and promote wellness.

1. AYUSH systems in brief

  • Ayurveda – based on the balance of the three doshas; diet, lifestyle (dinacharya, ritucharya), herbal medicines and panchakarma.
  • Yoga and Naturopathy – asanas, pranayama, meditation, diet therapy, hydrotherapy; emphasis on prevention and lifestyle.
  • Unani – based on the four humours; herbal and regimental therapies.
  • Siddha – a traditional system of Tamil origin.
  • Sowa-Rigpa – the traditional Himalayan (Tibetan) system.
  • Homoeopathy – based on the principle of "like cures like" with highly diluted remedies.

2. AYUSH in community health services

  • Mainstreaming (co-location) – AYUSH doctors and dispensaries at PHCs, CHCs and district hospitals under the National Health Mission, offering patients a choice of system.
  • National AYUSH Mission – support to states for AYUSH hospitals and dispensaries, medicines, education and medicinal-plant cultivation.
  • AYUSH Ayushman Arogya Mandirs – AYUSH dispensaries and sub-centres upgraded to provide comprehensive primary care with an AYUSH focus on wellness.
  • Yoga and wellness activities at AAMs, schools and communities; International Day of Yoga (21 June).
  • Use of AYUSH in programmes – for example, nutrition and anaemia, care of the elderly, NCD prevention and palliative care.

3. Indigenous and local health traditions

  • Home remedies, kitchen herbs, traditional birth practices and local healers; many are harmless and culturally valued, some are beneficial, and a few are harmful (for example, applying cow dung to the cord, branding).
  • The nurse encourages useful practices, discourages harmful ones respectfully, and builds trust with traditional healers to refer serious cases early.

4. Precautions and role of the nurse

  • Ask every client about the use of AYUSH and home remedies; watch for interactions with allopathic drugs and for unregulated products.
  • Never stop prescribed treatment for chronic disease (insulin, antihypertensives, ART, TB drugs) without medical advice.
  • Promote yoga, healthy diet and lifestyle; coordinate with AYUSH practitioners in the team.

Conclusion AYUSH and indigenous systems add cultural acceptability, choice and a strong wellness focus to community health services; safe integration with modern medicine benefits the community.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Delivery of Community Health Services
question: What is the Programme Implementation Plan (PIP) under the National Health Mission?
answer_html:
• The PIP is the annual plan of a state under the National Health Mission, prepared from district health action plans, which in turn are built from block, PHC and sub-centre plans.
  • It lists activities, targets, human resources, infrastructure and budgets for all programme components.
  • The PIP is appraised by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, and the approved plan is issued as a record of proceedings, which is the basis for releasing funds and monitoring progress.
  • It makes planning bottom-up, evidence-based and accountable.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Delivery of Community Health Services
question: What is the Drugs and Vaccines Distribution Management System (DVDMS)?
tags: drugs and vaccines distribution management system
answer_html:
• DVDMS (also known in many states as e-Aushadhi) is an online supply-chain management software for drugs, consumables and vaccines in the public health system.
  • It records procurement, warehouse stocks, indents from facilities, issue, receipt, consumption and expiry, and generates alerts for stock-outs and near-expiry items.
  • It improves transparency, reduces wastage and stock-outs and supports the free drugs service initiative.
  • Facility staff can view their stock and place indents online, and managers can see stocks across the district.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Delivery of Community Health Services
question: What is the Pradhan Mantri Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission (PM-ABHIM)?
tags: Pradhan Mantri Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission
answer_html:
• PM-ABHIM is a centrally sponsored scheme launched in October 2021 with an outlay of about ₹64,180 crore for 2021–26 to strengthen health infrastructure at all levels.
  • Its components include support for building-less AAMs in rural and urban areas, block public health units, integrated public health laboratories in districts, critical care hospital blocks, and strengthening of disease surveillance and research for pandemic preparedness.
  • It complements the National Health Mission by filling critical gaps in infrastructure and public health capacity.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
unit_title: Management of Delivery of Community Health Services
question: What is a Mahila Arogya Samiti (MAS)?
answer_html:
• A Mahila Arogya Samiti is a community-based group of women formed under the National Urban Health Mission in urban slums, covering about 50–100 households, with the urban ASHA as its member secretary.
  • It promotes health awareness, hygiene and sanitation, nutrition and use of services; monitors local health services; mobilises the community for outreach sessions; and uses a small annual untied grant for local health needs.
  • It is the urban counterpart of the village health, sanitation and nutrition committee.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: (a) Explain the job responsibilities of the Multipurpose Health Worker (Female)/ANM at the sub-centre. (6 marks) (b) Describe the job responsibilities of the Health Supervisor (Female)/Lady Health Visitor at the PHC. (5 marks) (c) Explain the role of the anganwadi worker in community health. (4 marks)
answer_html:
Introduction Primary health care in villages is delivered by a team – the multipurpose health workers at the sub-centre/AAM, supervised by health supervisors at the PHC, and supported by community workers such as the ASHA and the anganwadi worker (AWW). Clear job responsibilities avoid duplication and ensure that every family receives all essential services.

(a) Job responsibilities of the MPW (Female)/ANM The ANM serves a population of about 5,000 (3,000 in hilly and tribal areas), working with the CHO at the AAM and with ASHAs in each village.

1. Maternal health

  • Early registration of pregnancies (using pregnancy testing kits through ASHAs); at least four ANC contacts; Hb, urine, BP, weight and abdominal examination; IFA, calcium, deworming and Td; identification and referral of high-risk pregnancies; birth preparedness.
  • Conducting normal deliveries at the sub-centre delivery point (if designated) and supporting institutional deliveries; postnatal visits; postpartum family planning.

2. Newborn and child health

  • Essential newborn care, supervision of home-based newborn and young child care by ASHAs, identification and referral of sick newborns.
  • Immunisation sessions as per micro-plan, maintenance of the cold chain at session sites, tracking drop-outs, reporting adverse events.
  • Management of diarrhoea (ORS, zinc) and pneumonia as per protocol; growth monitoring with the AWW; vitamin A and deworming.

3. Family planning and reproductive health

  • Maintenance of the eligible couple register; counselling; distribution of condoms and pills; injectable contraceptive and IUCD insertion (if trained); follow-up of acceptors; RTI/STI counselling and referral; safe abortion referral.

4. Adolescent health – counselling, weekly IFA, menstrual hygiene, referral to adolescent-friendly clinics; school health activities.

5. Communicable disease control

  • Fever surveillance with malaria rapid tests and blood smears; treatment as per protocol; TB case finding, sputum collection and treatment support; leprosy case detection; reporting of unusual events under disease surveillance.

6. Non-communicable diseases – population-based screening for hypertension, diabetes and oral, breast and cervical cancers with the CHO; follow-up of patients on treatment.

7. Nutrition, water and sanitation – nutrition education, anaemia control, chlorination of water sources, promotion of latrines and hand washing.

8. Health education and community work – Village Health, Sanitation and Nutrition Days (VHSND), group meetings, home visits; coordination with the VHSNC, AWW, school and panchayat.

9. Records, reports and vital events – registers (ANC, immunisation, eligible couples, births and deaths, stock); monthly reports; updating the RCH portal; registration of births and deaths.

10. Support and supervision of ASHAs – monthly meetings, verification of their work and incentives, replenishment of ASHA drug kits.

(b) Job responsibilities of the Health Supervisor (Female)/LHV at the PHC

  • Supervision – supervises the ANMs of the PHC area (usually several sub-centres), making regular planned visits with checklists; checks the quality of ANC, immunisation, deliveries, family planning and records; observes ANMs at work.
  • On-the-job training and guidance – demonstrates correct techniques, corrects mistakes supportively, organises refresher training and ASHA training.
  • Clinical services at the PHC – conducts or assists in ANC, postnatal, family planning, immunisation and adolescent clinics; helps in conducting deliveries and managing emergencies in the labour room; IUCD insertion.
  • Logistics – ensures that sub-centres have adequate drugs, vaccines, contraceptives, equipment and registers; checks stock and cold chain.
  • Meetings and reports – holds monthly meetings with ANMs; compiles and verifies reports for the PHC; reviews data and helps prepare micro-plans.
  • Community work – participates in VHSNDs, school health, health camps and IEC; investigates maternal and infant deaths and outbreaks with the team.
  • Coordination – liaison between the medical officer, ANMs, ASHAs, AWWs and supervisors of other departments; reports problems and achievements to the medical officer.

(c) Role of the anganwadi worker in community health The AWW runs the anganwadi centre (usually one for 400–800 population) under the Integrated Child Development Services, now part of Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0.

  • Supplementary nutrition – take-home rations and hot cooked meals for children 6 months–6 years, pregnant and lactating women and, in some areas, adolescent girls.
  • Growth monitoring – weighing and measuring children, identifying underweight, stunted and wasted children, recording on the Poshan Tracker and referring severely malnourished children.
  • Early childhood care and education for children aged 3–6 years.
  • Health and nutrition education – breastfeeding, complementary feeding, hygiene, anaemia prevention.
  • Support to health services – mobilising beneficiaries for immunisation, ANC and health check-ups; jointly organising the VHSND with the ANM and ASHA; maintaining records of births, deaths and children's growth.
  • Convergence – member of the VHSNC; links with schools, self-help groups and the panchayat.

Related role – the ASHA – the ANM works closely with the ASHA, who acts as a health activist in her village: she mobilises women for ANC, immunisation and institutional delivery, escorts them, makes home-based newborn and young child care visits, provides first-contact care (ORS, zinc, paracetamol, contraceptives, pregnancy testing kits), supports TB and NCD follow-up, and records births and deaths; she receives task-based incentives verified by the ANM.

Joint working (the ANM–ASHA–AWW platform) – the three workers prepare a common list of beneficiaries, jointly organise the VHSND, share data on pregnant women and children, and meet monthly at the sub-centre to review due lists and drop-outs; the CHO at the AAM coordinates this team and adds curative, NCD and other primary care services.

Common problems of ANMs and their solutions – heavy workload and many registers (simplified digital records, task-sharing with the CHO), long distances and lack of transport (travel allowance, mobility support), inadequate supplies (regular indents, online drug systems), insecurity in remote areas (residence near the sub-centre, safety measures), and lack of recognition (supportive supervision, awards, career progression).

Work planning of the ANM – a monthly work plan divides her time between fixed sessions at the sub-centre/AAM, VHSND and outreach sessions in each village, home visits to high-risk mothers and newborns, school visits, meetings with ASHAs and the VHSNC, and record keeping; the plan is shared with the LHV and the CHO so that supervision and support can be planned.

Personal qualities needed – sincerity, punctuality, good communication in the local language, respect for community customs, ability to work in a team and to take decisions in emergencies.

Nursing importance

  • Clear understanding of each worker's role allows the CHO and nurse to plan teamwork and avoid gaps in services.
  • The ANM–ASHA–AWW team (often called the "AAA" platform) is the backbone of community health and nutrition in India.
  • Supervisors who guide rather than inspect improve the morale and performance of frontline workers.

Conclusion The ANM delivers a wide range of services at the sub-centre, the LHV supervises and supports her, and the AWW provides nutrition and early childhood care. Working together with the ASHA, they ensure that every mother and child in the village receives continuous care.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain the area-wise job responsibilities of the District Public Health Nurse (DPHN).
answer_html:
Introduction The District Public Health Nurse (DPHN), also called the District Public Health Nursing Officer, is the senior nursing administrator of community health services in a district. She is responsible to the district health officer (chief medical officer) and guides all public health nursing personnel – PHNs, LHVs, ANMs and, indirectly, ASHAs.

Area-wise responsibilities

  1. Administration and planning
    • Plans public health nursing services for the district as part of the district health action plan; assesses staffing needs and helps in recruitment, posting and transfers of nursing staff.
    • Prepares job descriptions, duty schedules and policies; participates in budgeting for nursing activities.
  2. Supervision and guidance
    • Supervises PHNs, LHVs and ANMs through planned visits to PHCs and sub-centres, using checklists; evaluates their performance; solves problems; ensures quality of services.
  3. Training and staff development
    • Assesses training needs; organises induction, in-service and refresher training of nursing personnel and ASHAs; guides nursing students posted in the district.
  4. Maternal and child health and family planning
    • Monitors ANC, institutional and home deliveries, postnatal care, newborn care, immunisation, nutrition and family planning services; participates in maternal and child death reviews.
  5. Communicable and non-communicable disease programmes
    • Supports nursing aspects of disease control programmes (TB, malaria, leprosy, NCD screening), outbreak investigation and control.
  6. School health and special groups – plans and supervises school health, adolescent, geriatric and occupational health nursing activities.
  7. Health education – plans IEC campaigns, supervises health education by field staff, observes health days.
  8. Supplies and equipment – ensures availability of nursing supplies, kits and equipment in the field.
  9. Records, reports and evaluation – reviews reports and HMIS data, prepares district nursing reports, evaluates programmes and recommends improvements.
  10. Coordination and liaison – with medical officers, programme officers, other departments (ICDS, education), NGOs and the community.
  11. Research and quality improvement – participates in surveys and studies; promotes evidence-based practice and quality standards.

Position and qualification – the DPHN is usually a senior nurse with a degree or post-graduate qualification in community health nursing and long field experience; she works from the district health office, reports to the district health officer and is supported by PHNs and LHVs at block and PHC levels.

Conclusion The DPHN is the leader and link between the district health administration and the nursing workforce in the field; her planning, supervision and training determine the quality of public health nursing in the district.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain the job responsibilities of the Multipurpose Health Worker (Male) and the Health Supervisor (Male).
answer_html:
Introduction The Multipurpose Health Worker (Male) works at the sub-centre/AAM along with the ANM and CHO, mainly for disease control, environmental health and men's health. The Health Supervisor (Male) at the PHC supervises several MPWs (Male).

1. Job responsibilities of the MPW (Male)

  • Malaria and vector-borne diseases – active and passive fever surveillance; blood smears and rapid diagnostic tests; treatment as per national guidelines; anti-larval measures (source reduction, larvivorous fish); supervision of indoor residual spraying and distribution of insecticidal nets; dengue, chikungunya, filaria and Japanese encephalitis control activities.
  • Tuberculosis and leprosy – identifying presumptive cases, collecting sputum, treatment support and contact tracing; searching for leprosy cases and supporting multidrug therapy.
  • Diarrhoeal diseases and outbreaks – reporting clusters; chlorination of wells and water sources; ORS distribution; participation in outbreak control.
  • Environmental sanitation – promotion of latrines and hand washing, safe disposal of waste, food hygiene in eating places and fairs.
  • Non-communicable diseases – screening of men for hypertension, diabetes and oral cancer; tobacco cessation advice; follow-up.
  • Family planning – motivating men for condoms and no-scalpel vasectomy; distributing condoms.
  • Immunisation and MCH support – assisting in sessions and mobilisation, cold chain support.
  • School health, occupational health of local workers, first aid, health education, especially among men.
  • Records and reports – fever and surveillance registers, vital events, monthly reports.

2. Job responsibilities of the Health Supervisor (Male)

  • Supervises and guides MPWs (Male) of the PHC area through field visits; checks surveillance registers, slides and stock.
  • Plans and supervises vector-control operations, spraying rounds and outbreak containment.
  • Ensures supplies – drugs, RDT kits, insecticides, chlorine – and maintenance of equipment.
  • Trains MPWs and volunteers; conducts monthly meetings; compiles and analyses reports; assists the medical officer in investigations and programme reviews.
  • Coordinates with panchayats, schools and other departments on sanitation and disease control.

3. Coordination – the MPW (Male) and MPW (Female) of a sub-centre divide the population and tasks, share data, and work as a team under the CHO; the Health Supervisor (Male) and the LHV jointly supervise the sub-centres of a PHC.

4. Challenges – vacancies of male workers in many states, large areas to cover, and seasonal workload during vector-borne disease outbreaks; multi-skilling and support from ASHAs help fill these gaps.

Conclusion The male health worker and his supervisor complement the female workers by focusing on communicable disease control, sanitation and men's health, completing the primary health care team.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Write any four criteria for selecting an ASHA.
answer_html:
• She must be a woman resident of the same village, preferably married, widowed, divorced or separated, in the age group of about 25–45 years.
  • She should be literate, with formal education preferably up to class 8 or above (relaxed only when no suitable candidate is available).
  • She should have good communication and leadership skills and be acceptable to the community, with preference to women from marginalised groups.
  • She is selected through a participatory process involving the gram sabha/VHSNC, generally one ASHA per 1,000 population (with relaxation for tribal, hilly and scattered habitations).

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: (a) Explain the concept and principles of supportive supervision in community health services. (5 marks) (b) Describe the methods and tools for supervising frontline health workers. (6 marks) (c) Explain monitoring of community health services – its meaning, indicators and tools. (4 marks)
answer_html:
Introduction Frontline health workers – ANMs, MPWs, ASHAs and AWWs – often work alone in villages far from their supervisors. Traditional supervision focused on inspection and fault-finding, which caused fear and poor morale. Supportive supervision is a facilitative approach in which the supervisor acts as a mentor and coach, helping workers solve problems and improve their skills, while monitoring keeps track of progress towards goals.

(a) Concept and principles of supportive supervision

  • Concept – a process of guiding, helping, training and encouraging staff to improve their performance continuously, through two-way communication, joint problem-solving and on-the-spot teaching, with an emphasis on the quality of services rather than on finding faults.
  • Supportive supervision versus inspection
Supportive supervision Inspection (traditional)
Focus on improving performance and quality Focus on finding faults
Two-way communication; worker participates One-way; orders and criticism
Joint problem-solving and on-the-job teaching Punishment and blame
Regular, planned and followed up Irregular, surprise visits
Builds motivation and trust Creates fear and hiding of problems
  • Principles
    1. Planned and regular – visits are scheduled, with clear objectives and checklists.
    2. Participatory – the worker takes part in identifying problems and solutions.
    3. Problem-solving and teaching – gaps in knowledge and skills are corrected on the spot by demonstration.
    4. Respect and recognition – good work is praised, privately and publicly; mistakes are corrected privately.
    5. Evidence-based – decisions are based on observation and data, not opinion.
    6. Continuity – agreed actions are recorded and followed up at the next visit.
    7. Supervisor's support – the supervisor solves system problems (supplies, transport, funds) beyond the worker's control.

(b) Methods and tools of supervision 1. Preparation for the supervisory visit – review previous visit notes, reports and data of the area; fix objectives; inform the worker; carry checklists, IEC materials and needed supplies.

2. Methods during the visit

  • Observation of work – watching the ANM conduct an ANC check-up, immunisation session or counselling; observing the ASHA's home visit.
  • Review of records and registers – completeness, accuracy, due lists, stock registers and cold chain charts; cross-checking a sample of records with beneficiaries.
  • Checking facilities and supplies – cleanliness, equipment, drugs, vaccines, BMW management.
  • Interaction with the community – visiting a few households to verify services and to learn about satisfaction; meeting the VHSNC.
  • Discussion with the worker – sharing findings, praising strengths, jointly identifying problems and solutions; on-the-job training by demonstration.
  • Recording the findings and agreed actions in the supervisory register or app, with a copy for the worker.

3. Tools

  • Standard supervisory checklists for sub-centres, AAMs, VHSND and immunisation sessions.
  • Supervisory visit plan (monthly calendar) and supervisory register.
  • HMIS and RCH portal data, dashboards and ASHA performance records.
  • Mobile applications for supervision used in many states.
  • Monthly review meetings at the PHC and block level; group supervision (cluster meetings of ASHAs with ASHA facilitators).

4. Follow-up – the supervisor takes up unresolved issues with higher authorities, checks the agreed actions at the next visit and recognises improvement.

(c) Monitoring of community health services

  • Meaning – the continuous tracking of activities and results against plans, using routine information, to identify problems early and take corrective action.
  • Types of indicators
    • input – staff in position, drugs and equipment available, funds released;
    • process – number of sessions held, home visits made, training conducted;
    • output – women receiving four ANC visits, children fully immunised, people screened for NCDs;
    • outcome/impact – institutional delivery rate, coverage achieved, reduction in IMR or MMR.
  • Tools – HMIS and programme portals, dashboards and scorecards, supervisory checklists, stock and cold chain records, maternal and child death reviews, surveys, community-based monitoring (VHSNC and Jan Arogya Samiti reviews, public hearings, social audits).
  • Monitoring versus evaluation – monitoring is continuous and concerned with activities and outputs; evaluation is periodic and measures outcomes and impact.

Example – supportive supervision of a VHSND session

  1. Before – the LHV reviews the sub-centre's due list and last month's coverage and carries the VHSND checklist.
  2. During – she observes the ANM checking pregnant women, giving vaccines and counselling mothers; she checks the cold chain (vaccine carrier, ice packs, VVM), infection control and waste disposal; she talks to a few mothers about the information they received.
  3. Discussion – she praises the ANM's careful counselling, notes that the BP of two women was not recorded and that one vaccine vial was without a date of opening; they agree on corrective steps; she demonstrates recording BP correctly.
  4. After – she records the findings and actions in the supervisory register, arranges a replacement BP apparatus, and checks progress at the next visit.

Qualities of a good supervisor – technical competence, good communication and listening, fairness, patience, a teaching attitude, punctuality, ability to solve problems and motivate, and willingness to act on workers' difficulties.

Barriers to supportive supervision and solutions

  • Too many workers per supervisor, lack of transport and time → realistic supervisory ratios, mobility support, cluster meetings.
  • Supervisors trained only to inspect → training in supportive supervision and mentoring.
  • Lack of follow-up on problems raised → a system of recording and escalating issues.
  • Fear among workers → building trust, confidentiality and recognition.

Supervision of ASHAs – ASHA facilitators (one for about 20 ASHAs) and the ANM support ASHAs through monthly cluster meetings, home-visit observation, verification of their work and grading of ASHA functionality on simple indicators, followed by targeted mentoring.

Example of monitoring – a block scorecard shows that the proportion of pregnant women with four ANC visits fell in two sub-centres; the supervisor finds that VHSND sessions were missed due to a vacancy and arranges an ANM from a neighbouring sub-centre until the post is filled.

Self-assessment by workers – supportive supervision encourages ANMs and ASHAs to assess their own performance with simple checklists before the supervisor's visit, so that the discussion begins with the worker's own view of strengths and gaps; this builds ownership and continuous learning.

Benefits of supportive supervision – better skills and confidence of workers, improved quality and coverage of services, accurate records, early solution of system problems, higher motivation and retention of staff, and stronger trust between the community, the workers and the health system.

Frequency of supervision – supervisors usually plan to visit each sub-centre at least once a month and to observe each worker's key tasks over a quarter, giving extra support to new workers and low-performing areas identified from data.

Nursing importance

  • Supportive supervision improves the skills, confidence and retention of frontline workers and the quality of care they give.
  • Monitoring with data allows the nurse supervisor to target support where it is most needed.
  • Community involvement in monitoring increases accountability and trust.

Conclusion Supervision that supports rather than inspects, combined with systematic monitoring of indicators and community feedback, turns supervision into a powerful tool for improving community health services.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain the Village Health, Sanitation and Nutrition Committee (VHSNC) – its objectives, composition, roles and use of the untied fund.
tags: Village Health Sanitation and Nutrition Committee
answer_html:
Introduction The Village Health, Sanitation and Nutrition Committee (VHSNC) is a community-level body formed in every revenue village under the National Health Mission. It provides a platform for the community to plan, monitor and take action on health, sanitation and nutrition, and it links the village with the health system.

1. Objectives

  • To create awareness about health, sanitation and nutrition and people's entitlements.
  • To prepare and implement a village health plan based on local needs.
  • To monitor health and nutrition services and support the ASHA, ANM and AWW.
  • To undertake local action on sanitation, water and nutrition, and help the poor in emergencies.

2. Composition

  • Usually a sub-committee of the gram panchayat, chaired by an elected panchayat member (preferably a woman) with the ASHA as member secretary/convener.
  • Members include the AWW, representatives of self-help groups, school teachers, community-based organisations, and representatives of SC/ST, minority and other marginalised groups; at least half the members should be women.
  • The ANM and MPW attend as invitees or members as per state guidelines.

3. Roles and functions

  • Conducting monthly meetings; maintaining records of births, deaths, pregnancies and disease outbreaks in the village.
  • Supporting the organisation of the Village Health, Sanitation and Nutrition Day.
  • Monitoring the attendance and services of health workers, availability of drugs, and the functioning of the anganwadi centre and school meals.
  • Promoting latrines, safe water, drainage, waste disposal and vector control.
  • Identifying malnourished children and high-risk mothers and ensuring they receive services.
  • Community-based monitoring – participating in public hearings and providing feedback to the PHC.
  • Mobilising the community during campaigns and outbreaks.

4. Untied fund

  • Each VHSNC receives an annual untied grant (generally ₹10,000) under NHM, kept in a joint bank account (operated by the chairperson and member secretary).
  • It may be used for village health activities such as sanitation drives, cleaning water sources, nutrition demonstrations, emergency transport or help for poor families, and IEC activities – as decided in a meeting, with proper records and accounts.

5. Role of the community health nurse – helps form and train the committee, attends meetings, provides data on village health, guides preparation of the village health plan and use of the untied fund, and acts on its feedback.

Conclusion An active VHSNC turns the community from passive recipients into partners who plan, monitor and improve their own health services.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain the planning, conduct and follow-up of a health camp in the community.
answer_html:
Introduction A health camp is a one-day or short-term organised event at which health services – screening, treatment, counselling and referral – are provided to a large number of people in a community, especially where regular services are difficult to reach. Camps can be general or special (eye, NCD, maternal health, dental, blood donation, disability certification).

1. Planning

  • Assess the need – identify the target group and the main health problems from data and community discussions.
  • Fix objectives – for example, to screen all adults over 30 years in a village for hypertension and diabetes.
  • Choose date, time and venue – convenient for the community (avoid market days and harvest time), with space, shade, water, toilets and electricity.
  • Form the team – medical officers or specialists, nurses, CHO, pharmacist, laboratory technician, ASHAs, AWWs, volunteers; assign duties.
  • Obtain permissions and involve the panchayat, VHSNC, schools and NGOs.
  • Publicity – announcements, posters, ASHAs' house-to-house information, social media groups.
  • Logistics – registers and forms, drugs, equipment (BP apparatus, glucometers, weighing scales), test kits, IEC materials, furniture, emergency kit, transport, refreshments for staff, BMW bins and bags.

2. Conduct

  • Arrange stations in a logical flow: registration → vital signs and screening → consultation → laboratory tests → pharmacy → counselling and health education → referral desk.
  • Ensure privacy for examination, especially of women; manage crowds; give priority to the elderly, disabled and pregnant women.
  • Conduct group health education on relevant topics.
  • Segregate and dispose of waste according to BMW rules.

3. Follow-up

  • Refer positive cases with referral slips; enter them in a follow-up register; arrange home visits by ASHAs and review at the AAM.
  • Ensure continuation of treatment, especially for chronic diseases.

4. Records and evaluation

  • Record the number of persons registered, screened, treated and referred; prepare a report; compare with objectives; collect feedback from the community and team; identify lessons for future camps.

5. Ethical and safety considerations – informed consent for tests, privacy and confidentiality, no unnecessary drugs or procedures, safe injection practices, emergency preparedness (adrenaline, oxygen where possible), proper waste disposal, and avoiding camps that are merely publicity events without follow-up.

Conclusion A well-planned health camp brings services to the doorstep, detects hidden disease and builds community confidence, but it is useful only when linked to follow-up and regular services.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain the training of frontline health workers (ASHAs and AWWs) by the community health nurse.
answer_html:
Introduction ASHAs and AWWs are the first point of contact for families. Their effectiveness depends on regular, practical training. The community health nurse, along with ASHA facilitators and block trainers, plays a central role in training and mentoring them.

1. Training needs assessment – observe their work, review records, discuss with them and the community, and identify gaps in knowledge and skills (for example, counting respiratory rate, using a thermometer, counselling for breastfeeding, filling forms).

2. Planning the training

  • Set clear learning objectives based on job tasks (for example, "the ASHA will correctly identify danger signs in a newborn").
  • Select content from the national ASHA training modules and programme guidelines (maternal and newborn care, child health, family planning, NCDs, TB, mental health, communicable diseases, nutrition).
  • Plan duration, venue (PHC, block, village), groups of manageable size (about 20–25), training materials and kits.

3. Methods (based on principles of adult learning)

  • Short interactive talks linked to their experience; demonstration and return demonstration (weighing a baby, measuring BP, preparing ORS, using RDT kits).
  • Role play for counselling and communication; case studies and problem-solving; flip charts, pictorial job aids and videos in the local language.
  • Field practice – supervised home visits and VHSND sessions.

4. On-the-job mentoring – during supervisory visits and monthly meetings, the nurse observes, corrects and reinforces skills; ASHA facilitators provide continuous support.

5. Evaluation – pre-test and post-test, skill checklists, observation in the field, improvement in service indicators; refresher training for weak areas; certification of skills where available.

6. Records – training register, attendance, materials distributed and evaluation results.

7. Example – a training session on danger signs in the newborn

  • Objective – ASHAs will identify eight danger signs in a newborn and refer correctly.
  • Method – a picture-card game, demonstration of temperature measurement and counting respiratory rate on a doll, role play of counselling a mother, and practice during a supervised home visit.
  • Evaluation – each ASHA correctly identifies danger signs on picture cards and demonstrates counting respiratory rate.
