8. Common problems and solutions – low literacy (pictorial materials, local language), long gaps between training and practice (immediate field practice and mentoring), large groups (smaller batches), and loss of wages or travel difficulties (training close to villages, allowances).

Conclusion Practical, competency-based training with continuous mentoring transforms ASHAs and AWWs into confident, effective community health workers.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain leadership in community health – approaches, qualities of a community health nurse leader and the development of community leadership.
answer_html:
Introduction Leadership is the ability to influence and guide individuals or groups towards achieving common goals. In community health, the nurse leads not only the health team but also community groups, and she must help develop leaders within the community so that health actions are sustained.

1. Approaches (styles) and their use in the community

  • Autocratic – the leader decides alone; useful in emergencies such as outbreaks or disasters when quick action is needed.
  • Democratic (participatory) – decisions are made with the team and community; best for planning health programmes, VHSNC meetings and health camps.
  • Laissez-faire – minimal direction; suitable only with experienced, motivated workers.
  • Situational – the leader adjusts her style to the maturity of the group and the situation – directive for new ASHAs, delegating for experienced ANMs.
  • Transformational – inspires the team with a shared vision (for example, "no mother dies in our block"), encourages innovation and personal growth.
  • Servant leadership – focuses on serving the needs of team members and the community.

2. Qualities of a community health nurse leader

  • A clear vision and commitment to community health; knowledge and competence.
  • Good communication – listening, explaining in the local language, negotiation.
  • Integrity, fairness and accountability; respect for community values; cultural sensitivity.
  • Decision-making and problem-solving ability; initiative and creativity.
  • Team building, delegation and motivation; conflict management.
  • Ability to work with leaders of other sectors – panchayat, education, ICDS, NGOs.
  • Emotional maturity, patience and empathy.

3. Developing community leadership

  • Identify natural leaders – panchayat members, SHG leaders, teachers, religious leaders, youth club members, retired persons.
  • Involve them in VHSNCs, health committees and campaigns; give them responsibility and recognition.
  • Train them in health issues, planning and monitoring; encourage women and marginalised groups to take leadership roles.
  • Support community-based organisations to take ownership of health activities (for example, sanitation drives, nutrition gardens).

4. Functions of a leader in community health – setting goals with the team and community, planning and organising activities, motivating and supporting workers, communicating clearly, managing conflicts, making decisions, representing the team at higher levels, and monitoring progress.

Conclusion Effective leadership by the community health nurse and the development of leaders within the community together make health programmes participatory, responsive and sustainable.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain financial management and accounting at the sub-centre/Ayushman Arogya Mandir – sources and activities of funds, accounting principles, books of accounts, basic accounting entries, payments and expenditure, fixed assets, statement of expenditure, utilisation certificate, budget preparation and audit.
answer_html:
Introduction Sub-centres and AAMs receive funds under the National Health Mission and other sources for local health activities. The CHO and ANM are responsible for spending these funds correctly and maintaining accounts. Financial management means planning, using, recording and reporting funds in a transparent and accountable way.

1. Sources and activities of funds

  • Untied fund – for local needs decided by the facility committee: minor repairs, cleanliness, consumables, patient amenities, emergency transport for the poor, printing of registers, IEC.
  • Annual maintenance grant – for maintenance of the building, water supply, electricity and toilets.
  • Programme funds – for specific activities such as VHSND, outreach sessions, NCD screening, campaigns and training (as per approved plans).
  • Performance-linked payments to the AAM team on the basis of service indicators.
  • Grants through local bodies and donations, where applicable.
  • Activities not allowed – personal expenses, salaries of regular staff, purchases not approved, or expenditure outside guidelines.

2. Accounting principles and policies

  • Funds are kept in a bank account in the name of the facility committee, operated jointly by two authorised signatories (for example, the CHO/ANM and the panchayat representative).
  • Every receipt and payment is recorded on the day it occurs (cash basis of accounting), supported by documents; expenditure only after approval of the committee and within the approved budget.
  • Cash in hand is minimised; payments are made through the bank or the public financial management system wherever possible.
  • Separate records for each fund; no diversion between heads without approval.
  • Transparency – display of funds received and spent at the facility; records open to audit and social audit.

3. Books of accounts

  • Cash book – daily record of all cash and bank receipts and payments, balanced regularly.
  • Bank book/passbook – bank transactions; periodic bank reconciliation with the cash book.
  • Ledger – head-wise accounts (untied fund, maintenance grant, programme funds).
  • Advance register – advances given to staff and their settlement.
  • Fixed assets register – equipment, furniture and other durable items purchased, with date, cost and location.
  • Stock register – consumables purchased and issued.
  • Cheque issue register, voucher file (bills, receipts, payment vouchers) and minutes of committee meetings approving expenditure.

4. Basic accounting entries and process

  1. Receipt of funds (bank credit) → entered in the cash/bank book and ledger.
  2. Decision to spend → approved in a committee meeting (minutes recorded).
  3. Purchase or service → bill obtained, goods checked and entered in the stock or assets register.
  4. Payment → by cheque or online transfer; payment voucher prepared, signed and filed with the bill.
  5. Entry in the cash book and ledger under the correct head.
  6. Monthly closing – balancing of the cash book, reconciliation with the bank statement.

5. Payments and expenditure

  • Follow purchase rules (quotations for larger purchases); avoid splitting bills; obtain receipts for every payment; pay incentives to ASHAs through the bank after verification; record advances and settle them promptly.

6. Fixed assets – every durable item is entered in the fixed assets register, labelled, verified annually and condemned through the proper procedure when unserviceable.

7. Statement of expenditure (SOE) – a periodic (usually monthly or quarterly) report showing the opening balance, funds received, expenditure under each head and closing balance, submitted to the PHC/block.

8. Utilisation certificate (UC) – a certificate, generally annual, stating that the funds received were used for the purpose for which they were sanctioned, with the amount spent and the balance; it is required before further funds are released.

9. Budget preparation – estimate needs for the coming year on the basis of the action plan, norms and previous expenditure; include maintenance, consumables, outreach and IEC; submit through the PHC for inclusion in the block and district plans.

10. Audit

  • Concurrent/internal audit – regular checking of accounts by auditors appointed under NHM.
  • Statutory audit – annual audit by chartered accountants, and audit by the Comptroller and Auditor General where applicable.
  • Social audit – review of expenditure by the community (VHSNC, public meetings).
  • Audit objections are answered promptly with documents.

Example – entries in the cash book of a sub-centre

Date Particulars Voucher no. Receipt (₹) Payment (₹) Balance (₹)
01-07 Opening balance – – – 6,500
05-07 Untied fund received from PHC (bank) R-1 20,000 – 26,500
12-07 Repair of water tap (bill no. 45) P-1 – 1,200 25,300
20-07 Printing of registers P-2 – 2,500 22,800
31-07 Closing balance – – – 22,800

Role of the facility committee – the Jan Arogya Samiti (or similar committee) of the AAM approves the annual plan and every major expenditure, reviews accounts in its meetings, and displays the summary of funds publicly; this ensures community ownership and transparency.

Electronic fund management – NHM funds are increasingly managed through the government's public financial management system, in which payments are made directly to bank accounts and expenditure is recorded online; this reduces cash handling and makes tracking easier.

Checklist before making a payment – Is the item in the approved plan and within the budget? Has the committee approved it? Is the bill genuine and in the facility's name? Have the goods or services been received and checked? Is the payment being made by cheque or online transfer? Has the voucher been prepared and signed?

Common errors and audit objections – expenditure without approval, missing bills or vouchers, cash payments of large amounts, splitting of bills to avoid procedures, unsettled advances, non-entry of assets, delay in submitting SOEs and UCs, and use of funds for purposes not permitted; these are avoided by following the guidelines and keeping records up to date.

Responsibilities of the CHO/ANM in financial management – prepare the annual budget with the committee, keep all books of accounts up to date, obtain approvals and bills, make payments through authorised channels, submit the SOE and UC on time, keep records ready for audit, and display the funds received and spent on the notice board of the AAM.

Financial reporting cycle – daily entries in the cash book; monthly balancing and bank reconciliation; monthly or quarterly SOE to the PHC/block; annual accounts, audit and UC; preparation of the next year's budget based on actual expenditure and the new action plan.

Transparency boards – a simple board at the AAM showing funds received, purchases made and balance available enables the community to see how public money is used and discourages misuse.

Nursing importance

  • Proper use of funds makes the sub-centre clean, equipped and responsive, which builds community trust.
  • Correct accounts protect the CHO and ANM from audit objections and allegations of misuse.
  • Financial discipline ensures the continued release of funds for future activities.

Conclusion Sound financial management at the sub-centre – planned budgets, approved expenditure, complete books of accounts, timely SOEs and UCs and regular audit – ensures that public money is used efficiently and transparently for community health.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain the functions of the Medical Records Department, the filing systems and the retention of records.
answer_html:
Introduction The Medical Records Department (MRD) of a hospital is responsible for creating, maintaining, storing and retrieving the medical records of patients. Medical records are essential for continuity of care, legal protection, research, teaching and hospital statistics.

1. Functions of the MRD

  • Registration of outpatients and inpatients, allotting a unique registration (unit) number; maintaining the master patient index.
  • Assembling and checking records after discharge for completeness (admission notes, progress notes, nursing records, investigations, consent forms, discharge summary).
  • Coding of diagnoses and procedures using the International Classification of Diseases (ICD); disease and operation indexes.
  • Filing, storage and retrieval of records for readmission, follow-up, courts and research.
  • Compiling hospital statistics – admissions, discharges, bed occupancy, average length of stay, deaths and causes; reports for HMIS.
  • Release of information with patient consent or legal authority; handling requests from insurance and courts.
  • Medico-legal records – safe custody; production in courts when summoned.
  • Digitisation and management of electronic records.

2. Filing systems

  • Alphabetical – by the patient's surname; simple but confusing for common names.
  • Serial numbering – a new number at each admission; records of one patient get scattered.
  • Unit numbering – one number for the patient for all visits, keeping all records together (preferred).
  • Terminal-digit filing – files arranged by the last digits of the number, spreading files evenly and reducing misfiling in large hospitals.
  • Colour coding and tracer (out-guide) cards help in quick retrieval and tracking of files.

3. Retention of records

  • Records are retained for periods prescribed by law and hospital policy – for example, inpatient records for at least three years as per professional regulations, longer for medico-legal cases (until the case is settled), records of minors, deaths and certain programmes.
  • Old records may be preserved by scanning or microfilming before authorised destruction.

4. Nurses' responsibilities – accurate, legible, dated and signed entries; no overwriting; completing records before sending to the MRD; maintaining confidentiality; following procedures for issue and return of files.

5. Types of medical records – outpatient cards, inpatient case files, nursing records (charts, care plans, medication administration records), operation and anaesthesia records, laboratory and radiology reports, consent forms, discharge summaries, birth and death records, and medico-legal records.

Conclusion An efficient MRD ensures that complete, confidential and retrievable records are available for patient care, legal needs and planning.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: What is a statement of expenditure (SOE)?
answer_html:
• A statement of expenditure is a periodic financial report (usually monthly or quarterly) prepared by a facility or programme unit under NHM.
  • It shows the opening balance, funds received, expenditure under each approved head and the closing balance for the period.
  • It is submitted to the PHC/block and district, where it is compiled to monitor the use of funds and to plan further releases.
  • It must match the cash book, bank statement and vouchers.
  • Errors in the SOE delay the next release of funds.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: What is a utilisation certificate (UC)?
tags: condition for release of further funds
answer_html:
• A utilisation certificate is a formal certificate, usually annual, issued by the authority that received a grant, stating that the funds were spent for the purpose for which they were sanctioned.
  • It gives the amount received, the amount utilised and the unspent balance, and is signed by the authorised officers.
  • It is a condition for the release of further grants and an important document in audit.
  • Delay in submitting UCs holds up funds for the next year.
  • It is prepared from the audited accounts.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: (a) Explain the types and magnitude of disasters in India. (4 marks) (b) Describe disaster and emergency preparedness at the community level, including the family and community disaster plan, the basic disaster supplies kit and mock drills. (7 marks) (c) Explain the common problems during disasters and the ways to overcome them. (4 marks)

diagram.caption: Community disaster preparedness
labels: vulnerability and capacity mapping → village disaster management plan and task forces → early warning and communication → training
kits and mock drills → response and relief → recovery and review → back to mapping
with the community and the health team at the centre

answer_html:
Introduction A disaster is a serious disruption of the functioning of a community, caused by a natural or man-made event, involving widespread human, material, economic or environmental losses that exceed the community's ability to cope using its own resources. India is one of the most disaster-prone countries in the world. Because the first responders in any disaster are the people of the affected community, community-level preparedness is the most effective way to save lives.

(a) Types and magnitude of disasters in India 1. Types

  • Natural disasters
    • geophysical – earthquakes, tsunamis, landslides, volcanic eruptions;
    • hydro-meteorological – floods, flash floods and cloudbursts, cyclones, storm surges, droughts, heat waves, cold waves, lightning, hailstorms, avalanches;
    • biological – epidemics and pandemics (cholera, plague, COVID-19), pest attacks.
  • Man-made (technological and social) disasters
    • industrial and chemical accidents (for example, the Bhopal gas tragedy of 1984), nuclear and radiological accidents;
    • major fires, building collapses, dam failures;
    • road, rail and air accidents; stampedes at religious gatherings;
    • terrorism, conflicts, chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear (CBRN) emergencies.

2. Magnitude – India's vulnerability profile

  • Nearly 59% of the land area is prone to moderate to very high intensity earthquakes.
  • About 12% of the land (over 40 million hectares) is prone to floods and river erosion.
  • Of the coastline of about 7,500 km, nearly 5,700 km is prone to cyclones and tsunamis.
  • About 68% of the cultivable area is vulnerable to drought.
  • The Himalayan and Western Ghats regions face landslides, cloudbursts and avalanches.
  • Heat waves have become more frequent and intense; urban flooding is increasing.
  • Large populations, poverty, unsafe buildings and climate change increase the impact of these hazards.

(b) Disaster and emergency preparedness at the community level 1. Hazard, vulnerability and capacity mapping

  • With the community, prepare a village map showing hazard-prone areas (river banks, low-lying areas, weak buildings), vulnerable households (elderly, disabled, pregnant women, young children, the sick, the poor) and resources (safe shelters, boats, vehicles, wells, health facilities, trained persons).

2. Village (community) disaster management plan

  • Prepared by the gram panchayat with the community, in line with the district disaster management plan.
  • Includes the risk map, early-warning system, evacuation routes and safe shelters, a list of vulnerable persons and who will help them, contact numbers, resources and stockpiles, and responsibilities of each group.
  • Task forces of trained volunteers – early warning, search and rescue, first aid and medical, shelter management, water and sanitation, relief distribution, and counselling.

3. Early warning and communication

  • Receive warnings from official sources (the meteorological department for cyclones and heat waves, flood forecasting agencies, tsunami warning centres, mobile alert messages) and disseminate them quickly through loudspeakers, sirens, mobile phones and volunteers.

4. Family disaster plan

  • Discuss likely hazards with family members; identify safe places in the house and a meeting place outside; decide evacuation routes; keep emergency contact numbers; assign responsibilities for children, the elderly and pets; keep copies of important documents in a waterproof pouch; learn basic first aid and how to switch off gas and electricity.

5. Basic disaster supplies kit (kept ready in an easy-to-carry bag)

  • Drinking water and ready-to-eat dry food for at least three days; ORS and water purification tablets.
  • First aid kit and a supply of regular medicines (for diabetes, hypertension, epilepsy, etc.), spectacles, hearing aids.
  • Torch with spare batteries, battery or solar radio, mobile phone with a power bank, whistle.
  • Copies of identity documents, health cards (including MCP card) and some cash.
  • Clothes, blankets, sanitary pads, soap and hygiene items, masks, a knife, rope and plastic sheet.
  • Baby foods and supplies (with breastfeeding promoted), and items for the elderly and disabled.

6. Training and mock drills

  • Train volunteers in first aid, CPR, search and rescue, fire safety and psychological first aid.
  • Conduct mock drills in schools, hospitals and villages to test the plan, warning systems and evacuation; review and improve the plan after each drill.

7. Preparedness of health services

  • Each PHC and CHC has a disaster plan with an emergency team, a stock of essential drugs, IV fluids, dressings, vaccines and disinfectants, arrangements for surge capacity, referral linkages and communication; staff are trained in mass-casualty management.
  • Line lists of pregnant women due to deliver, dialysis and chronic patients, and bedridden persons are kept for priority evacuation.

8. Mitigation – safe construction (earthquake- and cyclone-resistant buildings), raised plinths and platforms in flood areas, embankments, mangrove and forest protection, drought-proofing, insurance and livelihood diversification.

(c) Common problems during disasters and ways to overcome them | Problem | Ways to overcome | |---|---| | Deaths and injuries (trauma, drowning, burns, crush injuries) | Rapid search and rescue, field triage, first aid, quick transfer to hospitals | | Contaminated water, diarrhoea, cholera, typhoid, hepatitis | Safe water supply, chlorination of wells and tankers, ORS, hygiene promotion | | Poor sanitation and waste | Temporary latrines, waste disposal, vector control | | Vector-borne diseases (malaria, dengue) and leptospirosis | Source reduction, insecticide spraying, nets, surveillance and early treatment | | Measles and respiratory infections in crowded camps | Measles vaccination and vitamin A for children, ventilation, masks | | Food shortage and malnutrition | Regular rations, community kitchens, supplementary feeding, support for breastfeeding | | Lack of shelter, exposure to cold or heat | Tents, blankets, cool shelters, warm clothing | | Disruption of maternal, child and chronic disease care | Mobile medical units, continuation of ANC, deliveries, immunisation and essential drugs | | Psychological trauma, grief, fear | Psychological first aid, counselling, support groups, referral | | Vulnerable groups – children, women, elderly, disabled | Protection from abuse and trafficking, separate facilities for women, child-friendly spaces | | Breakdown of communication and transport | Satellite phones, radio, alternative routes, coordination centres | | Management of the dead | Dignified identification and disposal; reassure that bodies of disaster victims rarely cause epidemics |

Role of the community health nurse

  • Participates in preparing the village and facility disaster plans; maintains the list of vulnerable persons.
  • Trains volunteers in first aid and hygiene; conducts health education on preparedness.
  • During disasters – triage and first aid, care of pregnant women and newborns, immunisation, water and sanitation measures, disease surveillance, psychological first aid and referral.
  • After disasters – rehabilitation, follow-up of injured and chronically ill, and support for restoring routine health services.

Legal and institutional framework (brief) – under the Disaster Management Act, 2005, disaster management authorities function at the national, state and district levels, with national and state disaster response forces; district disaster management plans guide village and facility plans.

Phases of disaster management – mitigation and preparedness before the event, response during and immediately after it, and recovery and rehabilitation afterwards; community preparedness links all these phases.

Conclusion India faces many hazards, but deaths and suffering can be greatly reduced when communities are prepared. Risk mapping, a community and family disaster plan, early warning, a ready supplies kit, trained volunteers and regular mock drills, together with prompt public health action during disasters, are the keys to resilience.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain the measures to reduce the potential consequences of an earthquake – before, during and after the event.
answer_html:
Introduction Earthquakes strike suddenly and without warning, and most deaths are caused by collapse of buildings and falling objects. India has large areas in high seismic zones (the Himalayas, the north-east, Gujarat and parts of the Indo-Gangetic plains). The consequences of an earthquake can be greatly reduced by preparedness and correct action.

1. Before an earthquake (preparedness and mitigation)

  • Safe construction – follow earthquake-resistant building codes for new buildings; retrofit schools, hospitals and old houses; avoid construction on unstable slopes and filled-up land.
  • Secure the home – fix heavy furniture, cupboards and water heaters to walls; keep heavy objects on low shelves; avoid hanging heavy items over beds.
  • Know safe spots in each room – under strong tables or against inner walls, away from windows and glass.
  • Family plan and kit – prepare a family disaster plan, keep an emergency supplies kit and learn to switch off gas, electricity and water.
  • Drills and training – practise "Drop, Cover and Hold On" in schools, offices and homes; train volunteers in first aid and search and rescue.
  • Hospital and facility safety – structural and non-structural safety of hospitals so that they remain functional; emergency plans.

2. During an earthquake

  • Indoors – Drop to the ground, take Cover under a sturdy table or desk, and Hold On until the shaking stops; protect head and neck; stay away from windows, glass and heavy objects; do not run outside during shaking; do not use lifts.
  • Outdoors – move to an open area away from buildings, trees, electric poles and wires.
  • In a vehicle – stop in an open place away from bridges and flyovers and stay inside.
  • In hospitals – staff protect patients in place, then evacuate according to the plan.

3. After an earthquake

  • Expect aftershocks; leave damaged buildings carefully; do not re-enter them.
  • Check yourself and others for injuries; give first aid; do not move seriously injured persons unless they are in danger.
  • Check for gas leaks, fires and damaged wiring; switch off mains; do not light matches.
  • Listen to official information; use the phone only for emergencies.
  • Search and rescue by trained teams; persons trapped for long periods may have crush injuries and need careful medical care during rescue.
  • Public health measures – safe water, sanitation, shelter, food, disease surveillance, continuity of care for chronic illnesses and pregnant women; psychological first aid for survivors.

4. Four key ways to reduce consequences (summary)

  1. Earthquake-resistant construction and retrofitting.
  2. Securing household objects and identifying safe spots.
  3. Regular drills of "Drop, Cover and Hold On" and community preparedness plans.
  4. Trained search-and-rescue, first aid and medical response teams with emergency supplies.

Conclusion Earthquakes cannot be prevented or predicted, but safe buildings, prepared families and communities, and correct actions during and after the shaking save many lives.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain the health problems in relief camps after a disaster and their prevention.
answer_html:
Introduction After disasters, many people are displaced and live in temporary relief camps (schools, community halls, tents). Overcrowding, poor water and sanitation, inadequate food and stress make camps high-risk settings for disease. Public health measures, often guided by internationally accepted minimum (Sphere) standards, prevent outbreaks.

1. Health problems

  • Water- and food-borne diseases – diarrhoea, cholera, typhoid, hepatitis A and E.
  • Respiratory infections, including pneumonia and tuberculosis, due to crowding and poor ventilation.
  • Measles and other vaccine-preventable diseases among children.
  • Vector-borne diseases – malaria, dengue, chikungunya; leptospirosis after floods.
  • Skin infections – scabies, fungal infections, infected wounds.
  • Malnutrition, especially among young children, pregnant and lactating women and the elderly.
  • Interruption of maternal care, immunisation and chronic disease treatment (diabetes, hypertension, TB, HIV, mental illness).
  • Psychological problems – grief, anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress, substance use.
  • Protection problems – violence, sexual abuse, trafficking of women and children.

2. Prevention and control measures

  • Site planning – adequate space per person, ventilation, separate areas for families, safe locations away from hazards.
  • Water – at least 15 litres per person per day of safe water for drinking, cooking and hygiene; chlorination and regular testing; safe storage containers.
  • Sanitation – sufficient latrines (as a guide, not more than 20 persons per latrine), separate and well-lit for women; hand-washing stations with soap; drainage; solid waste disposal.
  • Vector control – removal of stagnant water, insecticide spraying, insecticide-treated nets.
  • Food and nutrition – rations providing about 2,100 kcal per person per day; community kitchens with food hygiene; supplementary feeding for vulnerable groups; promotion of breastfeeding and avoidance of uncontrolled distribution of infant formula.
  • Immunisation – measles vaccination with vitamin A for children, catch-up of routine immunisation, tetanus for the injured.
  • Health services – camp clinic or mobile medical unit; ANC, delivery arrangements and newborn care; continuation of chronic disease medicines; referral system.
  • Disease surveillance – daily reporting of diarrhoea, fever, rash and other syndromes; rapid investigation and response to outbreaks.
  • Health education – hygiene, safe water, food safety, and early reporting of illness.
  • Psychosocial support – psychological first aid, child-friendly spaces, counselling and referral.
  • Protection – safety of women and children, separate bathing areas, registration of unaccompanied children.

3. Role of the nurse – camp health assessment, organising clinics and immunisation, supervising water and sanitation, surveillance, health education, care of vulnerable groups and maintaining records.

Conclusion With adequate water, sanitation, food, shelter, immunisation and surveillance, outbreaks in relief camps can be prevented and the health and dignity of displaced people protected.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain the health hazards of floods and cyclones and the community health measures to deal with them.
answer_html:
Introduction Floods and cyclones are the most frequent disasters in India, affecting millions of people each year, especially along the eastern coast, the Ganga–Brahmaputra plains and, increasingly, cities. Besides immediate deaths and injuries, they cause major public health problems in the weeks that follow.

1. Health hazards

  • Immediate – drowning; injuries from debris, falling trees and collapsed houses; electrocution from fallen wires; snake bites as snakes seek shelter; hypothermia.
  • Short-term
    • water-borne diseases – diarrhoea, cholera, typhoid, hepatitis A and E, due to contaminated wells and pipes;
    • leptospirosis from contact with flood water contaminated with rat urine;
    • vector-borne diseases – malaria, dengue and Japanese encephalitis after water recedes;
    • respiratory infections and skin infections (fungal infections, infected wounds) in crowded shelters.
  • Other effects – loss of food stocks and crops leading to malnutrition; damage to health facilities and loss of medicines; interruption of immunisation and maternal care; mental stress; loss of livelihood and displacement.

2. Community health measures

  • Before – early-warning dissemination; identification of safe shelters (cyclone shelters, raised buildings); evacuation plans for vulnerable persons; stockpiling of ORS, chlorine tablets, medicines, antivenom, bleaching powder and dressings at PHCs; raising plinths of hand pumps and latrines in flood-prone areas.
  • During – timely evacuation; rescue by boats with trained teams; first aid and transfer of the injured; keeping away from fallen electric wires; protecting drinking water.
  • After
    • Safe water – boiling or chlorination; disinfection of wells; distribution of chlorine tablets; ensuring that hand pumps are safe before use.
    • Food safety – discard food soaked in flood water; community kitchens; supplementary nutrition for children and mothers.
    • Sanitation and vector control – temporary latrines, drainage of stagnant water, safe disposal of carcasses and waste, anti-larval and spraying measures, mosquito nets.
    • Leptospirosis – avoid wading in flood water without boots; early treatment of fever; chemoprophylaxis for high-risk workers as per state guidelines.
    • Disease surveillance – daily reporting of fever, diarrhoea and jaundice; rapid response teams.
    • Health services – mobile medical units and health camps; continuation of ANC, deliveries, immunisation (including measles) and chronic disease treatment; repair of damaged facilities.
    • Psychosocial support for affected families.

3. Role of the nurse – health education, distribution of ORS and chlorine, surveillance, first aid, care of vulnerable groups, and organising clinics and immunisation in affected areas.

Conclusion Early warning and evacuation save lives during floods and cyclones, while safe water, sanitation, vector control and surveillance afterwards prevent a second disaster of disease.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain disaster response – emergency relief measures and life-saving techniques, including field triage.
answer_html:
Introduction The response phase begins immediately after a disaster strikes. Its aims are to save lives, reduce suffering, prevent further damage and meet basic needs. The first hours (the "golden hours") are critical for survival of the injured.

1. Organisation of the response

  • Activation of the disaster plan and an incident command system at the district (district disaster management authority) with clear leadership, roles and communication.
  • Deployment of local volunteers, police, fire services and the national and state disaster response forces; coordination with health, water, food and transport departments.

2. Search and rescue

  • Ensure scene safety first; rescue by trained teams using proper equipment; locate trapped victims; give first aid at the site; move victims carefully to the casualty collection point.

3. Mass-casualty field triage (START method) Triage sorts victims according to the urgency of their need, so that the maximum number of lives are saved with limited resources.

  • Green (minor) – walking wounded; directed to a separate area.
  • For those who cannot walk, assess:
    • Breathing – not breathing even after opening the airway → black (dead/expectant); breathing more than 30 per minute → red (immediate).
    • Circulation – no radial pulse or capillary refill more than 2 seconds → red; control severe bleeding.
    • Mental status – cannot follow simple commands → red; can follow commands → yellow (delayed).
  • Victims are tagged with coloured tags and re-triaged regularly.

4. Life-saving first aid priorities

  • Airway and breathing – open the airway, recovery position, CPR when appropriate.
  • Control of bleeding – direct pressure, pressure bandage, tourniquet for life-threatening limb bleeding.
  • Treatment of shock – lay flat, raise legs, keep warm, IV fluids by trained staff.
  • Fractures – immobilise with splints; cervical spine protection in head and neck injuries.
  • Burns – cool with clean water, cover with clean dressings; wounds – cleaning and dressing; tetanus prophylaxis.

5. Evacuation and medical care – transport by priority to hospitals or field hospitals; hospitals activate mass-casualty plans; tracking of every patient.

6. Emergency relief measures

  • Shelter, clothing and blankets; safe water, food and cooking facilities; sanitation; lighting.
  • Medical camps, immunisation, disease surveillance and supply of essential drugs.
  • Psychological first aid and family tracing; protection of vulnerable groups.
  • Dignified management of the dead – identification, records, handing over to families, respectful disposal.
  • Communication to the public and restoration of essential services.

7. Role of the community health nurse – triage and first aid, care in field hospitals and camps, maternal and child care, immunisation, surveillance, health education, psychosocial support and documentation.

Conclusion An organised response with rapid search and rescue, field triage, life-saving first aid and timely relief saves the maximum number of lives and lays the foundation for recovery.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain the planning and conduct of a community mock drill for disaster preparedness.
tags: coordination with district disaster management authority
answer_html:
Introduction A mock drill is a rehearsal of the actions to be taken in a disaster, based on a realistic scenario. It tests the disaster plan, trains the community and responders, identifies gaps and builds confidence. National disaster management guidelines and training modules recommend regular mock drills in communities, schools and health facilities.

1. Planning

  • Form a planning committee – panchayat, health staff, school, police, fire services, volunteers and the district disaster management authority.
  • Set objectives – for example, to test the early-warning system and evacuation of vulnerable persons to the shelter within 30 minutes.
  • Choose the scenario according to the main local hazard – flood, cyclone, earthquake, fire, chemical leak.
  • Assign roles – warning team, evacuation team, search and rescue, first aid and triage, shelter management, communication, and observers/evaluators with checklists.
  • Arrange resources – sirens, stretchers, first aid kits, triage tags, vehicles, shelter arrangements, water.
  • Inform the community and authorities in advance to avoid panic; plan for safety of participants (no real risk-taking).
  • Conduct a table-top exercise before the field drill.

2. Conduct

  • Start with the warning signal; teams carry out evacuation, search and rescue of "victims" (volunteers with simulated injuries), triage and first aid, transfer to the "hospital", and shelter management.
  • Observers note timings, strengths and problems (delays, confusion, missing equipment, communication failures).

3. Debriefing and follow-up

  • Hold an immediate debriefing with all participants to discuss what went well and what did not.
  • Prepare a written report with recommendations; revise the disaster plan, fill resource gaps and plan further training.
  • Repeat drills periodically (for example, before the monsoon or cyclone season).

4. Mock drills in schools and hospitals – school drills teach children "Drop, Cover and Hold On" and evacuation; hospital drills test mass-casualty management, fire safety and evacuation of patients.

5. Role of the nurse – member of the planning team, trainer in first aid and triage, organiser of the medical post during the drill, and evaluator of the health component.

6. Common gaps found in drills – warnings not reaching all households, unclear evacuation routes, no plan for disabled and bedridden persons, lack of stretchers or first aid materials, poor communication between teams and confusion about who is in charge; each gap becomes an action point for the revised plan.

Conclusion Regular, well-planned mock drills turn written disaster plans into practised skills, so that communities respond quickly and calmly when a real disaster strikes.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: List the contents of a basic disaster supplies kit.
answer_html:
• Drinking water and ready-to-eat dry food for at least three days; ORS and water purification tablets.
  • First aid kit and regular medicines; spectacles and hearing aids.
  • Torch, spare batteries, radio, mobile phone with a power bank, whistle.
  • Copies of important documents in a waterproof pouch and some cash.
  • Clothes, blanket, soap, sanitary pads, masks, rope, knife and a plastic sheet; supplies for babies, the elderly and the disabled.
  • The kit is checked every six months and expired items replaced.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: What are the components of a family disaster plan?
answer_html:
• Knowledge of the hazards likely in the area and the warning signals.
  • Safe places inside the house and a meeting place outside; the evacuation route to the nearest shelter.
  • Emergency contact numbers and an out-of-area contact person.
  • Roles of each member, especially for the care of children, elderly, sick and disabled members and pets.
  • Keeping a disaster supplies kit and copies of documents ready; knowing how to switch off gas and electricity; practising the plan.
  • Reviewing the plan every year and before the monsoon.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Write the early warning systems for disasters in India.
answer_html:
• Cyclones, heavy rainfall, heat waves and cold waves – warnings by the India Meteorological Department, with colour-coded alerts.
  • Floods – flood forecasts by the Central Water Commission and state agencies.
  • Tsunamis – the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre at the national ocean information services centre (INCOIS), Hyderabad.
  • Landslides and avalanches – warnings by geological and snow research agencies.
  • Warnings reach people through radio, TV, location-based mobile alert messages, sirens and local volunteers; last-mile dissemination by panchayats and health workers is essential.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain the treatment and disposal technologies for biomedical waste.
answer_html:
Introduction Biomedical waste must be treated to make it non-infectious and safe, and then disposed of without harming people or the environment. Under the Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016 (amended in 2018 and 2019), the method depends on the colour-coded category of waste. Most facilities send their segregated waste to a common biomedical waste treatment facility (CBWTF).

1. Treatment according to category

Category Type of waste Treatment and disposal
Yellow Human anatomical and animal waste, soiled waste (dressings, cotton, plaster), expired or discarded medicines, chemical waste, discarded linen, microbiology and laboratory waste (after pre-treatment) Incineration or plasma pyrolysis; deep burial only in rural or remote areas without access to a CBWTF, with prior approval
Red Contaminated recyclable plastic – tubing, IV sets, catheters, urine bags, syringes without needles, gloves Autoclaving, microwaving or hydroclaving, followed by shredding or mutilation, then sent for recycling
White (translucent, puncture-proof container) Waste sharps – needles, syringes with fixed needles, blades, scalpels Autoclaving or dry-heat sterilisation, followed by shredding or mutilation or encapsulation; final disposal through iron foundries, secured landfill or sharps pit
Blue (cardboard box with blue marking) Broken or discarded glassware, metallic body implants Disinfection (sodium hypochlorite) or autoclaving, then recycling

2. Main technologies

  • Incineration – controlled burning at high temperatures in a double-chamber incinerator with pollution-control devices, reducing waste to ash; used for anatomical and soiled waste; the ash goes to a secured landfill.
  • Plasma pyrolysis – very high-temperature decomposition of waste using a plasma arc; little pollution.
  • Autoclaving – exposure to saturated steam under pressure (for example, 121 °C at 15 psi for the prescribed time) to kill micro-organisms; used for plastics, sharps and laboratory waste.
  • Microwaving and hydroclaving – disinfection by microwave energy or by steam in a rotating vessel.
  • Shredding and mutilation – after disinfection, plastics and sharps are cut into pieces so they cannot be reused.
  • Chemical disinfection – 1% sodium hypochlorite for glassware, spills and some liquid wastes.
  • Deep burial – in a lined pit, layered with lime and soil, only where permitted.
  • Encapsulation and sharps pits – sharps sealed in containers with cement or kept in a concrete pit, mainly in remote facilities.
  • Pre-treatment – microbiology and highly infectious laboratory waste and blood bags are sterilised or disinfected at the source before being sent for final treatment.
  • Liquid waste – treated in an effluent treatment plant or disinfected before discharge into drains.

3. Requirements and safety – untreated waste must not be stored for more than 48 hours; transport in closed, labelled, bar-coded containers; records and annual reports to the pollution control board; training, personal protective equipment and hepatitis B immunisation of waste handlers.

Conclusion Correct segregation followed by category-specific treatment – incineration, autoclaving with shredding, disinfection or secured burial – renders biomedical waste safe and protects health workers, the public and the environment.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain biomedical waste management at the sub-centre/PHC and during outreach activities.
answer_html:
Introduction Small facilities such as sub-centres, AAMs and PHCs generate biomedical waste every day – sharps from immunisation, dressings, placentas, laboratory waste and expired medicines. Outreach sessions and home deliveries also produce waste in the community. The nurse and CHO are responsible for managing it safely according to the BMW Rules.

1. Segregation at source

  • Keep colour-coded bins and bags (yellow, red, white puncture-proof container, blue box) at every point of generation – labour room, dressing room, laboratory, immunisation room.
  • Segregate immediately after use; never mix biomedical waste with general waste; fill bags only up to three-fourths and tie securely.

2. Waste from immunisation and outreach sessions (VHSND)

  • Use auto-disable syringes; cut the needle and nozzle with a hub cutter immediately after injection; collect needles in a puncture-proof container and plastic syringe bodies in red bags.
  • Bring all waste from outreach sites back to the sub-centre/PHC in closed containers; never leave it at the session site or burn it in the open.

3. Waste from deliveries – placentas and soiled pads go into yellow bags and are sent for incineration or, where permitted, placed in a deep burial pit; sharps in the white container.

4. Storage and transport – a designated, secure, ventilated storage area; collection by the CBWTF vehicle within 48 hours; where the facility is linked to the PHC, waste is transported there in closed containers.

5. On-site disposal in remote facilities (with approval) – a deep burial pit for anatomical and soiled waste and a sharps pit for disinfected sharps, located away from water sources and habitation, fenced and covered.

6. Records and reporting – BMW register with daily quantities by category, handover records to the CBWTF, accident register, training records; the facility submits an annual report to the state pollution control board.

7. Safety of health workers

  • Training of all staff; personal protective equipment (gloves, aprons, masks, boots); hepatitis B and tetanus immunisation of waste handlers.
  • Needle-stick injury – wash with soap and water (do not squeeze or use bleach), report immediately, assess risk and give post-exposure prophylaxis as per national guidelines.
  • Spill management – cover with absorbent material, pour 1% hypochlorite, wait, then clean with gloves.

8. Role of the nurse/CHO – ensures supplies (bags, bins, hub cutters), trains staff and ASHAs, supervises segregation, maintains records, and educates the community about not reusing or scavenging medical waste.

Conclusion Even small facilities generate dangerous waste. Correct segregation, safe handling of sharps during outreach, proper storage and linkage with a CBWTF or approved pits protect health workers and the community.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain the management of biomedical and sanitary waste generated in households and the community.
answer_html:
Introduction Biomedical waste is not produced only in hospitals. Households and the community generate sanitary waste (used sanitary pads, diapers), sharps from home treatment of diabetes, dressings from home care, and expired medicines. Careless disposal exposes waste pickers, sanitation workers and children to injury and infection and pollutes the environment.

1. Types of household and community waste of concern

  • Sanitary napkins, tampons, diapers and incontinence pads.
  • Used insulin needles, pen needles and glucose-testing lancets.
  • Dressings, bandages and catheter or colostomy bags from home care of bedridden or post-operative patients.
  • Expired or unused medicines and syrups.
  • Masks and waste from home isolation of infectious patients.

2. Safe management practices

  • Sanitary waste – under the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016, used sanitary pads and diapers are wrapped securely (in newspaper or pouches provided by manufacturers) and placed in the dry waste bin for separate collection; municipalities arrange incineration or other safe disposal; incinerators for pads in schools and public toilets.
  • Sharps at home – collect in a rigid, puncture-proof container with a lid (a thick plastic bottle can be used), never recap or throw loose needles in household waste; hand the closed container over at the nearest health facility for disposal.
  • Expired and unused medicines – do not throw them in drains or open dumps; return them through take-back arrangements at pharmacies or health facilities where available; never share prescription medicines.
  • Dressings and home-care waste – put in a separate, double-tied bag; follow instructions of local health authorities for collection; during outbreaks, follow special instructions for home isolation waste.
  • Hand hygiene after handling any waste.

3. Role of the community and local bodies

  • Municipal bodies and panchayats organise segregated collection of sanitary and domestic hazardous waste and its safe treatment.
  • Self-help groups and schools promote safe disposal and environmentally friendly menstrual products (reusable cloth pads, menstrual cups) where acceptable.

4. Role of the nurse and ASHA

  • Educate families of diabetic patients, bedridden persons and adolescent girls on safe disposal.
  • Provide sharps containers or advice, accept sealed sharps containers at the AAM for disposal.
  • Include waste disposal in school and adolescent health education; work with the VHSNC and sanitation workers.

Conclusion Simple practices – wrapping sanitary waste, using sharps containers at home, returning unused medicines – and proper municipal collection prevent injuries and infections from household biomedical waste.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Write the specifications of a deep burial pit for biomedical waste.
answer_html:
• A deep burial pit is used only in rural or remote areas without access to a CBWTF, with prior approval of the pollution control authority, for human anatomical and soiled waste.
  • It is dug about 2 metres deep, filled with waste up to about half, each layer covered with lime and then with soil (about 10 cm) so that animals cannot reach it.
  • It is located away from habitation and water sources, in an area not prone to flooding, with a fence and lid, under the supervision of the facility; the date and quantity of each burial are recorded.

question: What are the main changes introduced by the Bio-Medical Waste Management (Amendment) Rules, 2018?
tags: phase-out of chlorinated plastic bags and gloves
pre-treatment of laboratory and infectious waste
answer_html:
• Chlorinated plastic bags (other than blood bags) and gloves were to be phased out by March 2019.
  • Laboratory, microbiological and highly infectious waste must be pre-treated at the source (sterilisation or disinfection) as per WHO/national guidelines before handing over to the CBWTF.
  • Bar-coding of bags and containers and GPS tracking of transport vehicles by CBWTFs; online reporting and display of annual reports on the facility's website.
  • A further amendment in 2019 simplified some compliance requirements for certain facilities.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain the Indian Red Cross Society – its history, organisation, principles and activities.
tags: international Red Cross and Red Crescent movement
answer_html:
Introduction The Indian Red Cross Society (IRCS) is a voluntary humanitarian organisation and part of the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement, which grew out of the work of Henry Dunant after the battle of Solferino (1859) and the Geneva Conventions. In India it was established in 1920 by an Act of the legislature (the Indian Red Cross Society Act, 1920).

1. Organisation

  • The President of India is the President of the Society, and the Union Health Minister is the Chairman of the managing body.
  • National headquarters at New Delhi, with state and district branches headed by the Governors and District Collectors respectively, and sub-district units across the country.
  • Thousands of members and volunteers, including the Junior Red Cross (schools) and Youth Red Cross (colleges).

2. Seven fundamental principles – humanity, impartiality, neutrality, independence, voluntary service, unity and universality.

3. Emblem – a red cross on a white background, a protective symbol under the Geneva Conventions; its misuse is prohibited by law.

4. Activities

  • Disaster preparedness and relief – relief materials (tarpaulins, family kits, utensils, clothing), relief camps, water and sanitation support, trained disaster response teams, regional warehouses.
  • Blood services – blood banks and promotion of voluntary, non-remunerated blood donation.
  • First aid training and certification for the public, industries, police and schools; ambulance services and first aid posts at fairs and gatherings.
  • Health and care – hospitals, dispensaries, maternal and child welfare centres, immunisation support, health education, HIV/AIDS awareness, home nursing and care of the elderly.
  • Restoring family links – tracing family members separated by disasters or conflict.
  • Promotion of humanitarian values and international humanitarian law; assistance to the armed forces and prisoners of war in times of conflict.

5. Role of nurses – nurses serve as Red Cross volunteers and trainers in first aid and home nursing, staff blood banks and relief camps, and organise blood donation camps.

6. Red Cross days and movement links – World Red Cross and Red Crescent Day is observed on 8 May, the birthday of Henry Dunant; the IRCS works with the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC).

Conclusion For over a century the Indian Red Cross Society has served the vulnerable in disasters, conflicts and everyday emergencies, guided by its humanitarian principles and powered by volunteers.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain the World Health Organization (WHO) – its objective, structure and functions, with its contribution to health in India.
tags: Global Centre for Traditional Medicine Jamnagar
answer_html:
Introduction The World Health Organization (WHO) is the specialised agency of the United Nations for health. Its constitution came into force on 7 April 1948, a date celebrated every year as World Health Day. Its headquarters are in Geneva.

1. Objective – "the attainment by all peoples of the highest possible level of health", health being defined in its constitution as a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.

2. Structure

  • World Health Assembly – the supreme policy-making body of all member states, meeting annually in Geneva; it approves policies and the budget and appoints the Director-General.
  • Executive Board – members technically qualified in health, elected by the Assembly; gives effect to the Assembly's decisions.
  • Secretariat – headed by the Director-General, with technical and administrative staff.
  • Six regional offices – India is a member of the South-East Asia Region, whose regional office is in New Delhi; WHO also has a country office in India.

3. Functions

  • Directing and coordinating international health work; setting norms and standards – International Classification of Diseases, International Health Regulations (2005), essential medicines list, guidelines on treatment and prevention.
  • Prevention and control of communicable and non-communicable diseases; global surveillance and response to epidemics and health emergencies.
  • Technical cooperation with countries – health systems, primary health care (Alma-Ata Declaration, 1978), universal health coverage.
  • Promotion of maternal and child health, nutrition, mental health, environmental and occupational health.
  • Research, training, information and publications (World Health Statistics, World Health Report).
  • International treaties such as the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control.

4. Contribution to health in India

  • Support to the eradication of smallpox (1977) and polio (India certified polio-free in 2014), elimination of maternal and neonatal tetanus and yaws.
  • Technical support to TB, malaria, kala-azar, leprosy, immunisation, NCD and tobacco control programmes; disease surveillance and emergency response.
  • Guidelines adopted in national programmes (for example, IMNCI, safe childbirth checklist, labour care guide).
  • The WHO Global Centre for Traditional Medicine is being established at Jamnagar, Gujarat.

Conclusion WHO provides global leadership, standards and technical support for health; India both benefits from and contributes to its work in disease control and health system strengthening.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain the role of UNICEF in child health and development, with its activities in India.
answer_html:
Introduction The United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) was established in 1946 as the UN International Children's Emergency Fund to help children in post-war Europe; it later became a permanent agency for children in developing countries. Its headquarters are in New York, and it received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1965. UNICEF has worked in India since 1949.

1. Objectives – to protect the rights of every child to survival, health, nutrition, education, protection and participation, with a focus on the most disadvantaged.

2. Main areas of work

  • Child survival and health – support to immunisation (vaccine procurement, cold chain equipment and management, communication for demand), newborn care, management of childhood illness, maternal health.
  • Nutrition – promotion of breastfeeding and complementary feeding, the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative (with WHO), micronutrient supplementation, management of severe acute malnutrition (nutrition rehabilitation centres), adolescent nutrition.
  • Water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) – safe water, sanitation and hand-washing campaigns.
  • Education – early childhood education, school enrolment and quality learning, especially for girls.
  • Child protection – against child marriage, child labour, trafficking and violence; birth registration.
  • Emergencies – relief and recovery for children affected by disasters and conflicts.

3. The GOBI-FFF strategy (child survival revolution) – Growth monitoring, Oral rehydration therapy, Breastfeeding, Immunisation, Female education, Family spacing and Food supplementation – low-cost interventions promoted by UNICEF since the 1980s.

4. Activities in India – technical support to the Universal Immunisation Programme, newborn care units and home-based newborn care, nutrition programmes and anganwadi services, sanitation campaigns, adolescent empowerment, disaster response, and evidence and advocacy for children's rights in partnership with central and state governments.

5. Relevance to nurses – nurses implement many UNICEF-supported interventions – immunisation, breastfeeding promotion, growth monitoring, ORS and zinc, WASH education.

6. Advocacy and data – UNICEF publishes The State of the World's Children report, supports surveys and data systems on child well-being, and advocates for policies and budgets that benefit children, including the Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989).

Conclusion UNICEF has been a key partner of India in improving child survival, nutrition, sanitation and protection, with a special focus on the most disadvantaged children.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain the roles of UNFPA, UNDP and the World Bank in health.
answer_html:
Introduction Besides WHO and UNICEF, several international organisations support health indirectly through population, development and financing programmes.

1. United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA)

  • Established in 1969; works for a world where every pregnancy is wanted, every childbirth is safe and every young person's potential is fulfilled.
  • Areas – sexual and reproductive health and rights, family planning and contraceptive supplies, maternal health and midwifery, adolescents and youth, gender equality and prevention of gender-based violence and harmful practices, ageing, and population data (support to censuses and surveys); publishes the State of World Population report.
  • In India – technical support to family planning, maternal health and midwifery initiatives, adolescent health, gender issues, and population and development research in partnership with the government.

2. United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)

  • Established in 1965; the UN's global development network, focusing on poverty reduction, democratic governance, climate and environment, and resilience to disasters.
  • Publishes the Human Development Report and the Human Development Index (HDI), which combines life expectancy, education and income.
  • Health-related support includes strengthening health systems and supply chains; in India it has supported digital systems for vaccine logistics (electronic vaccine intelligence network) and other health technology initiatives with the Ministry of Health.

3. World Bank

  • Created in 1944 at the Bretton Woods Conference; comprises the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (loans to middle-income countries) and the International Development Association (low-interest credits and grants to poorer countries).
  • Provides loans, grants and technical advice for health, nutrition, water and sanitation, education and social protection; its World Development Report 1993 – Investing in Health introduced the disability-adjusted life year (DALY) as a measure of disease burden.
  • In India it has financed national and state projects for disease control (TB, HIV, malaria), nutrition, health systems strengthening and pandemic preparedness.

4. Comparison

Agency Main focus Example of work in health
UNFPA Population, reproductive health, gender Family planning, midwifery, prevention of gender-based violence
UNDP Human development, poverty, governance Human Development Index, digital vaccine logistics
World Bank Development financing Loans for disease control and health systems

Conclusion UNFPA, UNDP and the World Bank complement WHO and UNICEF by supporting reproductive health, human development and financing, all of which are essential for improving the health of populations.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Explain the functions of national voluntary health agencies in India – Indian Council for Child Welfare, Family Planning Association of India, Tuberculosis Association of India, Central Social Welfare Board, All India Women's Conference, Hind Kusht Nivaran Sangh and Voluntary Health Association of India.
answer_html:
Introduction Voluntary health agencies are non-governmental organisations that work for health and welfare, often filling gaps in government services, reaching marginalised groups, pioneering new approaches and advocating for policy change. Several national agencies have contributed to community health in India for decades.

1. Indian Council for Child Welfare (ICCW) – founded in 1952; works for the welfare of children through crèches, balwadis, child guidance centres, training of child-care workers, support for children in difficult circumstances and advocacy for child rights, through state councils.

2. Family Planning Association of India (FPAI) – founded in 1949; a pioneer of family planning in India, it provides sexual and reproductive health services, counselling, information and education through clinics and outreach, and advocates for reproductive rights.

3. Tuberculosis Association of India – founded in 1939; raises public awareness and funds through the annual TB seal campaign, trains health workers, supports TB clinics and research, and works with the national TB programme.

4. Central Social Welfare Board (CSWB) – set up by the Government in 1953 under the leadership of Durgabai Deshmukh to promote voluntary social welfare; it gives grants to voluntary organisations for the welfare of women, children and persons with disabilities (crèches, short-stay homes, awareness programmes).

5. All India Women's Conference (AIWC) – founded in 1927; works for women's education, health, legal rights, family welfare, literacy and the removal of social evils such as child marriage and dowry.

6. Hind Kusht Nivaran Sangh – the national leprosy relief association, working for leprosy control through case detection, treatment support, rehabilitation, health education and removal of stigma.

7. Associations for the blind – national associations for the blind work for prevention of blindness, eye camps, education, training and rehabilitation of visually impaired persons.

8. Voluntary Health Association of India (VHAI) – a federation of state voluntary health associations and member organisations, founded in 1970; it promotes community health, trains community health workers, supports grassroots NGOs, publishes health materials and advocates on issues such as tobacco control and health rights.

Functions common to voluntary agencies – service delivery in under-served areas; health education; training; research and innovation; advocacy; mobilisation of community and funds; partnership with government programmes.

Conclusion National voluntary agencies have played a pioneering and complementary role in India's health care, especially for women, children, persons with disabilities and neglected diseases; the community health nurse should know and collaborate with them.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: What is the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO)? Write its functions.
answer_html:
• The FAO is a specialised UN agency founded on 16 October 1945 (celebrated as World Food Day), with headquarters in Rome.
  • Functions – to achieve food security and fight hunger; improve agricultural productivity, fisheries and forestry; promote nutrition; set food standards jointly with WHO through the Codex Alimentarius Commission; collect and publish data on food and agriculture; and help countries during food emergencies.
  • It also supports nutrition-sensitive agriculture and the control of animal diseases that affect humans.
  • India works with FAO on food security and nutrition programmes.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: What is the International Labour Organization (ILO)? Write its role in health.
tags: ILO WHO committee on occupational health
answer_html:
• The ILO was established in 1919 and became a UN specialised agency in 1946; its headquarters are in Geneva. It is unique in having a tripartite structure of governments, employers and workers.
  • Role in health – sets international labour standards and conventions on occupational safety and health, working hours, child labour, maternity protection and social security; works with WHO on occupational health (the joint ILO/WHO committee gave the classic definition of occupational health); supports countries in improving workplace safety.
  • It received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1969.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: What is the Voluntary Health Association of India (VHAI)?
answer_html:
• VHAI is a national federation of state voluntary health associations and member organisations, founded in 1970, with its headquarters in New Delhi.
  • It works to make health a reality for the people through community health programmes, training of health workers, support to grassroots NGOs, publication of low-cost health materials and advocacy on issues such as tobacco control, rational drug use and health rights.
  • It also conducts research and runs health projects in partnership with state associations and the government.

subject: Community Health Nursing II
question: Name the international agencies working in health in India and state their main areas of work.
answer_html:
• WHO – norms, standards and technical support for disease control and health systems.
  • UNICEF – child health, immunisation, nutrition, WASH and protection.
  • UNFPA – reproductive health, family planning and gender; UNAIDS – HIV/AIDS response.
  • UNDP and World Bank – development, health systems and financing; FAO – food security and nutrition; ILO – occupational health and labour standards.
  • Non-governmental and bilateral partners – the Red Cross movement, CARE, JHPIEGO and private foundations support maternal and child health, family planning, training and innovation.
  • All work in partnership with the Ministry of Health and state governments.
